Are we celebrating!?

You don't know what? Czech flag day! I consider statism to be the greatest and most dangerous world religion of the present and past; like most religions it has different churches (in the form of individual states); they have their sacred symbols (flags, insignia), places (palaces, monuments), texts (constitutional documents, founding declarations) and songs (marchs, hymns), holidays (celebrations of victory, formation), celebrations (parades, military parades), relics (standards, crown jewels), officials (politicians, officials), symbolic gestures (salutes, laying of wreaths), saints (honored by statesmen, national heroes) and ceremonies (elections, coronations). Many states celebrate their flags on various important days for them (coronations, deaths, battles, enactment of flags, etc.); in the Czech Republic it could be March 30, which is the day of approval of the 106-year-old Act 252/1920.
In 2020, it was proposed by the Czech Vexillological Society, which at the time interested few people; six years later, Babiš probably needed to act as a patriot, so he proposed it in the amendment to Act 245/2000. So do we have it? Czech flag day in the law? Nope. Not even a week before the big day, the senate returned it. That they wouldn't want to weed out the legislation with such nonsense? But somewhere! Murray Newton Rothbard's One Hundredth Birthday

Today, the "Father of Anarcho-Capitalism" Murray Newton Rothbard would have celebrated his hundredth birthday if he were alive; I see the greatest contribution of his work in the consistent and logical introduction to the consequences of two trends - which were seemingly not very related - anarchism (anarcho-individualism) and the Austrian school of economics. Early anarchists typically did not understand economics very well, while proponents of the Austrian school of economics did not apply their (otherwise correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and came to a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This knowledge and full understanding of it changed my life greatly; Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.

Murder is murder

What would you say to a person who would murder someone he doesn't even know and excuse it by saying he's not responsible because his boss told him to do it? That's probably a pretty absurd defense. But why do we accept it for soldiers in the army? I understand that in case they have to enlist, desertion is punishable by death, so they were compelled to do the same by force; but why remove the responsibility from the soldiers who signed up for it voluntarily? After all, it is only their risk to murder someone who has done nothing to anyone in the course of their profession; even a professional driver probably has a higher chance of killing someone than the average person, but we don't tolerate it either. Why should murder in war not be murder? Just because it
the state pressures the people with its propaganda
? Will you say that "there is no other way"? Then imagine how much better the world would be if people weren't taught that sometimes murder isn't murder when it suits the powers that be.

Subsidy for domestics
Corruption and gambling

I recently listened to a (years old) recording of a kind of discussion with Petr Gazdík; in it he explained, based on his past and "life story and background", why he would never take a bribe. Let us suppose for a moment that he was telling the truth, and that he is seriously a proud incorruptible man; immediately afterwards, with considerable pride in his voice, he declared that the gambling lobby would never break him and that he would fight against gambling for the rest of his life, otherwise he would not be able to look in the mirror. That person is very likely not even aware that they are pushing
violent persecution of some group of people and trampling on their property rights
; and you know what's worse than a politician initiating aggression towards you? Well, much worse is a politician initiating aggression towards you who cannot even be bribed to stop it. Even if all those who "mean it well" sit in the parliament (and we are far from that), the state will not start working in our favor; on the contrary, sometimes it can be even worse.
Owning a reputation

To answer the question of whether I am infringing by damaging my reputation
property rights
(and thus I am attacking and the victim can defend himself with force), one must first determine whether the reputation can be owned. My reputation is actually people's opinions of me; reputation is what others think. And can I own the thoughts and opinions of others? Certainly not. So how could I own my reputation? It is not possible; it is not my property or decision what others will think of me. Therefore, when someone slanders me, it is appropriate to respond to it, refute the slander or ignore everything (it depends on the decision of each of us); however, it is not adequate to use physical violence and limit the freedom of speech and property rights of the slanderer, since he did not attack my property, since I do not own my reputation (that is, other people's opinions). He may have harmed me, but that in itself does not constitute a violation of property rights; if my partner leaves with him, it can also harm me, but it is not appropriate to solve the situation with violence.
Anti-capitalism

On my beautiful journey through life, I meet many opponents of anarchism or capitalism, most often both. Anti-capitalists typically dislike greed, selfishness, that some have little and others have much, inequality... These phenomena are seriously present in capitalism; but its regulations do not disappear. Greedy selfish people go into the service of the state, where they continue to dig (depending on the regime, they may focus on power, acquaintances, etc. instead of money), only the selfishness is not used to satisfy the needs of customers; and although inequality can be reduced by state interventions, it is only in such a way that the well-being of society is significantly reduced, because inequalities arise from the growth of well-being - the market is not a zero-sum game (voluntary exchange increases the benefit of both parties); inequalities typically arise when someone improves the lives of a lot of people a little, while improving himself by leaps and bounds. Anti-capitalists criticize the things they don't like, but they miss the fact that these are not the consequences of capitalism, but features of the world that socialism declaratively changes, but in reality only transforms them into something much worse.
Anti-anarchism

On my beautiful journey through life, I meet many opponents of anarchism or capitalism, most often both. Anti-anarchists typically resent the idea of a society without a central authority usurping a monopoly on violence. "Society cannot function without rules," they say; and they are right! But even the anarcho-capitalists do not care about the functioning of a society without any rules, they do not want to have those rules dictated from above by a central authority, but support their market emergence on a decentralized basis. Let everyone determine their own rules on their property, in their business; simply where he bears responsibility at the same time. And if several people collaborate on something, let them freely agree on the terms of collaboration; and if they don't suit them, they don't have to cooperate. If it becomes too complicated for people, there is nothing against it if they voluntarily start following uniform standards; but let those who do not wish such a thing be forced to do so, even if they were in the minority. Anarchy is not the absence of order; just the absence of a central authority.
Freedom? Democracy?

We often hear the phrase "freedom and democracy"; in reality, "freedom or democracy" is more valid.
Democracy tends to be the nemesis of freedom
. What is democracy? High-flown talk aside, this is the tyrannical rule of the majority; yes, violent, because against people who do not obey the laws dictated by the majority,
the state routinely uses violence
. Will the majority decide to disarm the minority? It will happen. Will the majority decide to raise taxes on the minority? It will happen. Will the majority decide to limit free speech? It will happen. Will the majority decide that we must solve the Jewish question? It will happen. That current non-democratic regimes are typically far less free? Sure; however, this does not change the above - just as the existence of an extremely toxic green toadstool does not make a poisonous red toadstool an edible mushroom.
Thirty-one years since the death of Murray Newton Rothbard

Today marks thirty-one years since the "Father of Anarcho-Capitalism" Murray Newton Rothbard left this world at the premature age of 69; his life's work was a consistent and logical introduction to the consequences of two trends - which were seemingly not very related - anarchism (anarcho-individualism) and the Austrian school of economics. Early anarchists typically did not understand economics, and the proponents of the Austrian school of economics did not apply their (otherwise correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and came to a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This knowledge and full understanding of it changed my life greatly; Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.
Murray Newton Rothbard was born on March 2, 1926; that means he would be 100 years old this year. In honor of this, the Freeport is hosting
the seventh conference
on the subject of freedom; and the first Saturday after his hundredth birthday.

A weak state?

I recently heard a wonderful argument in a discussion: "The state is too weak to defend itself against oligarchies and corporate influence." Erm... that's a rather idiosyncratic interpretation. So what about that? How to "strengthen the state"? More officials, more money, more control, more laws? Why it doesn't make sense and it won't lead to anything,
I have already explained many times
; here, however, it is even internally contradictory to the person's faith. If they believe that the state is controlled by oligarchs and large corporations (which is certainly true to a large extent), then how can the "strengthening" of that state (controlled by oligarchs and corporations) take place so that it is no longer controlled? After all, those subjects will also intervene in the entire process; and there is no reason to suppose why they should have less influence here than anything else. Do we want to get rid of them? Then let's get rid of the state! It makes no sense to claim that they control the state, but at the same time call for its strengthening; it's like upgrading the enemy's weapons.
State versus family

Before, families were pretty solid units; parents took care of their children, who they then relied on in their old age, which of course still happens today, but to a lesser extent. Why? Modern socialist states came up with theirs
social policy and pensions
; thereby reducing the motivation of families to maintain good relations. Does that sound cynical? Is it much more complicated? Relationships aren't just about money, are they? Love can't be bought? Yes, sure! That's all true. I am not saying that if parents and children were more economically dependent on each other, there would be a paradise on earth, I am far from it; it's just that the motivation of the parent to maintain good relations with the offspring is higher if the parent knows that he will be dependent on the offspring one day, and on the contrary, the motivation of the offspring to take care of his parent is lower when he knows that the state does it anyway - and especially when he knows that this is a fundamental role of the state, which is constantly emphasized to us (
since childhood
), in addition, the state in question still pays from taxes (which means it has less resources).

No toilet, yes education?

We all know from experience with socialism that the state is not able to provide even such banalities as toilet paper or menstrual pads - in short, things whose need can be easily estimated and calculated; the reasons are explained by the Austrian school of economics, but let's leave the theory aside for a moment. Almost no one disputes that when the state tries to provide consumer goods, it fails; unlike the market. But why do so many people, despite the state's inability to provide absolutely trivial needs, believe in its ability to provide things that are much more complicated (education, health, justice, security...)? Especially when they witness the state failing in this day and day; above all, we must not give the market a chance, because "it certainly wouldn't work" (although there is no indication of this). So why do people still believe it? Well, one thing the state doesn't do so badly -
propaganda indoctrination always worked for him; and it is not surprising that the target is small children

Old times

Sometimes I hear complaints about "modern consumerist over-technological society" and its separation from "nature" (as if we are not even part of it); they say it's bad that people live in cities, use technology and don't have contact with the wild. I don't quite understand this rant; I don't understand why anyone lives a self-critical life. Why does he complain about "society" instead of giving up technology himself and spending time in the countryside instead of the city? Well, there are not many achievements of modern times, such possibility of social enjoyment, so many job opportunities and the like; yes, that's all true - welcome to the "idyllic" life of our ancestors (or rather, a "taste" of it; in reality, it was worse)! I don't see the "disease" of today in the cities or the "separation of man from nature"; I think the "disease" of today is rather how often we want something, but we are not willing to pay the price, but we complain that others who don't need it live badly.

Taxation of gambling

What will happen to slot machine or roulette addicts if the state (even more) taxes gambling? Let's start with what will definitely not happen - these people definitely do not calculate that with a higher tax burden it is not really worth playing it anymore, and they will not stop doing it. How do I know? Well, if they were capable of it, they would have calculated it and stopped playing, because it didn't pay off for them even before; they'll lose enough of the games they put in the boxes anyway - and because they're addicted, they'll play enough of those games. The amount of tax that the state imposes on gambling only determines in what proportion the money of the addicts is divided between the gambling operators and the goons from the government; it does nothing to help addicts. Taxing cigarettes or alcohol can really reduce consumption, because it makes a difference whether a smoker pays three or five thousand a month for his bad habit; however, a gambling addict will pay whatever he can for his habit (that's the point of the addiction), so the tax won't help.
Hope from the post office

For a very long time, postal services were something that various states claimed to have monopolies; and people universally believed that it was actually necessary - everyone necessarily "knew" that the free market "wouldn't work" (just as everyone "knows" today in many other fields). Today it is clear how things are; a state monopoly for the delivery of parcels is completely out of the question in the vast majority of countries. Abolishing the state post office is not something that has broad public support, but here and there someone can be found, and above all, counter-arguments have already shifted from the position "only the state has to do it" to "in most cases, the private sector is more efficient". It's great to see an industry where public opinion has shifted from "the state must have a monopoly" to "OK, let it have competition" to "somehow we could do without the state (although we don't want to yet)". So when do you think the cancellation (or rather complete privatization) of the Czech Post will take place? Will we live to see it? And when will Czech Television start ringing the bell?

Do the laws of the market apply?
Christian Darwin

Ridicule of Christians - and creationists in particular - is quite common in the atheist Czech Republic (and as a Christian - albeit one who believes in evolution - I sometimes laugh heartily at such jokes); such insinuations are sometimes thoughtful, sometimes less so, however how about the following comment: "Christians (Creationists) are completely out of their minds because they believe in Darwin whose theories don't make sense." Isn't that absurd? It is indeed; and maybe that's why I've never heard this phrase. But I heard another - no less absurd: "Austrian economics is completely out of the question, because it assumes perfect competition, perfect information and perfect people pursuing their economic interests." This is no less nonsense than the Darwin thing; the Austrian economic school not only does not use any "homo economicus under ideal conditions" models, it even criticizes them very harshly, which does not prevent many from pushing these things into the Austrian economy anyway.
State subsidy of science

What would people do without state subsidies for science and research? So, above all, they would have more of their own resources (money), which they could decide for themselves; then basically two cases can occur: Either the person who has the money left in his pocket and the state did not collect it, decides to use it to finance some research (either directly or indirectly through the purchase of the product of the company that conducts the research - for profit or for another reason), the state is not needed for this; or would the person in question decide to spend this money (or part of it) in any other way - but what does this mean? That according to his own standards, what he spent his money on (whatever it was) brings more benefit to the person in question than the research that the state wants to force him to finance would bring him more benefit. It can be argued that the person in question will not correctly foresee all the consequences, but no one can do that at all; and if someone feels that someone else is doing it wrong, let them teach him, but
do not force him
!
Lists of allergens

I participated in a debate about whether the state should force restaurant owners to provide diners with a list of allergens; defense
violent coercion
she relied on two arguments: The first was that "after all, no one will miss out if she writes down the allergens"; the second concerned saving the lives of severe allergy sufferers. If "no one is missing" was a valid argument for violating property rights, then for example thieves who robbed many people of only a few crowns (rounding "errors") did not actually do anything because "no one was left". And the rescue of allergy sufferers? Don't be laughed at! Those who have such a severe allergy that they are at risk of death from anaphylactic shock have to take much more care (find out about the food, ask the staff, eat in "proven" places); relying on listings that sellers paid off just because someone pushed them is nothing more than another fruit of the government's efforts to make us irresponsible ignoramuses, which can't end well.
The paradox of the social contract

If children are not capable of legal action, so parents or the state must decide for them up to a certain age, how can they be bound by a so-called "social contract" from the moment of their birth, which cannot be terminated and binds them to unconditional obedience to the state until death?
Thirty years since the death of Murray Newton Rothbard

Today marks thirty years since the "Father of Anarcho-Capitalism" Murray Newton Rothbard left this world at the premature age of 69; his life's work was a consistent and logical introduction to the consequences of two trends - which were seemingly not very related - anarchism (anarcho-individualism) and the Austrian school of economics. Early anarchists typically did not understand economics, and the proponents of the Austrian school of economics did not apply their (otherwise correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and came to a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This knowledge and full understanding of it changed my life greatly; Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.
Murray Newton Rothbard was born on March 2, 1926; that means he would be 100 years old next. Twenty-nine years since the death of Murray Newton Rothbard

Today it is exactly twenty-nine years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers and geniuses - Murray Newton Rothbard, the "father of anarcho-capitalism" left this world at the age of 69; his life's work was a consistent and logical introduction to the consequences of two trends that were seemingly not very related: anarchism (anarcho-individualism) and the Austrian school of economics. Anarchists were often wrong in economics, and the proponents of the Austrian school of economics did not apply their (correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and came to a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This knowledge and full understanding of it changed my life greatly; Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.

The right to water

Sometimes we can hear from some that we have the "right to water" as a "basic human right"; such a belief is most likely based on the fact that we biologically need water to survive. However, this does not entitle anyone to force another to provide something. While the negatively defined right to water means that no one may take water from another, the positively defined "right to water" says that everyone must be provided with water; however, the dark side of positive "rights" is that someone must be forced to provide water by force, which is not ethically acceptable. In connection with this, one can encounter the fear that someone will have a monopoly on water and control everyone; however, that doesn't make sense because (ground) water is everywhere - it just depends on how deep you dig. So if the price of water rises above a certain limit, it will pay for people to dig wells; far from each having their own, they can join forces, share the water, and the monopolist is out of luck.

Medicinal grass

Someone recently asked me if I was in favor of legalizing cannabis for its medicinal effects; and guess what? I am not in favor of legalizing cannabis for its medicinal effects; I'm a supporter
full legalization (or decriminalization - it depends on the terminology, everyone means something different) of all drugs
(including marijuana) regardless of effects. It is not relevant to me whether weed heals. I know it is made into salves; I also know some shavers - they don't use it as medicine, although they sometimes tell themselves that shaving is not harmful, but that's their business. I understand the health argument, but it actually bothers me at the same time; it kind of suggests that if weed wasn't healthy, it's actually okay to ban it. But a free man shouldn't beg anyone for permission to put anything he sees fit into his body, even if it's cyanide. People like to talk about freedom, but when it comes down to it, "we need some regulation."
A crisis of values

We hear around us about a crisis of values, a crisis of elites, a crisis in politics, a crisis of civilization and a crisis of everything. I am convinced that we would have heard such talk at any time (historical records indicate this), sometimes there were also crises in the supply of goods, food, construction, industry - depending on what the state was in charge of. Where socialism thrives, there is crisis; in the Czech Republic before 1989, for example, practically everywhere, since 1989 in education, the social system, healthcare (i.e. state sectors) and logically also in values, elites, politics... Not that our "civilization" (as a whole) is in a "crisis of values" (although some like to claim that); ordinary people are still the same and there is no problem with them. Politicians are in a "crisis of values"; and rather than a "crisis" it is a long-term condition; and that
the condition is inherent, it is not a failure of individual politicians; and as long as we have a state, the problem will not go away
.

Contributions to collective defense

It is generally believed that
in a free market society people would pay little for collective defense (army) against an external enemy
; but how much is "little"? The only way to know "little" is to lose the war (and even that doesn't mean it was "little" for sure, she may not have had a chance to reverse the outcome at all); conversely, keeping an army at a time when there is no threat may be "too much". All this can be ascertained ex post; ex ante we know nothing. So if people in a free market society pay less for collective defense (army) than in a state, that doesn't necessarily mean it's "wrong"; for it is not clear how much is "correct". The budget of the army of the Czech Republic is (even relative to the state budget) many times lower than the army of the USA; is it wrong The answers will certainly vary and there will be different opinions with different rationales; then why is it "clear to everyone" that it would be a disaster in a stateless society (even if people paid handsomely less)?

explanation,
how the free market deals with monopolies
, I have already devoted enough time, text and words; but even if someone came to the conclusion that he needs "protection" from monopolies, the interesting question is what he is actually calling for. After the antimonopoly office? After all, he himself is a monopoly on solving problems with monopolies; Do you feel the paradox? How should the state help the person in question? A state that itself usurps a monopoly on violence in a given area; is this goat turned gardener supposed to protect the garden? What is the internal logic of establishing the most brutal monopoly to protect us from supposed monopolies? Sweatshops

Sweatshop is a (derogatory) term for factories where people work in miserable conditions for low wages; they tend to be in developing countries where poor people do not have a better livelihood. In the rich part of the world (ours), some people find it terrible (even though our ancestors had to work like that to be well off today) and protest by not buying products from sweatshops; it is of course their business where they shop, I just feel that they are missing something: If someone wants to help the poor, they should buy goods from companies where the poor are employed in better conditions; if this is not possible (or if the desire to help is not so strong that the helper overcomes the obstacles), buying goods from a sweatshop is at least something. Buying from a competitor (perhaps local) is even worse for those poor people from the third world; so when a person who actually helps criticizes those who buy sweatshops, it makes sense, but it's absurd when he criticizes someone who doesn't do either.
Supermarkets versus small shops

Supermarkets compete with small shops, which sometimes go out of business because of it; does it harm society? This in itself is clearly not; competition is desirable. Another thing is state interference, which affects small businesses worse than large ones, which can more easily dissolve it in costs (formerly EET, control reports, various standards and clouds of unnecessary administration; the mandatory closing of large stores on holidays is rather an exception that harms the large ones). However, market forces cause customers to get what they want: a supermarket may offer many types of goods and lower prices, a small shop may offer a more personal approach or high quality of some product segments; it is impossible to objectively say which of these is better, as human preferences are purely subjective. So everyone buys where it will bring them more benefit; some stores can handle it, others not, which is not bad, quite the opposite – the consumer expressed that something else would bring him more benefit.
Problem: Multitasking

Public administration is notorious for "problems" with someone winning a (typically construction) contract because it's the cheapest, but then screwing up on multiple jobs; an absolute classic is winning a tender with a price that doesn't even cover the costs. And for many years (I remember it since I was little) it has been "solved" what to do with it; I can't help but ask: How about selling those orders as fixed time – fixed price? The responsibility will be borne by the supplier; of course, the official is more likely to make mistakes, the space for corruption will decrease, but why isn't anyone else calling for such a solution? I wouldn't worry about finding a supplier; especially if the conditions for tendering change so that it is not a constant game of the five big firms. Most people will answer that it would be nice, but "there is a lack of political will"; and they are right - they are missing and always will be. As long as the state is the contracting authority, there will probably be no (well-intentioned) modifications
they will not have the desired effect
.

East and West Germany

Post-war devastated (and rebuilding) Germany was divided into two states in 1949: NSR (West Germany) and GDR (East Germany); in the first mentioned, a kind of socialism was implemented (quite a light version), in the second, rigid socialism. Although this situation was unhappy for the East Germans, from our point of view there is only one positive: The division of Germany was almost a laboratory experiment on the subject of socialism; the initial position of both countries was the same – property conditions, culture, history, mentality of the population, all of this was comparable on both sides of the artificial line. Then followed a social experiment lasting four decades; and the result was completely unambiguous and overwhelming, confirming the theory of the Austrian economic school to the letter -
socialism just doesn't work
. But the chilling question is: "How many more such experiments will have to take place before socialists learn their lesson?"
Pricing

In discussions with various greens, I come across bizarre examples of "market failure": A house made of wood is more expensive today than a house made of some "complex industrial shit"; land with natural wealth of "incalculable value" is worth buying for an office building. For them, such things are "market failure" that must be addressed by the state; it has to do with misunderstanding
pricing process
. The fact that something is commercially worthwhile to build somewhere indicates that people want it more than the thing that is not worth building there; when it pays to build with a material, it is obviously more efficient than building with a more expensive one. Self-centeredness and humility prevent some people from accepting that when others wish for something different, such a wish is not "inferior" to theirs; instead, they call for their wish to be enforced by force, which they back up with phrases of "incalculable value" (but this is demonstrably not true from their point of view either; if something really was of incalculable value to them, they would sell everything they have to help it).

Twenty-eight years since the death of Murray Newton Rothbard

Today it is exactly twenty-eight years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers and geniuses - Murray Newton Rothbard, the "father of anarcho-capitalism" left this world at the age of 69; his life's work was a consistent and logical introduction to the consequences of two trends that were seemingly not very related: anarchism (anarcho-individualism) and the Austrian school of economics. Anarchists were often wrong in economics, and the proponents of the Austrian school of economics did not apply their (correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and came to a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This knowledge and full understanding of it changed my life greatly; Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.

Text
Marriage for all

increases
state power. But by the same logic, we could say that if we change the building code so that more people can build,
will increase
with the power of the state, which makes absolutely no sense; or we could argue that the state has no business issuing trade cards to people (and everyone should be able to run a trade without a permit), but as long as it issues them, the fewer people who get them, the better - which doesn't make any more sense. If the state regulates, for example, the possession of arms, business, the production of alcohol, or anything else, it is certainly not the case that the more permits it issues, the less freedom; it's the exact opposite. And I almost don't want to believe that it isn't obvious to someone; rather, I think the idea of gays having sex clouds some people's logic a bit.
Seat belts

In discussions of regulation, opponents often cite seat belts to me as an example of good regulation; if they don't happen to know I'm an anarcho-capitalist, they often seize on the argument by trying to pass off the belt argument as something we can agree on. Why is mandatory seat belts such a mantra? After all, it is up to each person whether the risk is worth a little discomfort; and it cannot be decided universally, because the risk is not flat-rate and the discomfort is purely individual. So how to defend the violent repression against the unaffiliated? Some argue that the entire society pays for his eventual treatment; that's a great argument against socialist healthcare, not for mandatory belts. Others argue that someone could fly out of the car and injure others; even leaving aside the improbability of that scenario, it would be an argument for strapping everything in a car, not just people. So why belts? I believe the status quo is an iron shirt.
Customs, so customs

When a country imposes a tariff on our products, so must we; that's similar logic to proclaiming that if someone jumps out of a window, we must too. By imposing a tariff on some goods, we limit competition to domestic producers, thus harming domestic consumers (when the tariff prevents them from buying a foreign product that they would otherwise buy, we take away their best option and force them to choose a worse one); this will happen completely regardless of whether the other side also imposes tariffs. Why tariffs do not make sense is explained in some detail by Austrian economics, and even by its predecessor Claude Frédéric Bastiat in the book "What is and what is not seen"; I don't have space for a comprehensive explanation here, but I would like to give the reader a thought: What if the family imposes duties on everyone around? What if the street does it? Urban district? The whole city? Can they help each other? No? So why should a state help itself, especially when some states have less population than some cities?

Is the Fed private?

Is the US central banking system (FED) private or public? De jure it's complicated - it's a non-profit, it's supposed to be politically independent (haha) and the Reserve Bank owns its shares, which theoretically makes it a private company; de facto (although it is formally written to the banks) its leadership is determined by the state (so much for political independence). It is something like the "private" enterprises of the Third Reich, which were formally owned by white horses, but the state determined what and when they were to do and how much to sell for and how much to pay employees. And that is precisely why a distinction must be made between "private" and "free market"; when something is private on paper but state in reality, it can do more harm than the state itself. So when you hear socialists claim that the Fed is evil because it is a private company, ask how much it is really controlled by those private "owners" and how much by state legislation; the only meaningful solution is to abolish the FED and most importantly
separation of money from the state

How to arrange that beautiful and ugly people have the same opportunities? And how to compensate abused and psychologically damaged children for their suffering, so that they have the same "starting line" as others? It is well talked about, but simply not feasible; and all efforts to get closer to it are absurd, because only a few aspects of the entire colorful spectrum of life can be equalized. The word anarcho-capitalism

I feel the need to respond to one of our writers who came up with

About half of them think anarchism is cool, but capitalism turns people off; on the other hand, the other half perceives the words exactly the opposite - it depends on the social bubble. In addition, there is already a fairly used and at the same time peaceful word that can be used to describe anarcho-capitalism - it is "voluntarism" (which is immediately more accurate than the "multiarchy" proposed by the foreword). So why do I still call this school of thought anarcho-capitalism?
On the one hand, because it is natural for me to name things with the most accurate names possible (I don't like to play with anything, authenticity is very pleasant to me), moreover, I don't want to retreat from unpopular terms (I prefer to clean them up); but especially with the word "anarcho-capitalism" I distinguish myself and interest the listeners (albeit sometimes negatively). Countless times I have heard anarcho-capitalists talk about freedom in such a way that the listeners didn't really mind, but they didn't understand at all that the speaker was not talking about the state and "reformed" democracy with some slight modifications. I have nothing against such an approach; on the contrary, I appreciate that some have taken this path - it is good if we address several targets at the same time. However, it wouldn't suit me; it is more natural for me to call anarcho-capitalism anarcho-capitalism (which the listener will remember better anyway) and then look for words that will best explain what it is.

The nonsense of protectionism

On the one hand, there is a broad consensus (among economists and, in fact, throughout society and perhaps also among politicians) that
voluntary exchange and division of labor leads to prosperity and benefit
; everyone understands that cooperation is the way to prosperity. It follows logically that anything which in any way restricts the exchange and division of labor causes the exact opposite, i.e. poverty and decay; the rate will of course vary according to the magnitude of such restrictions. Therefore, whenever someone proclaims protectionism, that is, the restriction of foreign trade in the name of "protection" of domestic entrepreneurs, logically
it goes against the welfare of society
; and why actually? For what reason do I need to "protect" some businessman just because he shares the same side of some artificial state border with me? If someone argues by exclaiming, "Nothing but a nation," I find it silly, but not necessarily inconsistent; but don't let anyone tell me that protectionism "helps the economy".
Imperfect information

State interventions tend to be justified by imperfect information on the free market; however, perfect information does not exist not only in the market, but also in the state. But the state needs a huge amount of information to plan its interventions; not only more than individuals need (they try to manage "only" their lives), but as much even as much (because the state tries to manage the lives of a huge number of individuals),
that it is realistically impossible for him to get them all
. And here comes an interesting moment: The better the decision the state has to make, the more information it needs, which is not free, the subjects have to give it at their own expense, which increases with the better the state has to be informed; paradoxically, the better the state can be in terms of decision-making, the worse it must be in terms of depriving people of their resources. And what is the optimal rate? In principle, this cannot be determined, because that information is needed; therefore, changes to the researched subject change the research methodology.

Spreading a bad mood

"In the Czechoslovak Republic, the old charity, which was always considered a grace that always humiliated the poor recipient and dulled his human consciousness, will no longer have a place. Today, we are putting social duty in the place of humiliating grace." (Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk) The gifted poor man was then grateful to his donor; and perhaps he experienced humiliation that motivated him to do things better. Then came social duty; then the person in question does not feel gifted, it is no longer the case that someone gave him something, now it is his "right". And if you explain to someone that they have a "right" to other people's money and they believe it, they have nothing to be grateful for; on the contrary, it is perfectly logical if he still complains, it is not good enough for him and he asks for more. Why should he act otherwise? We cannot grant someone a "right" to something and at the same time ask them to be grateful for it; if you are "entitled" to something, gratitude excludes it, because it only makes sense when you get something you didn't have to get.
Politicians and politics
Practical politics

Politicians like and often brag that they are not theorists, but practical men who are absolutely uninterested in any theory because they need results; the voter demands it. On this basis, they often reject libertarian theories, saying that they have more important things to do; but what kind? What is their "practice" based on? A politician is not someone who stands somewhere with a shovel, screwdriver, wooden spoon or mason's trowel (although he would like to present himself that way) - in principle he is not a practitioner, because whenever he regulates, prohibits, taxes or subsidizes something, he does so on the basis of some theory; the theory that something will increase "social utility", that something will help someone, protect someone, and so on. None of this is practice with which he has experience, those decisions always flow from some theory, whether the politician wants it or not; so let's not be silenced by populist rants about the needlessness of theories, because politics is based on them - not to mention that they are flawed theories.
Internet anarchy

"Anarchy is a beautiful theory, but it can never work in practice!" This is the frequent objection of statists against anarchy. But is it really so? Of course, it cannot yet be proven whether it will work across society (until it is tried); and the opposite can certainly not be proven either. But what we can evaluate are individual areas; and a non-negligible part of our society is the Internet, in which free market anarchy reigns in practice (it is true that states sometimes enter here as well, but not in such a way that they ensure its operation, only sometimes they take someone down). People can - and to some extent do - harm themselves on the Internet; however, as a result, the Internet works (the pests globally are not able to "destroy" the efforts of those who create something valuable) and is perfectly usable even without regulations; I consider it one of the biggest "miracles" that cash-on-delivery e-shops work on an anonymous network, although competitors can spam them with fake orders. How is that? I don't know; but it's amazing.
Parasites everywhere

We hear complaints about parasites everywhere from time to time; workers complain about the "nemakačenka", some people don't like people on benefits, others generalize it to "gypsies", in extreme cases you can even hear that the parasites are self-employed (I'm not just talking about the famous saying of the parasite Mládek, sometimes other parasitizing civil servants are heard with similar nonsense). What about that? Unfortunately, nothing within the company's current setup; as long as there is violent redistribution and
protection money called taxes
, there will naturally also be parasites, because that is the basic principle of redistribution - solidarity differs from parasitism only by the consent of the donor (or victim), so involuntary on the one hand implies parasitism on the other. It is sometimes said that non-voters should not complain about the results (which I don't think); but now I say that those who want to stand should not complain about parasites.

Reforms

We often hear that we need absolutely fundamental reform of education, healthcare, judiciary, police and many other things; what do they have in common? All these fields are managed by the state. Have you ever heard about the urgent need for fundamental reform of the hotel industry, food industry, construction industry or even IT? So I don't. Where the free market works at least to some extent, there is no need for major reforms, as these industries reform themselves little by little as customers need; those who do it right make money, while those who reform wrong go bankrupt. On the contrary, almost everything the state does requires reform because it works poorly; and no wonder
it can't even work properly in principle
. And fully aware of these connections, I do not see how anyone can even stand up for the state; whatever the state manages doesn't work well, whatever was left to the market started to work better - so why not sell other sectors to the market as well?
The 2021 Education Conference is moving from February to May

The Freeport is also (hopefully) organizing another conference this year; it was originally supposed to be held in February, but government measures forced us to move it to May 22. will you come
If so, please

or
conference website

I consider the topic of education to be absolutely crucial to a free society; I will be happy if you also bring your friends and acquaintances who might be interested in the topic.
Rational action

Everyone knows that people do not always act rationally; Ludwig von Mises assumes the opposite in one of the basic books of Austrian economics (Human Action). Does this mean that the entire Austrian economy is standing on water? No; it just defines rationality differently. While Mises assumes that people act rationally, he explicitly defines such action as an effort to constantly maximize one's utility (taking into account the fickle and emotional state of man, incomplete information, "non-economic" desires, changing preferences, and so on); according to his definition, even a drug addict risking his life for the next dose acts rationally. And since Mises strictly adheres to this definition, it is correct; however, it creates a confusing impression on the uninformed reader (in my opinion, this is an unfortunately chosen definition). So if you encounter the assumption of Austrian economics that people act rationally, don't be alarmed; it means something other than what you probably mean.
Where can the economy grow?

Many economists, philosophers and thinkers warn us that the capitalist economy is growing too fast, which cannot last forever; her days are said to be slowly numbered, so nothing but downfall and misery await us. But why should such doomsaying come true? Yes, we are doing great, we live in wonderful times, we are surrounded by wealth; but is there really nothing to improve? Of course it is! We can constantly invent more and more things that we wish to have; but we don't have them at the moment because it would cost us a lot of resources. But it is the hard work of people all over the world that keeps lowering these prices; the same goods can be produced more and more cheaply (and now I don't just mean financially, but in terms of the total volume of resources - including human labor). What could stop such progress? Lack of mineral resources? Hardly; substitutes are still being found for scarce resources. Great wars of states? Yes, you might... but that's not a problem with a capitalist economy.
Twenty-six years since the death of Murray Newton Rothbard

Today it is exactly twenty-six years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers and geniuses - Murray Newton Rothbard, the "father of anarcho-capitalism" left this world at the age of 69; his life's work was a consistent and logical introduction to the consequences of two trends that were seemingly not very related: anarchism and the Austrian school of economics. Anarchists were often wrong in economics, and the proponents of the Austrian school of economics did not apply their (correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and came to a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This knowledge and full understanding of it changed my life greatly; Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.
A dynamic market

In discussions about the impossibility of economic calculation in central planning, we often come across that the discussants imagine the pricing process as something that will one day end and the prices will be "set right"; with these assumptions, he then tries to figure out how such a thing could be possible in socialism (although Ludwig von Mises has already shown that it is not). However, the reality is far more complex, as the free market is not an "achievement of a state", but a "process"; therefore, the central planner's task is not only to find the "right" prices or allocation mechanism without money (and he already fails in this task), but above all to be able to adapt to constantly changing conditions and to receive, evaluate and react to information from the whole world in real time, which is simply and simply a superhuman task, ergo
central planning can never work well
(and of course this also applies to education, healthcare, the social system and the like).
From my taxes...

"And I still have to pay for it with my taxes," the right-wing conservative faces; I ask why he thinks it's unfair, to which I get an indignant answer that he doesn't want this, it's his money, so he should have the right to decide. Well, that makes sense... and if I don't want to pay for state education, health, courts, police and military, it's my money, will they support me? Oh, won't support? Come on, is that "something else"? Um; and how is it different? There are ad hominem arguments, or some very illogical appeal to the social contract and similar nonsense. And no wonder, the difference is only in individual preferences; he wants to pay the military, police, judges and teachers, but he doesn't like paying the non-profit Auto*Mat. I don't like paying either (which is wrong), the cycling activists want both (also wrong); after all, only what the person in question wants is correct... and when the wishes of similar ones are added up, a solid drink comes out.

Fighting addictions

Addictions are crap; I also know people who are comfortable with such a state, or at least they say so (and no one but themselves can know how it really is). Whether it's addiction to drugs, gambling, porn, or any other person, I don't think there's anything to stand for (and addiction to air, water, and food isn't honey either, it's actually just as stupid as any other addiction, only we can't do anything about it); and because addictions are a problem, people usually call for state repression, which is wrong. For one thing, it has been consistently and repeatedly made clear for decades that repression is simply not the answer; above all, there is no moral justification for violence (taxation) perpetrated on entire societies in order to perpetrate further violence (war on addictions) on certain groups (especially providers of "pleasure"). Regardless of the "social benefit" (which is dubious anyway), such a thing is not excusable; what could it be?
The rich and the poor

When we talk about poor and rich people in society, we often treat them as fixed groups; therefore, whoever warns against the "opening of the scissors between the rich and the poor" (regardless of the fact that he often mistakenly focuses only on relative wealth and ignores the absolute), typically talks about it in such a way as if it were two more or less fixed groups of people, which is usually understood by the listeners as well (judging by the reactions). But the fact is that probably in the entire history of mankind it has never been so easy for the poor to become rich (or the rich to become poor); we don't have a strictly class or caste society, we don't have insurmountable family ties that would determine whether a person will be a lord or a commoner all his life. The information on how many poor people become rich (or at least middle class) varies (from country to country and statistics from statistics), but even according to pessimistic "leftist" estimates, it is tens of percent.

As an adult, I look forward to Christmas like a little boy; far more than when I was a little boy. I love the versatility of these holidays: They are Christian-spiritual; capitalistically material; and for me personally, anarchistically non-violent, because we arrange them with our loved ones in our own way and in such a way that we only do what we really want to do. Move to Somalia!

Statists often objected to anarchists that
the state initiates aggression against its citizens
, when he collects taxes under threat of violence, counter that if someone doesn't like it, they can move away (and Somalia is the most frequently recommended destination); I find this argument absolutely illogical to the point of desperation, but unfortunately it makes sense to many, so it's not out of the question to deal with it. So where is the flaw in the logic? Actually everywhere; if I criticize someone attacking someone else or threatening him with violence, it is of course true that the victim can run away, defend himself, dodge, deceive the attacker and so on, but none of this changes anything about my criticism of the behavior of the attacker, because it is absolutely unrelated to what defense strategy the victim chooses or does not choose. It's like using the argument in defense of the rapist that the victim should have been careful, besides, she didn't even have to be there and could even move to Somalia; if she didn't, she has nothing to complain about.
Interest-free loan

Interest free loans are something that people sometimes expect from the government for example for students and such; many assume that it doesn't really cost anything because the borrowed money will be paid back anyway. Bridge error; interest is a natural fee for a service (loan), which is neither risk-free nor cost-free (it is associated with an opportunity cost). So asking for a loan without interest is like asking for any other service for nothing; it is a common thing between friends, which is understandable, because friends help each other (not only by lending money). In another context, however, it should be remembered that an interest-free loan is not "free" for the lender; even if the money were to just lie there and he had nothing planned with it, he can never know when he will need to dispose of it unexpectedly, just as the risk that the debtor will not return it (even if he wanted to) cannot be excluded -
and of course this risk is not "free"
(because it is always better not to undergo it than to undergo it).
Social contract

The social contract is an artificial construct whereby everyone implicitly agrees that the state takes our resources under threat of violence and provides us with services in return; the catch is that some of us explicitly disagree—and are unlucky because the state is stronger. Let's imagine an analogous situation with the mafia, which starts collecting protection money in some territory and declares it a social contract; everyone implicitly agrees—and whoever doesn't is supposed to move away, because staying means agreeing. What makes it different? That the mafia does not provide as many services to the people as the state? For one thing, she doesn't take that much money from them, but above all - if she was providing services, is it all right? It is not! And just as I can't go sweep someone's snow (without asking) and demand money for it, neither should they do it; he's doing it from a position of strength and the social contract is just lofty bullshit to defend that
whoever has the bigger stick beats the others with it
.
Anarcho-capitalist extremists

Anarcho-capitalists are often accused of extremism by their opponents; what does such an accusation mean? We are blamed that
we completely reject offensive violence
and not only partially; it is not unlike if the object of criticism was that we are extremist opponents of murder and rape. We should not be so militant and immeasurable, but on the contrary willing to compromise; and how? For example... rape and murder are bad, but when Pepa does it, it's nothing against anything; and we can have a reasonable dialogue about whether or not Franta could also do it sometimes. Above all, no extremism, let's approach compromises, let's not rush and not be controversial; yes, and certainly let's not say it in full, so as not to discourage more conservative-minded individuals, after all, we must not scare people who would label anyone who radically condemns rape and murder as an extremist. And the calls to not be "extremists" sound about as absurd to many of us.
About the disappearing theater

If arts funding were left to the free market, it probably would
there have been big changes
; no one can predict what the changes would actually be, new forms of art would emerge, old ones would disappear, some cultural stands would not survive, others would. I am convinced that not all theaters would perish, on the other hand, I do not suppose that they would all support themselves; this is a frequent argument of the opponents of the free market in this area - so let's take a closer look at such a disappearing theater. The fact that the theater is not able to earn money for its operation (and I do not mean only from admission fees, but also from voluntary donations and the like) means that people value the resources it consumes more than what the theater brings to them (and this includes all emotional and cultural values, not only economic ones); that is, it should not exist in this form - it is simply not worth it to the people, so it should be reformed or disappear.
Minimum wage

Proponents of the minimum wage most often argue about helping the poor or weak and "social justice"; at first glance it also looks quite logical - after a possible increase in the minimum wage, the poorest workers will have more money. This may indeed be true to some extent for some, which is great to see; but then there is another thing that is not so easily seen: By setting the minimum wage to a certain limit, it is not worthwhile for employers to employ workers whose work will bring them less value than the limit set by the state; and this will affect precisely the least qualified, i.e. potentially the poorest. After all, unemployment is a phenomenon caused in principle by only two factors: Either someone does not want to work for the kind of money that other participants in the labor market value their work for, or they would agree on some contractual price, but their state outlaws the agreement, which
damages both (!) parties
.
Civilian casualties

I believe the generally held belief that civilians should not be murdered in wars is correct; however, I don't take it dogmatically in the sense of "it is so because simply because", but because someone who doesn't do anything to anyone shouldn't suffer just because he was born on the "wrong" side of the border. Sometimes people tend to condone the killing of civilians depending on what atrocities their fellow citizens have committed, which is something I strongly disagree with; everyone should be responsible for themselves, not for the actions of others just because they belong to the same nation. So I refuse, for example, to excuse Bombardier Harris for the massacres of German civilians by saying that the Germans started the war (for they were different Germans than those whom Harris burned); I do not excuse Hiroshima and Nagasaki with the attack on Pearl Harbor (other Japanese were attacked there than those who then died of radiation).
So we could continue
; a person is responsible for his actions, not for any state or nation.

Class conflict
Exploitation of poor countries

People and companies from richer countries often buy labor or minerals from people in poorer parts of the world; sometimes we hear that we are "exploiting" the poor countries. Such a thing can apply on the assumption that we would force their inhabitants to do something (or if the state or some other criminal organization forced them to do something by force); but if there is no aggression in the sense of coercion, I dare say that - regardless of the desperate conditions of the poor - their exploitation is not taking place. How is that? Trade with us improves their situation compared to the situation where we would not trade with them (and the same applies to us, there is no such thing); if someone, as a result of his poverty, gives up, for example, mineral wealth, in order not to die of thirst or hunger, his situation is indeed bad, but it is definitely better than he would be if he did not receive a similar offer (if this were not the case, he would simply refuse it and thus remain in the state he was in before).
Representative democracy

Sometimes I indulge in
principled general criticism of democracy
(no specific type of it, but democracy in general); however, now I would like to focus specifically on representative democracy. Who becomes a representative in such a system? What are the best predispositions for getting the voters' votes? Well, being likable, popular, well-known, able to entertain people... and other similar positives. And what does a "good leader" need? Most likely, wisdom, decisiveness, morality, perspective... "surprisingly" completely different qualities. Therefore, in order for it to work at least as theoretically as it should according to the supporters of representative democracy (another thing is that in principle it cannot for far more serious reasons), it must happen that the darling of the crowds is also a capable leader (let's leave aside the fact that people follow a capable leader voluntarily); how can anyone want to rely on something like that?
Parasitism

Modern liberals (and I don't mean classical liberals, but those "leftists" in the sense of American Democrats) like to label as parasites those who work illegally, or operate in some gross violation of the labor code; conservatives (classic "right-wingers" in the sense of American Republicans) on the other hand typically call those who receive social benefits, subsidies and the like as parasites. I think both of these groups are wrong. "Leftists" more, because the one who works for black money is definitely not a parasite on anyone, he just doesn't allow himself to be robbed by the state; "Right-wingers" are a little less wrong, however, those who take benefits or subsidies only take what someone (the state) offers them. The real parasite is the entity that robs us of those funds
it prepares with the threat of violence - that is, the state
. Inciting hatred towards one or the other is just the cover maneuvers of politicians and the creation of illusory goals; the one who steals is not an actor in the gray economy or a "sock" - it is the state.
Transportation of goods

"We live in a crazy time when some things that we can make locally, we prefer to import from the other side of the world," warn some. Is it really wrong? The answer is not so simple in today's distorted (regulated, subsidized and taxed) market, where it can vary; however, in the free market, the unequivocal answer is "No, it's not wrong!" The reason for importing goods that we can produce locally is typically that it is cheaper (even with imports). No, it's not a market failure; on the contrary, it is a question of finding the best way on the market, which in the given case consists in that import. People obviously value resources consumed by production elsewhere and imports less than resources consumed by production locally (if this were not the case, it would have to be cheaper to produce it locally); this can happen, for example, as a result of the fact that people value their time (and work) differently in different places, or that there are better conditions for the production of certain goods.
Wars without states?

When the word "anarchy" is spoken, most people think of apocalypse, conflict, chaos and warfare; how far are these ideas from reality? V
historical anarchies
was certainly no more at war than in territories usurped by states; many will argue that this does not mean much, as the situation may be different today than before. So be it, it may be so; nevertheless, I believe that a society without a state will be more peaceful. Why? Because wars are expensive; and when states go to war, those who decide on wars do not pay for it, they finance it with foreign money, while if a private individual wants to go to war, he pays for it from his own money. I'm not saying that there will never be any conflicts in anarchy, there certainly will be, because sometimes it pays off anyway (either economically or out of hatred); however, I am convinced that there will be fewer of them, but above all, their scope will be significantly reduced, as society will be decentralized, which makes a world war, for example, a rather unlikely scenario.
The free market is only for the rich

Statists often argue that a free market would only serve the rich because there is no incentive to provide services to the poor because they can pay less; it may look like that at first and very superficial glance, but let's think about it more deeply. Suppose the statement is indeed true; we live in a society where all companies are competing to offer better and more luxurious services to the rich, while no one does anything for the poor. How do you best earn in such a company? Well, of course, not by stuffing yourself into the harsh competition of the luxury market, but by starting to provide goods (obviously not so luxurious) to the poor; instead of making a million from one customer, you'd rather make a hundred of them ten thousand each. After all, if the aforementioned thesis were true, car companies would only produce the most expensive cars, no one would build cheap apartments, only villas and so on...
Supporters of the free market

In conversations with die-hard anti-capitalists, I am often struck by how wrong these people are about what I—as an anarcho-capitalist—actually think; they push me all sorts of ideas that I don't agree with at all; for example, they make me a defender of the current banking system, big corporations and the like. But such things are ultimately understandable, because no one can properly understand everything; however, an absurd situation occurs at the moment when I explain why I do not think this or that and do not want to, to which the discussion opponent will not react by revising his views, but by forcefully asserting that I simply think so! What follows from this? Personally, I think that these people simply put the label "capitalism" on any economic or social phenomenon that they don't like; that they are anti-capitalists then follows from the fact that for them "capitalism" is synonymous with "the bad that I don't like". what is it Another win for newspeak?

Corporations and States

Many people (especially those who call themselves "leftists") dislike big corporations and argue that we need states to protect us from them; they don't even realize how much they help those corporations with this attitude (especially when they show it in the elections). It is precisely the states that favor giant corporations over smaller companies on practically all fronts; as? First, the really big players can interfere in legislative processes and eliminate their competition; yes, officially they shouldn't, but it happens (and calling for help from the state through which it happens is absurdly naive). Second, corporations will once again adapt better to the legislative and administrative burden that states distort the market. Third, large firms receive subsidies more easily; they have whole departments that can deal with it. And fourthly, we have the old familiar investment incentives; they also do not apply to small players. Does it really make sense to call for a big state "against" corporations?
Who does nothing wrong...

All kinds of totalitarian practices - especially, but not limited to, wiretapping - are often defended in the way: "Whoever does nothing wrong has nothing to fear." (And so it doesn't need encryption, secure lines... and especially privacy.) This thesis is nonsensical, on the one hand, because the state also considers tax evasion, for example, "bad", which is nothing more than trying not to get robbed; even if we ignore this aspect, the statement shows the incredible naivety of the speaker, because he perceives the state as some perfect entity free of human error or ill will (which is far from unusual). But the state is made up of people; therefore, it is not true that those who do nothing wrong have nothing to fear, because they can certainly be afraid of the misuse of information that the state collects about them (and it can be a legislative misuse even in violation of the law). It kind of reminds me of another statement, "People are evil, so we need a state." Um... and who will run the state? Aliens?
The complexity of society

Sometimes one can come across the claim that in "primitive societies" the state may not have been absolutely necessary, because they were very simple communities, but today, as a result of the complex and complex "modern society", it is needed and "could not do without it"; few statements could be so far from the truth. How is that? Well, small communities are the only ones where socialism can work in some way, because people there know each other and can perform economic calculation "off the top of their heads" (they can simply estimate each other's preferences), for example the family; the larger and more complex society we live in,
the more difficult it is to perform economic calculation in it without a free market
. The reality is therefore exactly the opposite of what the above statement might seem: The more complex and complicated a society we have, the more difficult it is to plan centrally and the more urgently it needs a free market for the proper allocation of resources.
Balanced budget

Many - often "right-wing" minded - people are calling for a balanced state budget; however, I - surprisingly for many - do not. Why not? Because there are two ways to achieve such a state: The first consists in reducing expenses, but the second in increasing income; a balanced budget can therefore be kept within the framework of a minimal state, but also of a huge socialist juggernaut (for example, before 1989 the Czech Republic was not nearly as indebted as it is now, but it was no paradise). I personally see it as paramount that the state should have the lowest possible income; of course, a state with low income and expenditure is by far the best, but I consider low income and high expenditure to be better than a classic large state (albeit with a balanced budget). I'm not saying you have to share my opinion, but I think we should definitely think about how important the "fight for a balanced budget" is compared to efforts to shrink the state.
Burden of proof
How can he not be an anarcho-capitalist…

...pacifist, vegan, Jainist, arbitrary anarchist? Pacifists reject violence entirely; if they are consistent, they must also reject states, and at the same time they would hardly be able to prevent anyone from trading (even if they themselves do not have to participate, but anarcho-capitalism does not require such a thing). Vegans are against the enslavement and killing of animals, often even using the formulation that they do not want to "take away the fruits of their labor"; theoretically they could be consistent statists, but only if they preferred foreign species to their own. Jains are great ascetics, they should not lie, kill, but above all their first vow is "not to take what is not given"; however, states are founded on the taking of what was not given. And finally, all anarchists - many of whom define themselves against anarcho-capitalism - reject the state, but often with it a voluntary hierarchy; but how can they prevent people from forming voluntary hierarchies without becoming a state?

A state-run and stateless society

How is a state-run society different from a stateless one? In technology? In the management of some sectors of the economy? In centralization and decentralization? Maybe as a result too; however, they differ primarily in the absence of a coercive monopoly. Instead of an entity forcing people to do what they don't want to do and pay for things that aren't worth their money, as there is today, in a stateless society it would be left up to them to decide what they want to participate in and what they don't; that would be the most fundamental change - all others would
resulted
only from this and at the end of the day no one can predict what exactly and how it would actually happen. People often fear that no one would have "it" firmly in their hands; yes, he really shouldn't, but anyone who would like to have someone to transfer some of their rights, freedoms, powers or responsibilities to can hire him... does that sound absurd? Yes; just as absurd as when it comes to the state.
Job creation

"Job creation" is seen as something desirable and positive; and indeed it often happens that way - if an entrepreneur employs someone, a job has been created, which typically enriches the company. However, we must not confuse the creation of a job with the creation of some useful value; if we create a job just so that someone has a job, values are not created that way - on the contrary. For example, if the government employs people to dig holes and bury them, clearly no value to society is created; however, the less obvious cases are more interesting. Whenever the state employs someone whom the people would not willingly pay, but must force them to do so,
there is waste
– people apparently value that money more than the products of the person's work; the same applies to jobs that do not fall directly under the state, but also to jobs in private companies that can fill them only because of subsidies. They are all variations on digging and burying holes...
Let's do business taxes!

Many (especially left-leaning) people rejoice when some politician raises their rich boss's taxes; the right question, in my opinion, is whether they even realize that if something like this happens, it will be them, among other things, who will have to earn from these high taxes. How is that? Heavily taxed firms have fewer funds; and since we live in a world of limited resources, taxed money will be missing somewhere. For example, in employee salaries; and even if not, the motivation of taxed entrepreneurs to increase those salaries in the future will decrease. Another place where scarcity can show is in the prices of a given firm's products; in the end, the customer pays those taxes as well (which is potentially also the rejoicing myopic leftists). And last but not least, the company may go bankrupt or be forced to cut costs by laying off some employees; So before you rejoice, ask who the bell is actually tolling...

What is a state?

Quite often in discussions about a free society I get that someone wants me to describe what I actually call a state; what else do I call a state and what no longer? A state is an entity that (negligibly successfully) usurps a monopoly on violence over some (negligibly large) territory it does not own; it is typically funded by involuntary contributions (it has the power to collect them, so why wouldn't it). Therefore, if one entrusts certain functions of today's state to a private company, it will not become a state just because of that, even if it will do "almost the same" as long as no one is forced to finance it and obey it. From this, in my opinion, it is quite clear why the state is such an evil: Relationships (business, personal, work... whatever) that are worth something are based on voluntariness; if something doesn't work on a voluntary basis, it's obviously not worth much, ergo it doesn't make sense to force it, because someone loses from it (if he didn't lose, he does it voluntarily).

First day of school 2020

It starts today
school year
; and with it another regular wave of euphemistically called threats and violence
compulsory school attendance
. If any entity other than the state allowed itself to threaten to forcibly remove children from parents who decide to educate them differently than this entity orders, we would consider it completely unacceptable. Why then?
the vast majority of people find it correct or acceptable
, that OSPOD kidnaps children from their parents only because they are educating them contrary to the ideas of the Ministry of Education, Culture and Sports, including in cases where
there is no abuse or neglect
? And what kind
educational models outside the scope of our legislation
do they even exist? Are they functional? Who is to decide that anyway? By what title does the state usurp a monopoly in education? And don't all the well-known disadvantages and problems that every monopolist causes arise from its monopoly position?
We will deal with these and many other questions
at tomorrow's lecture at 7 p.m. in (de)Central
together with Gabriela Ježková; and now
the next day - on Thursday - on the live stream of Free Port Studio
with Zdenka Staňková!

therefore, they resume their standard operation; and with Stokami the whole
Free port
. Videos will be released this weekend
