And then there are the holidays, which affect quite a few of us in some way, be it school children, their parents, university students, teachers, visitors to various festivals and the like; The readership and viewership of texts and videos of the Free Port decreases every year during this period. We look forward to seeing you again in September <3
Comparative advantage

Comparative advantage is one of David Ricardo's greatest discoveries; and what does it actually mean? Let's imagine a successful lawyer who is also a very good cyclist; yet it may be profitable for him to hire a messenger (on a bicycle) to deliver his package, though a lawyer could do it better and more quickly himself, yet, by attending to his work, he earns so much more that it pays him to send someone else with the package. This example is not exactly earth-shattering, and no one probably has a problem imagining it; But what does it mean? That mutual trade can pay off even when one party is no more efficient than the other; this is also true in international trade - even for states, one of which is "backward" in all respects, it can be mutually beneficial to trade. The concept of comparative advantage replaces the concept of absolute advantage (according to which a trade pays off when each party does something better than the other), which was introduced by Adam Smith.
We know what was wrong

Ex post we often know very easily what went wrong in the past; we condemn slavery, torture, witch trials, serfdom, racism, Nazi and Communist regimes (at least mostly). Yet all those things were socially accepted and even desirable in "their" time; no one then thought of what horrors it was, although some pointed it out. How is that possible? Were people evil back then? I don't think so; I would say they are still more or less the same. So how could they do such a thing? Well, it was just normal back then and "everyone knew" it "was reality" and "there was no point in going head against the wall" and no practitioner cared about "castles in the air and naive theories" because everyone "lived in the here and now"; the only thing necessary for the triumph of evil is for good men to do nothing. And so I ask: Will we allow our descendants in the distant future to see how blind we are now to evil just because "everyone knows that
we need the state
"?
Public media

Let's imagine a medium owned by a private person, but it does not have to make money from itself; everyone has to pay it, regardless of whether it brings anything of value... and this is actually a public media (its owner is the biggest and most dangerous monopoly - i.e. the state - which, of course, promotes its interests through it like any other owner). The justification for such (mostly absurdly expensive) media is that they are supposed to be carriers of content that does not make money; but what does that mean? That people are simply not interested in that content, or rather they are more interested in the resources that the medium consumes; so we will "logically" force them to pay. They say we also need the public media to inform us about "crisis situations"; erm... when something critical happens (natural disasters, terrorist attacks...), does the private media keep quiet about it? No! On the contrary, they push back another agenda just so she can talk about what the people want.
Deceiving the consumer

Deceiving consumers is prohibited by law: No one may deceive consumers, in particular by providing false, unsubstantiated, incomplete, inaccurate, unclear, ambiguous or exaggerated information, or withhold information about the real characteristics of products or services or the level of purchase conditions; all this under a fine of up to fifty million crowns. But how does the state treat its citizens, i.e. the consumers of its services? What does he tell them?
in schools
? For example, open lies about the fact that the free market cannot provide certain services (healthcare, social system, judiciary, money, etc.), therefore the state must (!) provide them; and it is not an "opinion", it is a demonstrable lie, because the market already provided those services in the past, until the governments took them over. And how would the state behave towards a businessman who would lie to his consumers in a similar way? Quite possibly similar to the mobsters who collect the booty; although the state itself does the same in a larger way and calls it taxes.
Bad banks

People often call for state protection from bad capitalist banks; such a call would be laughable if it were not for crying. Why? Today's banks are not "bad capitalist" but "bad state". A free market bank has a business policy, provides people with its services, or issues money at its own discretion, and it is up to people to accept this money; if she misbehaves from their point of view, they can just get rid of her money.
Today's banks have a huge advantage from the state
, who gave them the ability to issue money, which he then forces people to accept, keep accounts in, and pay taxes in; it basically gives them the power of a cartel that they forcefully impose on us all. It is therefore paradoxical to call on the state to "protect" us against "bad banks"; it would be enough for the state to stop giving them the disgusting force-enforced privileges (control over the money they all have to receive) and let the free market solve the problem.
Anarchy and Capitalism

"
Capitalism is the ultimate expression of anarchy and anarchy is the ultimate expression of capitalism.
" In my opinion, this quote best describes the essence of the life work of its author - Murray Newton Rothbard. Unfortunately, many (especially anarchists of other directions) do not understand it; so I would like to give them an explanation. Pure capitalism – i.e. a completely unregulated market – can only exist without state power, as any – even the smallest – tax distorts the market environment; the condition of pure capitalism is therefore a stateless environment, i.e. anarchy. And vice versa? In anarchy there is no central power to regulate anyone; people can freely exchange their goods and own the means of production, which is capitalism - even if they decide to live in communes and own the means of production communally (as long as no one is prevented from doing their own thing, which is the essence of anarchy, it will always be capitalism).
Interest
Prison

Imagine someone doing something to you;
then what about that?
If it wasn't all that bad, you might welcome compensation; if it was something unforgivable that ruined your life, you might want to hurt that person as well (I personally find revenge unfortunate, but let's leave that aside for now). But who would use their money to build some kind of bizarre zoo on their property,
in which he would lock the offender
, guarded him there, fed him at his own expense and released him after a while? Apparently almost no one. So why in this way
we deal with those who break the law
? It is enough to obscure the circumstances of the payment a little, to hide from the people the fact that they are the ones who pay, to spread the costs among those who are not affected... and then it stops being absurd and we have a prison; a massive waste of resources, gathering criminals in one place where they learn the "craft" from each other and then releasing them into society - that's the state.
Price, cost, supply and demand

Most libertarians quite rightly understand the subjective theory of value and reject the cost theory; and indeed, the value of a property is purely subjective, changing with time and place, there is no such thing as "objective value". The price then depends on supply and demand; libertarians understand this too and take it into account in their reasoning. But sometimes they automate these thoughts so much that they fall into a logical trap and tend to claim that the price does not depend on the cost. However, this is nonsense; although price is determined not only by cost (and nothing else), but also by (among other things) cost! This does not contradict the law of supply and demand, price really depends on supply and demand, but supply is affected by (among other things) costs; of course, this is not contradicted by the fact that the found gem, for which I did not have to do anything, is worth the same as the hard-to-excave one, however, if it were possible to find clouds like this, it would already be reflected in the price.
Peace with drugs in the Cherubín teahouse

Today at 7 p.m. we can meet live for the first time after the corona crisis - come and talk about drug issues and the war against drugs
to the Cherubín teahouse
. We like to return to the tea room for its unusually pleasant atmosphere; come try it too!
Abortion from the point of view of the NAP

Sometimes during discussions about
non-aggression principle (NAPu)
the topic of abortion will come up; the child is the owner of his body, so it might seem that the mother has no right to end his life. But beware! There is a difference between killing someone (that is, that he would live without me, but as a result of my actions he will die - this is a clear violation of property rights to his body) and not helping him to survive (that is, that he could survive with my help, but as a result of my inaction, he will die - this is not a violation of property rights); I'm not saying it's virtuous to let someone die, but it's not aggression in my opinion. To step over a wounded man in the street I consider abominable, but to do violence to an unhelpful one inexcusable; I have similar criteria for not giving a transfusion to a dying person... and also for a mother who refuses to give her body for the child's survival. I personally don't like it, I don't agree with it, but in my opinion it is not a violation of the NAP and no one should force her to continue her pregnancy.
Good bankruptcy

When a company goes bankrupt, we perceive it as something bad or unfortunate; and indeed it is bad for its owners and employees. But from other people's point of view it is a necessary and healthy cleansing process; to understand this idea, we need to ask ourselves the situation in which businesses fail. This happens when the company's costs exceed its expenses in the long term, causing it to find itself at a loss; but what does that mean? That people value the resources a business consumes more than the goods it creates; that is, it wastes (consumes something valuable and produces something less valuable). The merciless market condemns such companies to extinction (or to a change in functioning); this is indeed unpleasant for the owner and employees, but good for everyone else, because someone more efficient will fill the vacancy on the market (otherwise he will suffer the same fate). Failure is a process that allows us to be surrounded by the best; others are doomed to go do something they are better at.
Social engineering

Anarcho-capitalists are sometimes accused of being social engineers because they "plan their utopia" which they then want to force on people; on the one hand, I can understand why some think this (anarcho-capitalism in their eyes can resemble some utopias planned by social engineers), on the other hand, nothing could be further from the truth. Anarcho-capitalists often talk about what a free market society might look like; however, they do it not because they wish to force it on someone in that form, but because they are constantly bombarded with questions like: "And how would this or that work without the state?" They then embark on various predictions that may at first glance resemble the utopian world of a social engineer; but the anarcho-capitalists only take it as an example, they wouldn't force it on anyone, because it contradicts the whole philosophy. We want to let people be free and not control anyone; this is the opposite of social engineering.
Property and human rights

Anarcho-capitalists are often accused of dealing only with
property rights (or non-aggression principle)
, but they cough up human rights and "man" as such; here, I fear, is a pure misunderstanding of what anarcho-capitalism, the principle of non-aggression, and property rights actually mean. It is not only about the ownership of inanimate objects, but also (actually above all) about the fact that a person owns himself, his body; various "human rights" follow from this (for example, not to be killed, restricted in movement, harmed, etc.). True, these human rights are not defined in the same way as those in the Charter of Fundamental Rights and Freedoms; mainly because, unlike LZPS, they are consistent (
The LZPS is not consistent, as it promises us rights that cannot be fulfilled without limiting some of the rights of other people
). Anarcho-capitalists are not indifferent to "human rights"; on the contrary – they are anarcho-capitalists because they really care.
Interest in politics
Lamenting the poverty of time

Socialists have always complained about the "poverty of the common man", typically advocating redistribution and robbery from the rich; however, I find it very interesting to see what they meant by "poverty" in which times. At first it meant when people didn't even have food; then it changed, the person who did not have enough comfortable housing was also called poor; over time, other conveniences were added; and today even the one who has something to eat, a place to live, a lot of free time and can even go on a more modest domestic vacation from time to time is already "poor". The state is supposed to help these "poor people". If the criteria of poverty will change like this, there will always be a reason to legalize robbery in the interest of the "poor" (they already live better today than the rich in the past). But what is it that keeps the poor doing better and better? By capitalism of course; the latter is not based on equality like socialism, but it creates so much wealth that "today's" poor have more than "yesterday's" rich.
Own housing for young people

We have a new "problem" in society: Young people do not have enough resources to buy their own housing, so they "have to" take out mortgages. All sorts of socialists lament where the world is going, what a horror it is and what we should do about it (ie how the state should solve it); and where is the world going? Well, to prosperity; this "problem" is completely illusory, because never in history have young people had enough resources to buy their own housing, this is nothing new. On the contrary, never in the past were the young (or even the old) so rich and so well provided for; we even live so well that we have forgotten that the initial state is poverty and wild inhospitable nature. Wealth, houses and technology are things that come with time; and the world is moving towards more and more young people owning their own homes... so that the socialists can whine that young people don't have their own jets.
Jobs

The doctrine of "job protection" is more or less based on the misconception of a limited number of jobs in the world (or in a country); however, this is a similar illusion to the thesis that the total wealth of the world is constant. However, neither of these is true; as wealth keeps increasing (just compare how we are now and how it was a few hundred years ago), people keep having more and more needs. Whereas before they were happy to have something to eat, today they want entertainment, travel, beautiful houses, cars... and when the time comes when they have all this, they will start wanting even more (other forms of entertainment, space travel, living on the seas or under the surface, hovercraft...). In connection with this, new jobs will be created all the time (and if one day machines do all the work, so much the better; people will not have to work, their needs will be met even without work, so they will have a lot of free time).
Let's regulate X!

X can mean offensive violence, violation of property rights (murders, robberies, rape, destruction of other people's property...); let's leave that aside for now and talk about cases where X is anything else (i.e. non-violent, property-rights-respecting activity). So what does the call to regulate X mean? In reality, it is a call for the use of offensive violence against someone who is looking out for his own and does nothing to anyone. It means: "That man over there is doing something to himself and for himself that I don't like; let's make him stop doing it and submit to my will." If we say this sentence to an ignorant person, he will most likely condemn it unequivocally; yet the vast majority of them will support some such regulation.
At the same time, it is the same thing
, it differs only in wording. It is fascinating how powerful state propaganda is; because of her, it is enough just to reformulate the same thesis into the words presented to us by the state as "desirable"... and lo and behold, a clear rejection turns into consent.
Capitalist insatiable

Many people dismiss crooked capitalists as "just after the money"; but what does it mean when someone in the free market (that is, without violating property rights) "goes after the money" and makes money? Such a person buys something (and consumes), sells something (not necessarily creates, but can); either it is an entrepreneur who buys resources (material, labor...) and transforms them into a product, or a speculator (or intermediary) who buys what he sells later (or elsewhere). In both cases, the value he consumed is less than the value he provided to others (even in the case of the speculator - let's not forget that value is subjective and changes over time, the cost theory of value has been disproved); his profit then expresses how much he has enriched society. Of course, a capitalist whose highest value is money may not be exactly the best life partner; to those who trade with him, however
it clearly benefits
.
Who "rules" in capitalism?

The first superficial answer might be that they are huge multinational corporations; however, for a deeper understanding, it is necessary to ask what makes the huge corporations so huge, where they actually get their influence. The truth is that they are given this size, power and money by their own customers, the "common people"; they are the ones from whom the power comes in the free market, they are the ones who rule in the free market society! If the economy were a ship, corporations are the helmsmen or the officers commanding the crew, but the customer is the captain who determines the course of the voyage; if a corporation does not serve those who voluntarily buy from it, it will not have access to their money and will lose its power. Someone may argue that a sufficiently large and powerful corporation does not need voluntary customers, because it can ignore their will and force them to pay; of course that risk exists... and such a corporation is then called in one word: the state.
Hated capitalism
World injustice

I often hear people on below-average pay talking hatefully about the "top 10 percent" and the like; they perceive it as a huge injustice that they are not among them. I find it utterly absurd; why? Because they typically belong! Even poor people in the Czech Republic are among the richest people in the world. We live in one of the richest parts of the world and here we are like pigs in the rye; all of us (even those factory workers and supermarket saleswomen) belong to the "top ten percent" (and many quite possibly even to the top five percent). Even those who live "from hand to mouth" here do not suffer from hunger (unlike masses of people around the world); unlike the majority, these people often have free weekends, work approximately eight hours a day and somehow make ends meet... but they complain that they don't have more free time, more money for better vacations, a car and the like. And when society gets even richer, they will complain that they don't have yachts, because some do.
Government of the people

Imagine a decentralized society where people express their will through market exchanges; what they like and what they want
voluntarily finance
, while they will simply not pay for goods they are not interested in, thus clearly expressing their preferences. Projects, the outputs of which people value less than the resources they consume, will simply not arise, because in this society there will be a lack of means to implement them, since no one will distribute them by force. In contrast, let's imagine another company that functions more or less like the last one... except, sort of
democratically elected government
it subsidizes some loss-making projects (against the wishes of those with whose money it does so) and taxes and regulates some profitable ones; as a result of these interventions, some things are created against the will of the payers and others are not created, although people would like them (they are prohibited or disadvantaged). The rather fundamental question then is: Which of the two variants is more "government of the people"?
Homo economicus

Economic man is a theoretical construct used in some economic models; this is a hypothetical person who only tries to maximize his (financial) profits, buy as cheaply as possible, sell as expensive as possible and, moreover, always behaves completely logically. This model was sharply criticized by Austrian economists (especially Ludwig von Mises) for its apparent discrepancy with reality; any conclusions drawn from similar assumptions cannot then be used for the real world, because in it people simply behave differently (although they always try to maximize their benefit, not only the financial one, but also the complex one, i.e. also the emotional one). The Austrian school of economics, on which, for example, anarcho-capitalism is based, counts on real people; in connection with this, I find it absolutely absurd how often homo economicus is presented to Austrians or anarcho-capitalists as a mistake in their thinking, although they themselves point to it.
State employee taxes

Why do civil servants pay taxes? Well... first of all, it must be said that they are paid formally, but not in reality. The state takes money under threat of violence from anyone who earns it in the private sector; those who are already paid by the state also theoretically pay taxes, but this is just an accounting trick: the state gives them X and takes Y; in fact, he could just give them X minus Y, take nothing, and it would come out the same. Why isn't that the case? Firstly, in order to make the civil servants themselves feel that they are not supporting themselves on other taxpayers (and they are succeeding, see the famous statement of the unnamed official: "If we, the civil servants, were not there, who would pay taxes on all those self-employed people?"); and secondly, to put these people in as much of a "normal light" as possible. But it should be normal to provide services based on voluntary payments; certainly not to be paid with money that belonged to someone
taken away under threat of violence
. Stop the state!
How much is a human life worth?

In connection with the coronavirus, many are beginning to address the cost of human life in the sense of how much money it makes sense to pay to keep someone from dying; and two currents of opinion are most common:
1/ Some calculation of GDP per capita, or the market price of the values produced by a person after deducting the costs of his education and the like.
2/ The value of human life is incalculable; and anyone who attempts such a thing is disgusting, inhumane and reprehensible.
I don't agree with either approach. The first does not take into account the non-monetary benefit; the other reality (its logical consequence would be to spend all existing resources only on saving lives; no one should devote their time or money to anything else). So what is my answer? The price of each of us is different; and to save each individual it makes sense to spend just as many resources as people (including him) are willing to voluntarily pay, but not more than he himself would wish. The universal price of human life is about as much nonsense as the statement that all men are the same.
Failure of the individual

Until
Freeport Forums
someone shared a strange text about police buzzing. Since it was only about the length of Stok, I asked the author if I could publish it here (under her name). She declined, saying she did not want to bring the police into disrepute because of an individual's failure. I respect her wishes; for those interested
I'm just posting a link
. However, I ask how obvious systemic defects of the state are people willing to excuse the failure of individuals? Yes, an individual has sinned; but what to expect if we give power to a handful of individuals selected from among those who want to be policemen under the present conditions? Or politicians - if people get power who first climb through internal party struggles to the top and then do the best PR in the election campaign, how will they govern? When a private firm cheats a customer, no one blames the particular employee at the counter where he signed the contract; so why does everyone in the state blame the employees, but almost no one blames the entire institution?
Dan Steigerwald in deCentral: The lecture will be, we have an exception from the government

Dan Steigerwald will be speaking at deCentral today; since Babiš is a big fan of anarcho-capitalism, we negotiated a government exemption for this event.
However, in case anyone doesn't believe it, the identical lecture will be repeated on the first Wednesday of the next month, i.e. May 6th.
I choose you, Prymula!

Because Vojtěch is a handsome man, but also a singer and a lawyer, Babiš pulled another ace up his sleeve: "I'm choosing you, Prymulo." An epidemiologist could be the winning horse in solving the epidemic! And wisdom is already falling from him; on the one hand, masks until there are zero infected, which I understand. But then we have a proposal to first ban discount events. Like seriously? Isn't it enough that government measures (some of which I think are reasonable) will hurt the economy and people won't have enough money? Will we still take away the opportunity to buy at a discount? In addition, I would be worried about the temporary nature of such a measure.
However, I consider the declaration of closing the borders for months to years to be much more fundamental. Yes, there were times when such a measure made sense; those were exactly the times when Babiš and Vojtěch told us that everything was under control and there was nothing to fear. Closing the borders in the past could have prevented the infection from reaching the Czech Republic. Now it's here; and it spreads. If its spread could be stopped and the infected isolated, of course closing the borders would make sense; but this will be done within the next few weeks (which is the question), or never (the infection will get out of control). If the infection will spread worldwide (which it probably will) and the prevalence of infected people in the Czech Republic will not differ significantly from the prevalence abroad, why keep the borders closed?
Profiting from someone else's misfortune is...

All my life - and especially in recent days - I hear that "profiting from the misfortune of others" is morally reprehensible, pathetic, scumbag and the like. Can someone (logically) explain why it is wrong when someone helps people in need and gets paid (perhaps a lot) for it? When I imagine myself in need, I would rather be the person who offers to help me for a lot of money than the person who offers nothing and just condemns the first one. An offer of help for big money can be rejected. So how can it be worse than no offer at all? Why is the one who helps dearly so often perceived worse than the one who doesn't help at all? At worst, I won't use expensive help, which makes it at least as useful as no help at all. And finally, it is not clear to me why people who so condemn "making money from other people's misfortune" usually respect firefighters and doctors, who live directly from other people's misfortune?
National self-sufficiency

The doctrine of "national self-sufficiency" has long been quite popular; and like many popular things it doesn't make much sense on closer inspection. First, let's ask why self-sufficiency should only be at the level of a nation; wouldn't it be even better to be self-sufficient at the city level? Street? Or even families? Or to make everyone self-sufficient? Such ideas obviously do not make sense, as they would plunge us into poverty through absence
division of labor
. But how does protectionism differ on a smaller and larger scale? Only in that it is more visible in the smaller; economic laws also apply internationally: Production (for example, food) within the state suffers from the same ailments as production (for example, food) within the household; it is more efficient for everyone to specialize in what they are good at (and then exchange the resulting product with others on the free market) than for everyone to do everything. For the division of labor means wealth; isolationism and protectionism poverty.
Usury

Most people condemn usury; however, I maintain that this is a clearly positive phenomenon. Why? If someone offers someone a loan with a dizzyingly high interest rate, there are two possibilities: Either the recipient rejects the offer, then nothing happened and the situation is the same as if the offer had not occurred; or they agree, which means that the borrower himself considers the situation when he takes the loan to be better than the situation when he refuses it (otherwise he would not borrow). What does this mean? That the creditor offered him a better alternative, whereby
improved his situation
(according to the borrower's own standards); this applies regardless of the borrower's desperate situation or the amount of interest. Whoever does not like it, let him compete with the lender and offer the poor man a loan on better terms; if he does not, the criticism of usury is then utter insolence from his mouth. Why? Especially because he didn't do as much for the borrower as the usurer, who at least offered him an alternative to a desperate situation (albeit a desperate one)!
Who would solve... the coronavirus without the state?

People have been asking me lately how pandemics would be handled in a stateless society; who would keep people in quarantine? Well, security forces, people with guns - just like today. Only they would not be subject to governments, but to private security agencies operating in the area. They would act in the interests of clients; and in the interest of health insurance companies, which should have a direct financial incentive to participate. So what would be the difference? First, in the responsibility of all actors – while a politician can screw up anything and bears no personal responsibility, market entities pay for mistakes (an unnecessarily extensive quarantine can bring a whirlwind of lawsuits and the recovery of compensation for restricting personal freedom; lax actions lead to loss of customers, reputation or money); and secondly, without the state, no one would come up with such stupid ideas as banning disease testing by private laboratories or regulating the price of respirators (which reduces the incentive to quickly produce more).
Pavel Ševčík at deCentral: Anonymity of Bitcoin and its risks

The topic of the past
lectures on anarcho-capitalism at the (de)Centrála club
was an introduction to cryptocurrencies, especially Bitcoin.
Today we will directly follow up on the previous lecture; Pavel Ševčík will talk about the anonymity of Bitcoin! Despite popular belief, Bitcoin is designed as a pseudonymous system, not anonymous; however, anonymity can be achieved with a little effort.
You are all also directly invited to the next lecture, which takes place on April 1; Dan Steigerwald will lecture. He will explain to us why socialists are right about everything; except for one small detail.
I'm looking forward to seeing you tonight at 7 p.m
of the (de)Central club
.
EU versus battery

The EU is not only trying to
unification of chargers
; is trying to force cell phone manufacturers to produce only devices with replaceable batteries. It might seem that such a thing would help us; but is it really so? First of all, there isn't much consumer interest in it; if it was, manufacturers would offer such phones as a competitive advantage. However, most people like to switch phones and buy new, faster, better-featured ones; on the other hand, those who put off buying a new phone for years (like me) can buy a power bank for a few hundred. And secondly, integrated batteries also offer technological advantages: their shape adapts better to the phone, which saves space or increases capacity; in addition, they are better insulated against moisture and dirt. Although I am one of those consumers who would appreciate replaceable batteries, I don't want to impose my preferences on others; let the market decide, not the EU.
EU versus chargers

For several years, the EU has been trying to force manufacturers to unify chargers for all mobile phones and some other devices. On the face of it, this is good customer service; but what about the second and third look? First, gradual unification occurs in the market even without legislation; USB-C is a fairly widely accepted standard, so anyone interested in it has a pretty decent choice. And secondly – let's imagine that the EU had managed to push through such legislation ten or fifteen years ago; what would happen As a universal adapter, something that was used to charge at the time would probably be promoted then; and over which it typically could not transfer data. If we had preserved the development with such legislation, we would probably not have reached what we have today, i.e. a single cable for both charging and data transmission. The question is: What will we lose in the next ten years if we maintain development at the current standard?
Totality yesterday, today and tomorrow

Totality does need some ideology to function, but not a specific one - almost any one can serve, even if some are more suitable. Of course, a totalitarian regime can be based on the divinity of the ruler, the purity of the race, the class struggle, but also on anything else from the practically endless number of possibilities that the human imagination offers. The way the state functions and its practices matter far more than a specific ideology. Totality does not lie in divinity, racial purity, or working class; it consists in controlling (almost) all aspects of people's lives, and it doesn't matter what ideology the state uses to justify these practices. In practice, this means, among other things, that every further regulation, every further extension of legislation, every further mandatory register and data collection, every further control of our lives – these are all steps towards totalitarianism; completely regardless of what we justify and excuse them with.
This is something that most people are unfortunately not aware of, so the individual ideologies of the past are demonized that we are wary of, but at the same time we are blind to the real totalitarian threats that we face every day. What are they like?
That's what I lectured about
on
Freeport Conference 2020: Totality yesterday, today and tomorrow
.

published an article on the Mises.cz server
, who inspired us to organize the conference.
How would the free market solve...?

If I had to say which question I answer most often in life, it would certainly be variations on the theme of how the free market would solve this or that; the paradox is that I can never answer with certainty. I only give people - for better or worse - guesses; not that I can't imagine various free market solutions, quite the opposite in my imagination, but firstly, I can never know which of the possibilities would arise, and secondly, I consider it very likely that the millions of entrepreneurs in the free market trying to get rich solving any problem will come up with something far better than I can ever think of. After all... if the free market could be predicted, it could also be centrally planned. So you can see my answers as a worst-case-scenario; imagine yourself (or others who have actually done so) how you would have estimated the form of capitalism today a hundred years ago. Life has more imagination than we carry in our dreams; and the free market likesmet!
Tax havens

Tax havens are (as a result of massive state propaganda) widely hated; the people who pay taxes there, the state (and, as a result, many citizens) try to portray them as pariahs. So are tax havens harming us? No! Quite the opposite. Firstly, it is necessary to realize that untaxed money is not "stolen" (on the contrary -
taxes are robbery
and not taking them away is a defense against it); secondly, this money will not disappear anywhere, only politicians will not decide how to spend it, but those who earned it (which is only good); thirdly, even a company that would pay no taxes at all is definitely a positive force in the economy as long as it sustains itself (it provides customers with values that they value, otherwise they would not willingly pay for them); and finally, fourthly, tax havens mean competition for tax hells (states with high taxes risk companies moving to states with low taxes). I am happy for every tax haven and entrepreneur who pays taxes there instead of here.
Are we living in capitalism?

Capitalists and socialists mostly agree on one thing; and Mises already agreed with Marx: Capitalism means that the means of production have private owners; in socialism, the state owns the means of production. So far we are clear. However, many sometimes forget that it is quite clear from this definition that "pure" capitalism or socialism will be rather exceptional states; we mostly live in a society that is to some extent capitalist and to some extent socialist (so capitalism and socialism is not binary). Because everyone tends to notice primarily things that don't work the way they wish, socialists like to say we live in capitalism, while capitalists say the opposite; how to find out who is closer to the truth? Even if we leave aside that, especially nowadays, it is not entirely clear what a "means of production" is, we come across the fact that there is a difference between who owns something de jure and who owns it de facto.
Let's imagine a hypothetical situation where the state completely decides on the means of production, but de jure the owners of the enterprises are "white horses" (they do not decide on anything); this state is undoubtedly de facto pure socialism (Hitler's National Socialism came close). In today's over-regulated world, the state does not have exclusive decision-making power, but with its regulations it de facto deprives the owner of the means of production of part of their ownership (not de jure); legislation enforces how they can deal with property, affects prices, salaries and working conditions, and in addition, we pay most of what we create to the state in taxes. To what extent the means of production are owned by the state and to what extent by the formal owner, it is impossible to say, as the degree of individual legislative restrictions is often subjective; we therefore live in partial capitalism and partial socialism (except for the sectors where the state is the de facto and formal owner; these are purely socialist).
Who is talking about market failure?

Have you noticed what examples people typically cite as so-called "market failures"? Well, the ones where their preferences differ from what others want, so the market will decide differently than they would like. A classic "market failure" is, for example, the demolition of a beautiful building in the name of allowing a supermarket to stand on the site; but what does that mean? Only so much that people's utility from that supermarket is higher than from that building; if this were not the case, those who want to maintain the status quo could buy the land for as much money as the buyers are not willing to spend (otherwise, they obviously get more use out of the land). The so-called "market failure" is then called by the statists who want the building and are not satisfied with the result of peaceful voluntary exchanges, while the supposed "correction" of the situation is to force free people to do what the statists force them to do instead of what they want.
GDP

Many people take this economic indicator very seriously; for some she is almost an idol. I am not claiming that this figure is completely useless, in reality it can be used to compare the wealth of different states very roughly (seriously very roughly) (at least by order of magnitude; if the GDP of one state is one percent higher than the GDP of another, it does not mean anything, the difference in large tens or small hundreds of percent does); however, its growth does not necessarily mean something good. There are a number of problems with this indicator; however, I consider the biggest to be mixing pears with apples (sometimes rotten) - the state adds its expenses to the value of the goods that are traded on the free market. Even if the state paid thousands of people to dig holes and bury them, GDP would increase despite the obvious futility of this activity (the same goes for all other state waste); on the other hand, the gray economy, which undoubtedly helps people, is not included in GDP... so watch out for that.
VAT on beer?

Alcoholic beer has a VAT of 21%; tapped on site has a VAT of 10%. Non-alcoholic beer has a VAT of 15%; VAT is 10% on the spot. On-site means beer at a store with facilities and not in a pitcher. Period, that's all. Although I welcome any criticism of Babiš, the government, or even the state, has this really become the most fundamental problem of the last few days? We live in a total legislative jungle of absolutely confusing and incredibly complex laws; running the smallest business means a lot of bureaucracy. And nobody really minds; not enough to make it a hot topic. Is VAT on beer really our biggest problem? Yes, let's criticize VAT on beer. But isn't the more substantial criticism of the existence of multiple VAT rates? And an even more substantial criticism of the existence of VAT itself? And the far more important criticism of the existence of taxation? And are taxes really what the state oppresses us the most?

Unreasonable profit

Recently, for the fourth time in my life, a communist (each time a different one) with whom I had a discussion claimed to me that due to the profits made by every entrepreneur in the chain of production (i.e. mining - ore processing - manufacturing of components - assembly of products), all products are five times overpriced, so that if production were nationalized, without those profits they would be available for only twenty percent of today's price (and since everyone said the same number, I assume that somewhere read but I couldn't find where); I'm not going to explain why this is nonsense, which I've already done anyway
elsewhere
, but I ask: If this is really the case, why instead of nationalization, why don't socialists simply create free market enterprises without profits that will produce goods five times cheaper and thereby crush capitalist competition to dust, if they can deliver goods to the people so much better than the greedy capitalists?
Gray economy

Politicians (and not only them) like to convince us of the harmfulness of the gray economy; it is said to harm society, which becomes poorer because of it, because people pay less taxes to the state. First of all, I would like to point out that the state and society are two different things; while society is all of us, the state is a parasitic entity that drains the productive ones of us. Above all, as a result of the gray economy, no money "disappears" anywhere; although the state cannot deal with them, they remain in people's wallets. So when the finance minister talks about how much money we are "losing" due to the gray economy, what he really means is that it is not he (the parasite) who is spending those resources, but us (the hosts); it's definitely not bad, on the contrary -
we know much better how to spend our money
, than some fool. Not to mention that even if we didn't know, it was our property and it was up to us what we would do with it; each the engineer, train driver and train driver of his own luck.
State and ownership

Is the state the guarantor of private property? He definitely claims to be one; and indeed it is to some extent. Specifically, to the extent that he tries to force himself
a monopoly on infringing the property rights of others
, in which he rebuffs other entities when they try to do the same; so yes, the state protects people's private property - but only against robbers other than the state itself. As a result of the state usurping this function, many even believe that without it private property would not exist at all; however, this is a deep mistake, because people probably started appropriating things long before the emergence of states (primitive man already used primitive tools), not to mention that even in times and places where the power of the state did not reach (for example, the USA during the time of colonization or Iceland in the early Middle Ages), the institution of private property did not disappear. So let's not be mistaken - property rights do not have to be enforced by state power.

Technological standards

Some people still believe today that we need the state to enforce technological standards; one socialist even told me in our recent discussion that without the state we wouldn't even screw in a screw because the thread would have a different width, pitch and tooth profile. Lack of humility or its excess?

Why did the state buy an e-shop for 400 megabytes?

Yesterday I wrote about
state e-shop for 400 mega
. Today I would like to answer the question, how can the state afford such a thing? Well, it's quite simple. The state is not a free market firm; not serving customers. It is a monopoly on violence; and as an organization it does not have to answer to the citizens for anything. In case of major misconduct, he can punish and replace someone from his ranks, if it helps PR; but he doesn't have to change anything about the principles of his operation, because of which those errors occur, because he has power, so it's easier for him to ban competition than to do things for people. The main problem with the 400 meg e-shop is not the price; it is the involuntariness of the whole transaction that allows it to take place under such conditions at all. And complaining about the prize is, as the anarcho-capitalist Dan Steigerwald said, "...like a woman who was raped in a park complaining about not getting a flower and then being left lying in the mud."
E-shop for 400 mega from erar

The state transport infrastructure fund bought the e-shop for highway signs for 400 mega without a tender; and everyone is on edge. Why? Well, because it's expensive. And because no sane person will buy an e-shop with five and a half items for 400 million crowns. Clearly an overpriced order! And how do we know? Simply; we know how much e-shops cost on the market. And we assume that government purchases should move in similar relationships as market ones. Well, when they differ by an order of magnitude, the hype in the media space begins. Just as Americans didn't like it when the U.S. Army
she bought a toilet seat for 45 thousand crowns or a hammer for 30 thousand.
.
We all know how much an e-shop (or a toilet seat or a hammer) should cost; but we know this only and only because there are also market prices in the corresponding industry; if they didn't exist, we have no idea. Well... and exactly this situation actually occurs in sectors where the state has a monopoly position; no one knows how much not only Pandora, but also services such as courts, police and education are supposed to cost. In those sectors, market mechanisms are almost absent, prices are more or less determined by states; and no one has anything to judge by how much they correspond to reality and how much someone would be willing to pay realistically for services of the given quality. We just trust the state that this will definitely not be overpriced; for when such excesses occur where they are easily discovered, certainly no civil servant or politician will allow himself to do such a thing where, in principle, it cannot even be discovered.
Surplus value

Surplus value is the cornerstone of the communist justification of revolutionary violence of the "proletarian working class" against the "exploiters"; and unfortunately, such an explanation makes sense not only to communists: Workers produce goods that have some value, the capitalist sells them, pays part of the money taken to the employees, spends part on other expenses related to production and keeps part (which is precisely the surplus value). However, this thinking completely ignores the subjectivity of value; nothing has an objective value in itself, that is attributed to goods by people. What does this mean? That there is no such thing as surplus value; the capitalist buys people's labor at the market price (for the worker, obviously, this price is higher than the value of that labor, otherwise they would not work for him; for the employer, it is the opposite, otherwise he would not employ them) and then sells the produced goods at the market price to customers (because for them their value is higher than this price).
There is no evil as evil

Totalitarianism is a state in which a state seeks to control almost all aspects of its subjects' lives on a vast scale.
Dictatorship is the rule of a narrow group (or individual).
Democracy is the rule of the majority.
Fascism is a totalitarian dictatorship with significant elements of egalitarianism (collectivism), nationalism, militarism and certain forms of progressivism.
Nazism is a combination of fascism with racism (the theory of a superior race) and anti-Semitism.
If we proceed from these (generally accepted) definitions, we reach the following (generally neglected) conclusions: Totality does not have to be a dictatorship; dictatorship does not have to be totalitarian (although it typically is). A democracy cannot be a dictatorship, but it can be a totalitarianism (and sometimes it is; the rule of the majority may want to control almost every aspect of its subjects' lives). Nazism and fascism are not the same thing; fascism need not be racist or anti-Semitic (Nazism is). Not every dictatorship or totalitarianism is fascism. A police state is totalitarian, but it doesn't have to have a dictator; even the rule of law can be totalitarian (if there are sufficiently repressive laws). Democracy means the rule of the majority, not freedom and certainly not "goodness" or "protection of minorities".

A quarter of a century since the death of Murray Newton Rothbard

Today is exactly twenty-five years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers and geniuses - Murray Newton Rothbard, the "father of anarcho-capitalism" left this world at the age of 69; his life's work was a consistent and logical introduction to the consequences of two trends that were seemingly not very related: anarchism and the Austrian school of economics. Anarchists were often wrong in economics, and the proponents of the Austrian school of economics did not apply their (correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and came to a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This knowledge and full understanding of it changed my life greatly; Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.
What if there was no X without the state?

You can put absolutely anything behind X... roads, schools, charity, research... just anything. After you do that, two possibilities arise: Either we need X so much that we are willing to voluntarily pay more than what the cost of that X is; or we don't need, which means the resources we're willing to sacrifice on X won't cover the cost. In the first case, anyone who starts providing X can make money (people will pay him more than what it costs to produce X if the condition above is met); there is no point in doubting whether X would be available, because without the state it might be difficult to provide it - what can be made, someone will take care of it. In the event that we are not willing to pay the above costs for X, then X will most likely not occur at all; and that's only a good thing, because under the circumstances providing it would be wasteful (people value X less than the resources expended on it).

NAP and veganism

O
I have already written a lot about the principle of non-aggression
; maybe that's why vegans ask me more and more often why I don't apply it to animals. The answer is that the principle of non-aggression is based on property rights that animals not only do not observe and understand, but are not (and it seems likely never will be) capable of understanding; then it makes no sense to me to recognize these rights towards them (if there were animals that understood property rights, I would reconsider my position). I completely understand and fully respect even those who do not want to use animals to increase their utility and I will not talk them out of it (I even consider it a certain virtue); however, I believe that choosing otherwise is not worse (nor better) in principle. And just as vegans question why I apply the NAP to humans but not to animals in general, one might ask why we don't just extend the NAP to all living things (which would mean starving to death). Does anyone know the answer?
"Our" resources

"Our" raw material wealth; "our" jobs; "our" country; and sometimes even "our" doctors (who, for example, brazenly dare to leave the Czech Republic, which was a huge issue a few years ago). We can often come across these - and many other similar - expressions in the sense that "our" means Czech; ideas and theses that arise from similar assumptions tend to be completely misguided. Why? Well, raw materials have an owner, ergo they are his; to declare them "our Czechs" denies this ownership; lands on the territory of the Czech Republic also belong to their owners, not to "us" all; and "our" doctors, that's total nonsense. What is especially mean about this argument is that it operates with a kind of quasi-property, which, however, contradicts property rights; therefore, whoever says: "My country, my rules," means the Czech Republic and indicates that "he has the right" to (jointly) decide here, thereby denying the very statement from which (my country, my rules) is based, with regard to the owners of specific plots of land in the given territory.

Anarchist at heart, capitalist at heart

Some time ago I spoke with an anarcho-communist; among other things, we discussed his idea that everyone should "have the right" to an apartment or a house, because housing and a sense of security are among the basic human needs. I countered that although most people probably feel that way, someone may prefer other things to housing. He looked at me sheepishly and came up with the analogy that it's like if he bought everyone chocolate and I'd blame him for spoiling them because someone would prefer a donut to chocolate; he apparently missed that the state and the socialists are buying these people with their money. But that's beside the point now; as I reflected on our conversation on the way home, one thing dawned on me: We both want the same thing. Seriously. And what is it? We want people to be happy. The only difference between us is that while he is some kind of intuitive supporter of an objective theory of value, I understand that value is subjective.
Sometimes you ask me why I feel closer to anarcho-communists than to the conservative right; and this is the reason: While I am separated from the anarcho-communist and his idea of "housing for everyone" by a different perception of the theory of value, from the conservative rightist and his "defense of the traditional family" (as a result of which, for example, homosexuals suffer, which he knows and doesn't care) I am separated by... I don't know... humanity? When an anarcho-communist tells me "a flat for everyone", I understand that my aim is to explain to him that we live in a world of limited resources and to show Bastiat's "what is not seen"; however, when a staunch conservative tells me that he rejects gay marriage because "it's unnatural" (which probably won't be his real reason, because he's also not in favor of throwing away antibiotics and dying of infections, because it's natural) and "marriage between a man and a woman is among traditional millennial values" (but he doesn't want slavery with an even longer tradition), what am I supposed to think?
Death to speculators!

Nobody likes speculators; we still forgive the unsuccessful ones, because they have already eaten it, but the successful ones are condemned by the majority society. What do I say to that? These reactions are not only illogical and absurd, but above all completely inverted; for the successful speculator helped others, while the unsuccessful one harmed others. The market is not a zero-sum game! Property prices are subjective and change over time. If there is an excess of something, the price will fall; in case of shortage it will rise. A clever speculator will buy in times of surplus (helping bankrupt producers by raising the price) to sell in times of need (helping consumers by lowering the price); the person in question essentially "smooths out" price fluctuations over time. When he gets it wrong, he can do the opposite, harming others and paying dearly for it himself (as much as he harms them); paradoxically, only criticisms of unsuccessful speculators can be considered justified, but they harmed themselves in the first place.
Economic cycles

People often think of business cycles (periods of rapid growth alternating with crises) as something that has always been there, sometimes even a feature of capitalism; however, both are mistakes. Business cycles occur as a result of (government-controlled) artificial interest rate reductions. The market has this fascinating property: If there are enough saved resources in society, due to the law of supply and demand, interest rates fall, which motivates people to invest and produce goods that they then sell easily (there are enough resources in society); the artificial reduction of interest rates motivates entrepreneurs to make the same investments, but then they will not find a market for the produced goods (society is poorer than it appeared from the false price signals).
I explained this phenomenon in more detail in my lecture on money.
However, those who are practitioners with no interest in theories can convince themselves empirically: As long as states did not artificially lower interest rates, economic cycles did not take place.
A zero sum game?

Many argue that envy is behind the hatred of the rich; and maybe they are right (certainly in part). However, I think that, in addition to envy, a role is also played by the generally widespread belief that the market is a zero-sum game, so that when someone gets rich, it must happen at the expense of another who gets poorer. However, this is clearly not true; if it happens between two people
voluntary exchange
, everyone subjectively values the good they gain more than the good they give up (if they didn't, they wouldn't voluntarily enter into such a trade). Even thanks to this, the wealth of the company is constantly increasing; let's see what conditions people lived in a few hundred years ago and compare it to how we are now. Society as a whole grows richer; even the poor get rich. In a free market, the person who improves the situation of others the most earns the most. Therefore, when a company makes a lot of money, it is not "at the expense" of customers; both sides will improve.

Che Guevara as a symbol

If there is interest in something, in our capitalist society it will typically be available sooner or later; and various objects with images of the revolutionary Che Guevara are no exception. Many even see it as a symbol of freedom; and I can't help but wonder. The murderer of hundreds of people, who, together with Castro, helped establish a harsh dictatorship in Cuba, in which he himself held important government positions (he was a minister), ran a bank (!) and intensively centralized all power in society, he apparently found a taste in murder (not only in combat), because he personally participated in mass executions, although he undoubtedly did not have to. When the powerful (el Che and Fidel) fell apart, he moved from Cuba to Zaire, then to Bolivia; in both places, as a professional revolutionary, he continued to harm people and spread suffering; however, he did not achieve his goals, failed, was captured and finally shot from head to toe. From the photos, I think he was a really handsome guy; is this the reason why someone puts it on a t-shirt?
Intellectual property

Many (by no means all) anarcho-capitalists (myself included)
they do not recognize intellectual property
; this certainly does not mean that I have anything against people contractually committing themselves to anything they deem appropriate - i.e. not to distribute a purchased book or even software (under the threat of an arbitrary fine for breach of contract). So what do I find unacceptable? For anyone to extend the validity of this contract to other individuals who have nothing to do with it at all. If person A creates a work, which he sells to person B, who contractually agrees not to distribute the content, but does so anyway, it makes no sense to prosecute person C for its further distribution, if he did not enter into any contract (and did not take possession of the work by infringing someone's ownership). Do you object that in practice it is difficult to prove something to person B? It certainly does; but if there is a crime that is difficult to prove, will we prosecute the innocent just because we can't find the perpetrator?
Some wonder why some of the anarcho-capitalists do not recognize intellectual property, although property rights are sacred to them; well, even if it sounds paradoxical, this is exactly the reason. Let us imagine a man who owns land, a pencil and paper; he sits down on his property and starts writing something there with his pencil on his paper. And this is the property that is sacred to us; he can do with his resources as he sees fit! To say that someone "owns" the text of a book, for example, is to ascribe to him partial ownership of all the pencils, paper, and other means of writing books in the entire universe; similar to when the state forbids people to take drugs, for example, it partially usurps property rights to their bodies, which we consider unacceptable (even if it is also only a limitation of one of the many activities we can do with our bodies; and it is no different in the case of those pencils and papers).
Subsidy four times differently

First: Subsidies cause corruption; beneficiaries bribe officials.
Second: Redistribution wastes resources; those who run them do not work for free.
Third: Subsidies harm small entrepreneurs; everyone pays taxes, but larger entities can more easily manage the administration and meet the conditions.
Fourth: Loss-making companies waste, ergo they should go bankrupt and make way for prosperous ones; redistribution saves them, thereby distorting the market, destroying the good and helping the bad.
The order in which I have listed the disadvantages of subsidies corresponds to how serious, in my opinion, the public perceives them (while everyone sees the former as a big problem, the latter are most likely not even realized by most people); however, their real harmfulness is probably almost exactly the opposite - while some corruption basically only causes money to be spent according to the needs of another, instead of being spent according to the will of one official, supporting the wasteful and incompetent pushes the more capable out of the market, thus harming customers who have to pay more money for lower quality services. And I'm not talking about that at all
the moral side of the whole thing, because the money that the state gives out has to be stolen from someone first
.
Marriage is everyone's private matter...

Yesterday
a text was published in Stoká
, whose author calls for the separation of marriage from the state (which is something we definitely agree with), but at the same time he is against the marriage of same-sex couples on the grounds that it would be a violation of the NAP, because he says the state forces him to consider homosexuals as spouses, while he wants to consider them deviant. However, I maintain that declaring two people married is not in itself against the NAP; something like this would happen even in a free society, where the two would not be declared husband and wife by the state, but by other free market institutions. The author could then continue to consider such a couple as deviant, which he can do even now. Of course, it would be best for the state not to interfere with the marriage at all; I agree with the separation (not only) of marriage from the state. But until that happens, I am a supporter of the greatest possible freedom and the least regulation in this area. Let same-sex couples get married, too; and not just couples.

Regulation of damages from regulations

Many state interventions cause so many problems that they "must" be solved by... the state; as? Naive readers, who might have already thought that by interfering with what causes them, I have to mislead them - they are "solved" by exactly what caused them, i.e. additional regulations. A typical example is the socialist healthcare system and the health tax (called health insurance), as a result of which there are further regulations in the name of the health of the population and the reduction of spending on their treatment. In order to maintain the second (linked) regulation, the existence of the first is usually argued; I am not surprised by the statists, but sometimes even libertarians fall into such a logical paradoxical trap, since they would be in favor of abolishing both, but as long as the first exists, they support the second. Examples: "The state is taking free market funds from us to solve the migration crisis, so entry into the country needs to be regulated." "Vaccination must be compulsory until health insurance is voluntary."
However, this reasoning is the road to hell for a libertarian; regulation that can be repealed without causing problems for anyone that would not have happened without the existence of other government interventions to look at. Example: Opening borders is a problem because of social benefits; the abolition of social benefits is a problem because of the labor code (people will have trouble finding work); repeal of the Labor Code is a problem due to obstacles in business (employees have worse conditions for starting a business when their employer does not suit them); removing barriers to doing business is a problem due to tax evasion; tax evasion is a problem because of pensions and so on. If we recognize any of those problems as serious enough not to disturb the regulation, taking into account the interpersonal incomparability of utility, then we cannot argue against anyone who declares any other to be serious; the only way, in my opinion, is always to deregulate.

Protection money

Let me quote something written by OC a long time ago - an anarcho-capitalist whom I respect very much, because he has inspired me in what I do for more than ten years; this is a (fictitious) letter you get after you move into a new house:
Dear Neighbor,
I welcome you to our quiet and pleasant neighborhood. Of course, I take care of her peace of mind, and it costs me a lot; therefore, it is only fair that these costs be spread over the other neighbors as well. Today is Monday; if you do not send CZK 50,000 to my account by Friday, I am afraid that my representative will personally come to you at the beginning of next week for CZK 100,000. If you throw him out of the door, he will come again and with him a group of armed men who will kill you if you are not spared and if you do not pay. If, against all odds, you should kill them or drive them away, the next day a group twice as large and better armed will arrive.
Everyone else on your street is happy to pay their annual fee, on time and properly; I hope that you will not become the disturber of our peaceful and friendly coexistence.
Your M.V., v.r.
Pretty crap huh? And if I told you that M.V. is the Minister of the Interior and that protection money is called taxes... would that change anything? If so, why? Feel free to write in the discussion xD

Free slavery

May I voluntarily sell or donate myself into slavery? There is no consensus on this issue among libertarians (neither famous authors nor in our community); and I with my answer: "Definitely yes!" I am adding to the side of those who are currently in the minority. However, I cannot answer otherwise; why? It would not be consistent with the non-aggression principle and basic libertarian principles. What does it mean that I am someone's slave? That I am his property, he owns me, he can give me orders and if I resist, he can even kill me. However, if we grant that people have the right to sell their organs (even if it costs them their lives), and also that they have the right to borrow things (both of which libertarians allow), then I can sell all my organs to anyone, and he can lend them to me for use as long as I obey his every command, or as long as he pleases; then I am his slave, he owns me and decides about me.
And whoever opposes this must question my right to sell my organs or the buyer's right to lend them to me; however, perhaps no libertarian will do that, so if he wants to be consistent, he must recognize the legitimacy of voluntary slavery. Despite this, some object, for example, that even if someone owns my body, he cannot directly control it, but this is not a condition of ownership; even animals can be owned and we cannot directly control their bodies either. The objection that the fact that I give up the possibility to act freely invalidates the contract at the moment of its conclusion also does not stand; if I sell or donate a heart to someone, I die, thus certainly giving up the ability to act freely in a much more definitive way, yet I would be hard-pressed to find a libertarian who would want to take away the ability to sell or donate a heart. So why couldn't I voluntarily become someone's slave? Whether we like it or not, this is a consistent consequence of the principle of non-aggression.

The Evolutionary Argument

People often ask me why, if anarcho-capitalism is so good, it hasn't won the "evolutionary battle" with states; I realize that his answer, "What is not, may be," seems rather silly at first glance, so please take a second look. Human society is still developing, that development will probably never end, and we can see from history that people believed a lot of nonsense and atrocities often took place in society, which seemed justifiable to everyone, but it only took a few (tens or hundreds) of years for everything to change; for example, slavery was here for many thousands of years and clearly won the "evolutionary battle" with societies without slaves, but then everything broke - the paradigm that had been valid since the beginning of the age collapsed and turned to dust in an instant. In order for this to happen, people fighting for the right cause must not have assumed that if slavery had been around for so long, it couldn't be that bad. But it was. It is. And always will be. Just like the states.
What a Wonderful World

Some time ago I received an interesting question in a discussion - someone asked me if, as a libertarian who sees taxes as theft and laws as aggression, the world seems terribly evil and bad to me; I would like to share my answer here. For I told him that certainly not, for I find the world an absolutely delightful and fascinating place; yes, of course we don't have as much freedom as I would like and we see bloodthirsty robber states around us, but that's not all! We must not forget all those cooperating people who are already working together and creating values; we must not forget the enormous progress (ethical and technological) that drives humanity forward. And things (except for the occasional ups and downs) are looking up; slavery has practically disappeared, there are fewer wars, the standard of living (of the poor and the rich) is rising, for the first time in history more people are suffering from obesity than hunger... and while not everything is perfectly fine, the world is a wonderful place to live.
Medicines, drugs and double standards

I find the topic of "drugs" interesting, as it is surrounded by many myths that are released into the world, especially by states, to defend their "war on drugs"; I dealt with their destruction
in a word
i
in writing
and added i
something more subjective
. Although some drugs are undoubtedly a reliable tool for slow (and sometimes quite fast) suicide, the state (since school years through various anti-drug programs) gives us every illegal drug in this way (it portrays the legal ones in a completely different light); then many don't trust the government (which is fine) so much that they automatically believe the opposite of everything the state says to be true (that's already dangerous). Some people - coincidentally often those "natural" and suspicious of pharmaceutical companies - then underestimate the drugs; although they are skeptical, for example, of vaccinations and often of antibiotics, they are not afraid to experiment with completely untested drugs or methods of their use; please don't let the state manipulate us to either side!
Parallel with slavery

As some have astutely observed, I relatively often compare the institution of slavery to the state on many different occasions; I would like to write a few lines about that analogy. It is not directly about us being slaves to the state (I probably wouldn't even call it that), but rather about the majority of people's attitude towards those two institutions: Today, although almost everyone considers slavery to be bad, it wasn't like that a few hundred years ago; and it is very interesting to see how people then looked at those who began to come up with ideas for its abolition. It was downright impossible. It would spell economic disaster. Slaves would not be able to take care of themselves. It was a beautiful theory, but unusable in practice. These were extremist and radical ideas. The idea that a slave could disobey a master was about as absurd as the idea that a citizen could disobey a policeman on duty. But the change came extremely quickly...

Security above all...

Those concerned are simply indoctrinated by state propaganda; it was explained to them that we need the state and that's just the way it is. Therefore, when we try to convince someone that the state is immoral, we do not start from scratch, but from the conviction of the person concerned that we are definitely wrong; what about that
