Who writes history?

Although I am not a historian and do not know anything about the academic sphere in this field, I would like to convey to you, dear readers, the assumptions of two historians that I found very interesting in my conversations with them; both argued that research grants are handed out by people who already have some idea of what happened in the past, while they don't want to fund research that is about something vastly different from their version. In my opinion, this may not be a conspiracy at all (I don't really like you, by the way, as a big fan of Hanlon's razor), it makes sense anyway - those people simply consider funding something they don't believe in to be a waste of money; however, the consequence of this – quite logical – approach is the severe complication of the possibility of correcting major errors in the current perception of history. If this happens, the reason is not malicious intent, but socialist subsidization of historical research; the solution would then be – similarly to many other places –
free market financing
.
Without the state, it would disappear!

When I talk about a stateless society, I often encounter objections that something (anything) would disappear without a state, so we need a state; interestingly, the counterargument is quite universal regardless of what it is specifically about. The absolutely fundamental question is: Does the given thing bring more benefit to people than how much benefit would be brought to them by the resources that the thing consumes? If the answer is in the affirmative, then the objection falls; people would buy it even without the state (either independently, or they would agree to it, but they would definitely give up the necessary resources, because the resulting product is more valuable to them). If the answer is no, then the thing should not exist and the state should not artificially keep it alive; why? Simply because people can use the necessary resources in a different way to bring them even more benefit; and since we live in a world of limited resources, we should not waste them.
Two interviews

If I wait somewhere, I read; that's why I don't even mind waiting. However, a few days ago I found myself in a situation where I had to wait and had nothing to read, so I just sat and thought; however, I was distracted from this by two conversations I witnessed. The actors of the first of them could be the owner or director of a company and probably his salesman; they were frantically figuring out what to do to make customers feel good and want to come back. The second interview was probably conducted by two nurses; they collectively cursed at how someone could afford to come without an appointment and shared tricks on how to "punish" the person in question (make him wait longer than necessary so that he doesn't allow himself to do this anymore). Can you see the difference? While some fight for customers, others harass; why? Well, the clients bring resources to one, while they drain them from the other; do the nurses think about it like this? Most likely not; and they probably don't even realize it.
Hatred of capitalism

Capitalism is hated by a lot of people (as is anarchy, but let's ignore that for now); why actually? But I think we should not ask "why" but "what"; what do these people really hate? Typically one of the following two things: Either the "wild capitalism" of the nineteenth century (compared to today) or contemporary (state-linked) corporations; hating nineteenth-century capitalism because people lived in worse conditions than today (though better than before) makes about as much sense as reviling the invention of the steam engine because today we have more powerful machines, while calling state-linked and over-regulated corporations (which sometimes make laws through lobbies and limit competition) capitalist shows a severe misunderstanding of the term. Capitalism means free markets and voluntary exchanges, not lobbying and bribing MPs; and it's up to us to explain it to people.
Respect for authority

Many often complain that "today's youth" (of course worse than the former - like everyone) has no respect for authority, which they would often like to solve with war, or at least strict discipline in school; but what will the youth learn by these means? To grovel before an authority that these people did not choose for themselves; how can such a thing even be considered a virtue by anyone? Respect and healthy humility are of course very desirable, however, they must come from within the person concerned - he himself chooses who deserves his respect, who is worth following; but if we impose on him whom he must obey, we only make him a puppet, dull his will, and teach him to "shut up and walk." Do you notice how often this can be encountered in, for example, schools? And no wonder; it is of course useful for the state to educate obedient citizens - the teacher can then easily be replaced by a policeman, official or politician. Do you really want this for your children?
Dead horses and their poo

Over a hundred years ago, someone in New York realized that there were too many horses; he found out how fast these horses were multiplying and approximated further developments: Sometime in the second half of the twentieth century, people in New York will be wading through a meter-long layer of horse excrement, not to mention a flood of dead horse bodies. Does this seem absurd to you? Well, yes to me; on the one hand, the author somehow forgot about cars (not that they existed in his time), but above all, that even without cars, people would have solved the given problem far before they had to wade through feces on the streets. How is it that when it comes to horses, everyone sees how absurd it is to think like this, but when someone comes up with sustainable development based on equally absurd assumptions, they take it seriously? At the same time, all models of sustainable development are based on just such predictions and the assumption that people will not react to emerging problems...

Key Libertarian Moments

I have spoken to many hundreds of libertarians in my lifetime; when it came to what led them to this way of thinking, there are usually some specific turning points that those concerned are typically very clearly aware of and remember - in my life, the biggest libertarian "aha-moments" were two (one related to the fire department, the other to the law) and a few other fairly fundamental ones. A beautiful moment was described to me by Dominik Stroukal, who was convinced by Murray Newton Rothbard and his commentary on the selling and buying of children; In short: The transaction is good for the seller, the buyer, but most importantly for the child! And what convinced you, dear readers? Please confide in the comments; I'm not just asking this, I'm trying to find the best arguments. I would like to find a strong common denominator in as many stories as possible; I then want to apply it to my rhetoric.
Let's blame Nemakachenka!

A lazy person who doesn't want to work and just depends on the social system is a favorite target of hatred, especially of right-wing conservatives; why is that? At first glance, a quite understandable idea: "He who does not work, should not eat." (In connection with this text, I recommend especially right-wingers to google who notoriously used this phrase.) But why should everyone work? If someone is satisfied with poverty or beggary in exchange for a certain freedom and a huge amount of free time, that is after all his business and only his business; and if he begs for a living, it is nothing against anything at all. The moment the state comes to ask for alms, a problem arises; but who is its originator? A beggar who is just taking advantage of what he (the state) has been told is his "right" or one who is handing out money from someone else? Blaming the former makes about as much sense as blaming instead of the thief for stealing the one whom the thief gifted.

What is the sentence that makes an anarcho-capitalist angry with a left-wing socialist and a right-wing conservative?

Drug and gun regulation are, at first glance, relatively unrelated topics; and upon a little more detailed research, we find that typically the proponents of deregulation of one would like to regulate the other with all the more vigor. But why? Logically speaking, the argument for deregulation of both is almost identical in principle. Do you disagree? So come and talk to Terezka and me; then you'll probably disagree even more. However, you will definitely get the opportunity to passionately debate the given topics and try to convince others of your opinion; or maybe learn something new.
We look forward to seeing you in the evening
Bar Nebe
!
Heaven on Earth

People often complain about how the "common man" is doing badly and his situation is getting worse and worse, so the government needs to intervene; frankly, I can't think of any popular myth at the moment that would be further from the truth (at least in Europe or America). First, the "common man" has never been better off in history than he is now; we have enough (often surplus) drinking water, food, we live in houses where there is heat and light, we enjoy a huge number of achievements of the modern age. Second, the situation of the "common man" has probably never improved so rapidly; virtually every conceivable metric shows that we are getting better. Thirdly, never has so little labor been required of the average man to support himself; so we have clouds of free time (compared to perhaps all conceivable periods in the past). And finally, fourthly, this is happening precisely despite government interventions; they can only make our great situation worse.
Inability to reconsider opinions

Anarcho-capitalists are sometimes called fanatics, and very often statists suggest that they are unwilling to change their views and admit mistakes; I find such a statement interesting and somewhat paradoxical. After all, almost all of us were brought up to be statist; almost everyone originally believed in the state. Anarchists for some reason had to go through at least one fairly fundamental change of mind and admit a mistake during their lives; the statists could also, but did not necessarily have to. How then can statists accuse anarchists of the inability to reassess opinions and think critically, when they have already demonstrated this ability at least once in their lives? Of course, it is possible that anarchists can be wrong in their views on the world and statists can be right, but the chance that someone has been fanatically manipulated is higher precisely with statists, because they believe what was instilled in all of us in elementary school.
Private is more expensive than state!

There is a very popular belief across society that is largely undisputed – the private sector is more expensive than the public sector; yes, it is recognized as having a higher quality, but in terms of price, in the eyes of almost everyone, the state is cheaper. But why should it be so? In fact, there is no reason for this, the state is not able to create goods more cheaply than a private person; on the contrary, it is more expensive because, in addition to the goods themselves, you also have to pay for bureaucracy, officials, central management and the like. The difference is that the payments are hidden, and while we see the full amount of the money we pay to a private company, with state services the taxes are separate (and moreover divided into many components, so that the state takes about two-thirds of what we earn); but above all, we are manipulated by similar myths from an early age through the state education system, whose goal is to spread propaganda. That's why we don't believe in dogmas and always ask for reasons.
Belief in socialism

Again, it was not so long ago that many people generally believed that the economy had to be centrally controlled or we would starve, because something as important as food production and distribution could not be left to the free market, so both were arranged by the state - and it seemed that way; after the revolution, what many feared happened... and lo and behold, suddenly things started to work better. And to the "big surprise" the other sectors that were privatized did the same; however, many remained in state hands to allow their notorious problems to continue. In connection with this, two questions come to mind: How is it possible that even if everything that the state no longer cares about prospers better, so many people still object that it would be different for exactly what is still state-owned? And how can anyone believe that the state, which cannot provide even such a primitive thing as toilet paper on the counters, will take good care of, for example, education or healthcare?
Anarchists and other anarchists

There is a rivalry between anarcho-capitalists and anarcho-communists (and not only between these two schools of thought, but also many others related to them; I take those two as an example for others); the anarcho-capitalists accuse the anarcho-communists of inconsistency, while the anarcho-communists in turn accuse them of not being real anarchists. I have nothing against it in principle, but it strikes me how little both camps know about their opponents, towards whom they define themselves; in fact, most anarcho-capitalists draw their knowledge of anarcho-communists from other anarcho-capitalists who mock and caricature them (the exact same thing goes the other way around). It is always sad to see criticism of capitalism like: "Capitalism is when the state gives privileges to banks." On the other hand, it (the anarcho-capitalist critique of anarcho-communism) is no better; therefore, I recommend to all who want to criticize the anarcho-communists to go and talk to them directly first.
Fluid gender and sexual identity

Recently, we can hear more and more about people who are not sure of their "gender" identity. Now I don't mean "pure" transsexuals, they are already clear about their gender, it's just that this "clarity" doesn't match their physical bodies, which can be solved with surgery; I'm talking about people who simply don't know, they feel they are alternately female and male, or even beings of completely different genders. I respect their identity (although sometimes I get a little confused about what gender to call them - and I only know a few), I don't think it's any of my business; that is why I am surprised by the increasingly frequent cries of defenders of family values, where the world is going and that this threatens the traditional family. What? How about? I cannot imagine the state a family must be in, threatened by the existence of someone somewhere who is not clear whether they are a woman or a man; I think that pro-family warriors should mainly take care of their families and leave others alone.
Tax against work

Interestingly, excise taxes are often defended as reducing consumption; a tobacco tax reduces smoking, an alcohol tax reduces drinking, a fuel tax motivates people to save fuel (and nature) and so on. This logic makes sense, taxes can indeed influence people's behavior; not that it would be good, that's it
it always ends up hurting someone
, but it works. The question then is, what effect does the income tax have in this sense? By taxing work, we actually demotivate the payers of this tax to work; because they will receive a lower reward for their work. Combined with various unemployment benefits and support, this is actually quite an effective tool to discourage people from working. More or less the same can be said about the VAT; although it has a different name, it has more or less the same effect, only not on employees, but on entrepreneurs. And how much different do you think it is in the case of such levies for social and health "insurance"?
Muh... the road?

Many people consider it a serious problem of a free society that even the road network would be owned by private owners; why it would not be such a problem, I explain for example
in his series on anarcho-capitalism
. However, it is noteworthy that although questions like: "What if someone doesn't want to rent me their road in the city?" we often hear, almost no one asks: "What if someone doesn't want to rent me their apartment in the city?" How is that? Well, apartment rentals work more or less on a free market basis and there is no problem with them in principle; and yet there is no reason why road owners should behave any significantly differently from apartment owners - everyone just wants to make money, and very few people are interested in owning land and doing nothing with it (in which case they can always sell it). Yes, sometimes there is an uncooperative owner of the road, just as today we sometimes encounter an uncooperative apartment owner; however, most of them behave normally.

Ankap versus an ideal world?

Often in discussions about anarcho-capitalism, one gets into a situation where the statist comes up with an example of what bad could happen to someone, and asks how the market would solve the given situation; it can be non-payment of health insurance and dying of an illness, or a child being abused by parents, and so on. Most free market advocates then begin to respond to such objections in various ways (charity and so on); nothing against that, but I think the very first thing that should be said is that even the existence of the state will not prevent such cases - many people die as a result of bad medical care in the socialist healthcare system, many parents abuse their children despite the laws. No one claims that anarcho-capitalism means an ideal world where evil never occurs; into the defense of anarcho-capitalism not against the state, but against the ideal world, but we allow ourselves to be manipulated by every acceptance of the objection: "What if <unlikely situation>?"

, invited me to an afternoon chat with them. If you're nearby, come check it out at 5pm!
Get used to the teacher, accept the politician

About the direct indoctrination of children in state schools, which they are forced to attend as part of compulsory schooling, otherwise the state will kidnap them from their parents and expose them to propaganda anyway
he wrote
i
he said
enough; however, I would like to mention another aspect of this monstrosity: Since children are forced from an early age to accept violently imposed authorities in the form of teachers, they grow into people for whom this model of behavior becomes completely natural, so that they then automatically accept other authorities that they did not choose - the state, government and politicians. The danger of schools is therefore not only in direct indoctrination, but also in the fact that everyone accepts involuntary authorities as the norm and "necessary evil"; of course, this does not mean that authorities (in general) are bad - I consider only those that are forcibly imposed on a person to be harmful. I do not believe that part of "preparation for life" should be involuntary submission; voluntary acceptance of authority yes, but it cannot be forced.
Compulsory school attendance

Most people perceive compulsory schooling as something beneficial, without any deeper societal discussion about it; because it is one of those things that "everyone knows" and "it's obvious"... so "obvious" that the vast majority of people don't even realize (and are surprised when confronted with this fact, they often tap their foreheads and find it absurd) that in reality compulsory schooling (regardless of its possible benefits) means threatening parents from the state that they will either send their child to school, or they will simply be kidnapped by a social worker and
forced to complete that indoctrination by the school anyway
. And what do I mean by indoctrination? Well, for example, just how one-sidedly compulsory school attendance is presented in schools, its benefits are talked about, but the disgusting violence it represents is completely hushed up; the state through schools teaches children how to be "good citizens".
Such a thing is not a coincidence, it is not even a conspiracy, it is quite a public matter; you only have to look at the White Paper, the National Education Program, it is quite openly discussed there - teachers of all subjects are supposed to make good citizens out of their students. Imagine if there was any other organization besides the state that would do something like this - forcing your children to get their education under the threat of taking it away by force; what if some church made your children religious? What if McDonald's turned your kids into "good customers" and you couldn't say no? Would this situation be corrected by the fact that the children would also learn other things there? And if not, why tolerate something similar to the state? Sure, the state has the power to enforce it; having power and using it however
doesn't mean it's ethical or excusable
.
An anarchist revolution?

Anarchy is (mainly due to the attitudes of many left-wing anarchists, i.e. anarcho-communists or anarcho-syndicalists) in the eyes of most people associated with (violent) revolution; I personally believe, however, that at least anarcho-capitalism cannot be achieved simply and simply through revolutions. Why not? Well, even if a revolution were successful and an anarcho-capitalist took power over the state, he basically has two options for what he can do: He will give people real freedom; but people today want a state, so the first thing they will do with that freedom is to establish a state. The second possibility is that he forbids them to form a state, thereby becoming the state himself. People can be forced by force to build a better tomorrow of socialism, to gas Jews in the name of Nazism, or to vote in a democracy,
however, they cannot be forced to freedom
; they have to want it themselves first, but if the overwhelming majority of people already want it, there is no reason to make a revolution.
Which brings me to another seemingly unrelated favorite question, such a dilemma; sometimes someone asks me in a discussion if I had a button that I could use to cancel the state overnight, would I press it (mostly they allude to the fact that if the state disappeared out of nowhere, chaos and violence would probably ensue). But such a choice is, in my opinion, pointless; either people want the state, but when I cancel it with a button, they immediately start it again, or they don't want to, but then there's no need for buttons. It makes no sense to decide whether to "uninstall" the state immediately or not, because the state can only be removed as quickly as the people themselves want; so if we want to abolish it, let us convince and show the advantages of freedom! I don't even think that the people would then democratically "vouch" for freedom, but rather that if the majority does not recognize the state, it will disappear regardless of any elections (but of course, as society changes, it will be reflected in those elections as well).
Dull masses?

Quite a few people (and I was one of them years ago) feel that "average people" aren't smart or capable enough, can't take care of themselves, and are generally the "dumb herd"; each of the elitists who proclaim this, of course, considers himself above average (how else; after all, most people consider themselves above average). But where does the belief that "almost everyone is a self-righteous idiot" come from? In my opinion, this is due to the fact that we all have things in our lives that do not interest us, we do not orient ourselves in them, and we do not even have a great interest in them, because our priorities are elsewhere, from which it follows that we all appear to be idiots in at least something; however, with ourselves we understand the reasons, we understand and we apologize for it, while with others we do not, because we see their shortcomings in what we ourselves consider essential.
Perhaps every person is a complex individual who has his own weaknesses and strengths; he develops what he considers important and stagnates in what he is not very good at. And just because we constantly see many people around us behaving unwisely from our point of view, the "average person" does not have to be demented; on the one hand, in many other things, we will behave unwisely from their point of view, but above all, we typically do not know the entire context of their actions, so what may seem stupid to us may simply be the result of the people in question having different set priorities and something different to us being important to them (which, by the way, complicates our assessment of their qualities). I recommend to anyone who sees idiots around him to think about whether he himself can often appear exactly the same to those around him; I am not saying that people are "equal" and "equally good", but rather so much that it is not much to judge.
The path of peace

I can't count how many times in my many years of being a libertarian I've witnessed anarcho-capitalists calling minarchists scumbags, minarchists calling anarcho-capitalists fanatics, and anarchists of all stripes waging their never-ending war over who is a real anarchist and who is just playing; these are simply disputes in which the ad hominem argument does not go far. I personally always regret it, especially when I know from experience how easily such unnecessary conflicts can be avoided in the vast majority of cases simply by not wanting to argue and behaving in a friendly manner; the opposing party almost always agrees to such negotiations after a while (it is true, recently one ankom told me to take a conciliatory approach and to go to hell with the understanding game; however, this happens only rarely), seriously try it sometime: Look for common ground, try to understand the discussion opponent.
I'm not saying you have to agree, just don't treat the person you're debating with as an idiot just because they have a different opinion; rather, try to look for common points of contact, it happens much more often than it might seem. Then you might be surprised to discover all sorts of interesting things; for example that
anarcho-communism is not necessarily inconsistent
. Let's ask ourselves the basic question, what are we trying to do: Convince people, or let off steam and send someone to hell? In the second case, everyone can handle it on their own, but I would like to remind you that by provoking an argument, you will drive your opponent into an emotional state in which he will not be willing to accept the opinions of others, which is counterproductive; not to mention that even from the point of view of those watching the debate, a civilized discussion looks better than demented bickering. I understand it's hard sometimes; however, I highly recommend it from my own experience.
Terezka in Brno!

Teresa
accepted the invitation of the Fola initiative and goes to give a lecture at the Brno company Živo u Palečka. The topic will be drugs, their regulation, decriminalization and the potential for use in medicine and not only there.
Come listen to it, discuss it, agree or disagree; there are no limits to differing opinions in debates.
So arrive at the company today at 6:30 p.m
Live at Palečko
.
Detection of indoctrination

On your own
the first lecture in Polis
I expressed an idea that many later returned to in conversations with me, as they considered it essential; that's why I'm going to write about her today. Being exposed to propaganda tends to result in indoctrination that partially blocks our critical thinking; we then approach things in such a way that we "know" everything in advance, we do not look for arguments and information with the aim of finding out the truth, but only to confirm our opinion. The bad news is that it's not just about statists and state propaganda, but even after seeing through, one can fall into the same trap on the opposite (or any other) side; I personally found myself operating this way a few years ago when thinking about anarcho-capitalism: I "knew" in advance where the truth was, and stopped approaching the arguments of opponents as something that could convince me. The good news is that in order to correct the situation, it is enough to realize and fully admit it, and the attitude itself will change.
How to detect such a state of mind? I'm afraid that everyone has such darkened corners; it has always fascinated me, I am actively working to uncover them and I believe it is a never-ending process. I consider the simplest method of detection to be our reaction to a thought which we encounter for the first time; if it is complex and we have never thought about it, we cannot quickly decide whether it is nonsense. If we know immediately that something "is completely absurd" and look for arguments in retrospect, we can be sure that we have been indoctrinated in this direction; as an example I like to use the analogy of a soldier who kills on the orders of a superior and an employee who kills on the orders of a boss... almost everyone immediately "knows" that this is an absurd comparison; only then are they looking for reasons why actually. It's not about whether the simile fits at all, but about the process: "I know what it's like right away; only then do I go looking for an argument." Maybe I will write about other detection methods sometime next time.
Child labor

Child labor is now considered a bad thing in our latitudes and civilization; and it's no wonder, because in such a rich society it doesn't make sense for children to work - firstly, they can get a much better job later thanks to their studies, and secondly, there is a huge difference between the value of skilled and unskilled work. In other times or parts of the world (in a poorer society), however, this unfortunately does not apply; children work simply so that the family can survive at all - not only does the family not have the resources to study them, but often not even to feed them. How to change such a situation? Only in such a way that the given society becomes rich; and certainly not by imposing a ban on child labor on them. Working in insane conditions sixteen hours a day is appalling; however, other options (starvation, for example) are even worse - if they weren't, they'd use them. However, by banning, we will force them to do exactly that - to choose the worse option.
Individualism does not lie in isolation

Libertarians are individualists by nature; however, many people understand the term a little differently than they do, because they assume that it is about isolating yourself from others, and you can often come across that someone contrasts individualism with cooperation, cooperation in a community of people. I don't want to argue here about which meaning of the word individualism is "correct", because I consider it irrelevant - after all, what's in a name? What they call a rose, even if called otherwise, would smell the same. However, I would like to point out that anyone who criticizes libertarians as those who reject cooperation has not understood the following fundamental difference: Voluntary cooperation is one thing, which is one of the basic ideas of the Austrian school of economics, by the way, but coercion is something completely different; no libertarian rejects peaceful cooperation, on the contrary, they all strongly condemn its coercion from a position of strength.
Excuse by authority

If a police officer does a prank (say, harassing citizens) within the limits of the law (or even required by law), a huge number of people tend to excuse it by saying, "He had to do it, he was just doing his job." I reject such an argument; partly because the guards in the concentration camp were "just doing their job", but above all because each of us is personally responsible for our actions. It's remarkable how everyone understands this in the private sector (everyone recognizes that it's absurd to excuse a murder, for example, by saying that the killer was ordered to do it by the boss), but so many people turn a blind eye to the same when it comes to the state (almost everyone excuses the murders of soldiers by saying that they were just following orders); why is that? Well, the state simply has better PR; propaganda takes place on all fronts, the youngest are already indoctrinated as part of compulsory schooling. When you excuse someone for "just doing their job," ask yourself if you would excuse them in the private sector.
whine about "today's"

The grass was greener and the girls more beautiful; we hear complaints all the time about "these days" and it's popular to exclaim how screwed up everything is. At the same time, we live in wonderful times, we are having a good time, never have so many people lived in prosperity; in the USA and Europe we are drowning in abundance, never before have so few hours of work been enough to provide a person with the basic necessities of life, never before have people also had so much free time. Even in the rest of the world, which is worse off than we are, people are getting richer like never before; there are more obese people than starving people in the world. So why the constant whining about bad times? The reasons are clouds; however, this one caught my attention: Imagine five amazing things that could happen to you within an hour of finishing reading this text; do you have Good; now think of five bad things. Wasn't the second one easier? To me, both are the same; however, the vast majority of people come up with bad things much faster. Why actually? Answer in the comments.
Urza in deCentral: Economic calculation

The topic of the past
lectures on anarcho-capitalism at the (de)Centrála club
there were abortions, euthanasia, vaccinations and other issues related to the right to make decisions about one's own life; and my wife Tereza gave a lecture.
Today we will talk about economic calculation; unfortunately, it is extremely neglected in today's world, most people do not know this issue at all, and a significant part of libertarians do know it, but they cannot explain it very well.
You are also all invited to the next lecture, which will also be on the first Wednesday of the month, i.e. June 5; the topic will probably be the property rights constitution I created for Liberland.
I'm looking forward to seeing you tonight at 7 p.m
of the (de)Central club
.
Voluntariness

When anarcho-capitalists define themselves against the state running or funding something, they very often face accusations that they are against the thing itself (for example, when they do not want the state to fund art, statists say they are against art as such); unfortunately, this is not always a targeted argumentative fallacy, as the person concerned very often does not really see the difference between "not wanting people to be forced to do something" and "not wanting that something". Still, voluntariness is one of the most important aspects of anything; there is about as much difference between a theater financed by admission and other voluntary sources and a theater paid for by the state as between two people making love, expressing their sincere love, and rape. This, of course, varies enormously morally, which is far from everything; even from a utilitarian point of view, coercion is a big problem.
Why? Because of
the impossibility of economic calculation
; anything that is voluntarily funded has the property that when it starts to consume so many resources that people would benefit more from them than from the resulting thing itself, it starts to generate a loss and something needs to be done about it (changed, canceled...), while when something is run by the state, there is no way to know if it is a god-awful waste of resources. By waste, people often refer to a situation where, for example, the state buys something expensive that can be obtained more cheaply; this is undoubtedly true, but the far more fundamental question is whether the state should buy this "something" at all! How do we find out what it brings
more benefit than the resources needed to do so
? Well, very simply; we'll let people decide whether to voluntarily purchase it or not. What are you?
will not buy voluntarily
, it obviously won't do them any more good than the resources they have to spend on it; and what will bring them more benefit, they will buy. Laissez-faire!
Night at Hollar: Limits of Anarchy

Lectures, discussions, screenings and, of course, unique parties. Already on Friday, April 26, another Night on Hollar will take place, this year with the subtitle Limits of Anarchy.
The present combines a fusion of endless possibilities and ever-present barriers, which naturally creates chaos in which each of us must find our own order. This year's edition of Noci na Hollar will go along the imaginary edge on the border between existing society and anarchy, in order to grasp at least some of the limits determining our view of reality.
The whole event will last from 16:30 until midnight; the conversation with me will last 90 minutes and starts at 5 p.m.
I'm looking forward to Na Hollar this afternoon!
Everything cannot be converted into money

The objection that everything cannot be converted into money is a relatively logical response to the efforts of some people to ignore the non-monetary benefit of various goods and consider only their financial benefit or price/performance ratio; on the contrary, however, it is not at all a logical answer to
conclusions of the Austrian school of economics
, which also sometimes converts a lot of things into money, but never without including a non-monetary benefit, taking into account all the subjectivity of value for each individual. So how does the Austrian school of economics convert goods into money? Well, the price of anything is equal to the higher of the following two values: The first is the highest offer, how much someone is willing to pay for that property, the second is the lowest offer, for which the owner of the property is willing to sell it; it naturally follows, among other things, that there can be (and are) things whose price expressed in money is infinite, but which are only those that someone owns and does not sell.
Therefore, if someone owns something that he is simply not willing to sell under any circumstances, it is not exchangeable for money at that moment; on the other hand, all other things that someone is willing to trade with can be "recalculated" to money, and this in a very meaningful way: The price of the property is the highest offer from possible buyers, or the lowest offer for which the owner will sell (the higher of the two values). This is an open market price and absolutely everything is included - artistic value, emotional value, commemorative value, charitable value, just everything; how is that possible Well, when someone sells or buys something, he includes in the price his knowledge, emotions, humanity, intuition and everything he is capable of; and precisely for that reason, it makes no sense to argue against a free market economy by saying that "some things cannot be converted into money" - people acting on the market "convert" into money exactly what and only what can be, and that includes all non-financial aspects.
Human preferences

Surely you know a lot of people who, on the one hand, agree with the restriction of freight traffic in the city, but at the same time they are bothered by paying more for goods (the price of which will increase as a result of such restrictions), or they sign a petition against the construction of a mall or a parking lot instead of a park, but then they shop or park there more than they ever went to the park, or they go to protest against factories that pollute the environment, but then they still buy and use their products a lot; they do so because many times they are not aware of the connections themselves, which is perfectly fine, no one can know everything. But what does that mean? That asking people their preferences (or letting them democratically vote on them) doesn't produce results that correspond to reality; their true preferences cannot be ascertained except by letting them act in a free market—
only by actions, not by words, does a person demonstrate what really benefits him
.
Ice creams

It has been a few decades since many people made a living as ice cream workers; they mined ice and sold it to people to keep their food cold. Then came the fridge; and thanks to profit-seeking capitalists, it soon became available to almost everyone in both Europe and the US, millions of refrigerators flooded households en masse. But... the icemen were losing their jobs in droves; today there is quite possibly not one in the whole world. And with elevator operators, for example, it's not much better; how many people lost their jobs because of automatic elevators? So I could go on. But would it make sense to "protect jobs" in those cases? No! It is only good that the ice-makers have been replaced, their work has lost its meaning, and people can refrigerate food better; those in question then went to do other things instead of the ice business, contributing to society. In retrospect, almost everyone understands that this is right; but why do so few people understand the same when it comes to the present?
Advertisement

Many of us see advertising as a necessary evil, some even want to limit or ban it, saying that the world would be a better place without it, and they don't like that ultimately the customer pays for advertising; so why not outlaw advertising? Even leaving aside the moral reasons, advertising has, among other things, an informational benefit for all who are exposed to it; after all, how else would we orient ourselves in the abundant supply of goods offered to us by capitalist entrepreneurs? Even just the message on the product packaging, or any information about the product anywhere, is a form of advertising. So we are only talking about measure; but how to determine the right one? Well, let companies compete in the free market; whoever advertises too much will also spend too much, thereby losing their competitiveness; the very fact that advertising costs are reflected in the final price of goods is the reason for reducing its quantity.
Street lighting

Sometimes we can come across the claim of statists that without the state and public budgets we wouldn't even have street lights; the truth is that where people would depend on it, there would be public lighting, but not elsewhere. But is it wrong? No; just the opposite. Where people purchase public lighting voluntarily,
they obviously benefit more from it
, than if they used the resources needed to build it differently; on the contrary, where they don't opt for it, they make it clear that they have a better use for those resources (otherwise they would voluntarily build lighting), so it's better for them not to have it there (and have something else instead). This is where the popular argument about black riders often comes in - people will be less motivated to pay when they know they can "ride" on others paying for them; this is really true, it is very difficult to exclude someone from the consumption of public lighting.
But is this a reason to forcibly extract resources? If it were, one can defend the forced selection of resources for anything just because there is black passengering, or some other objective (physical and given by the nature of the world) reason why the given thing is made more expensive by some externality. Non-excludability from consumption is a property of a given good that makes it more expensive – just as a swamp on a plot of land increases the price of building in that place, black passenger traffic increases (for payers) the price of public lighting; yes, if the conditions were different (the land was dry or black passenger traffic was more solvable), the goods in question would be cheaper, but that (in no case) is not a reason to forcibly force people to pay for it if they are not voluntarily interested - that good will still bring less benefit than what the resources they paid for it would bring to people (if it wasn't the case, they will pay voluntarily).
Regulation to protect the weak

Regulations are mostly defended on the grounds that the state protects the weak; for now, let's leave aside whether the forceful enforcement of such protection is morally justifiable and look at its concrete effects on small, large and huge firms. A large company has its accounting and legal departments, which can deal with the new regulations as needed and adjust the processes in the company so that they comply with the regulations. Huge companies (in addition to the above) often have lobbyists and other means with which they can influence legislators and block seriously unpleasant, expensive or threatening regulations. However, small companies do not have any of the above options, and any regulation of their business can be potentially liquidating or very painful for them. This protection of some weak ones ultimately only endangers other weak ones, and often very fundamentally; please let's not forget that.

The industrial revolution

As such, the Industrial Revolution is rightly considered a very progressive period in human history; however, I see a remarkable contradiction in how the "wild capitalism" of that time is perceived. So before we condemn capitalism, please consider the context.

Drivers; why?

Totally
the first text in Stoké
(i.e. except
the welcoming one
) dealt with the meaning of driver's licenses (or state licenses to drive motor vehicles); I present in it several arguments why this is nothing more than useless bullshit. Yet their existence is considered self-evident, right, justified and meaningful by almost everyone; therefore, I would like to point out here again the main reason why, in my opinion, they are absolutely useless: In theory, they are supposed to prevent people who can't drive from endangering others on the roads; but if someone is so irresponsible as to get into a car and drive off into traffic without having acquired even the minimum set of skills that can be learned in a driving school, and is willing to risk property, health and human life (including his own) to do so, how could the threat of a police check, a possible fine or a driving ban (not that he is allowed to do so now) deter such a person?
Democrats-liberals, libertarians, Republicans-conservatives

Dividing the political spectrum into left and right is relatively problematic, as these concepts are already incredibly desecrated, media-twisted and unclear; in the Czech Republic, it is basically the case that wherever a political party places itself, that is where the media presents it (completely regardless of the program and possible activities in the parliament). In the USA, the situation is a bit clearer, there are traditionally two fundamental political camps: Democrats (let's say leftists) and Republicans (let's say rightists); while Democrats defend personal freedoms and suppress economic freedoms, Republicans do exactly the opposite. For some reason, most libertarians tend to identify with Republicans (given the choice); and I ask the plenary a question for discussion: "Why?" I personally find the libertarian philosophy equally close to and far from both camps (we promote personal and economic freedoms); however, why do so many libertarians see it differently? Thanks for the answers.
There is no "insurance" like insurance

What is insurance? A voluntary contract between an insurer and an insured, which typically obligates the insured to pay relatively small fees to the insurer, who will pay the insured a relatively large amount of money in the event of a loss event defined by the contract; it is essentially a high-odds bet on an unlikely event that the insurer takes because it sets a favorable rate, while from the insured's point of view it is essentially a service fee. A tax is something completely different - by its very nature it is not voluntary, people are forced to pay it under the threat of violence (from the state), it is something like an extortion (but taxes have better PR); moreover, the amount of taxes is typically not related to what services and to what extent the payer receives them, but is determined in some other way (very often it depends, for example, on his income, or on how much he spends, etc.).
And then we have such things as health "insurance", or social "insurance"; what is remarkable about them is that they have very little in common with insurance, in fact only the name, however they are not voluntary and the amount of the "insurance premium" does not depend on the risks, the probability of a harmful event, or the amount of the insurer's payment (if it occurs). These payments have all the characteristics of a tax, while practically none of the characteristics of insurance (in particular, for example, social "insurance" is paid more by the insured and the rich, who are logically less likely to use it, and vice versa); however, because it would not sound good that we are taxed at approximately sixty to seventy percent, the state is trying to create an illusion in the citizens that this is not actually the case, if it calls rather large taxes by another name, but Shakespeare rightly noted that: "What by name? What roses are called, even called otherwise, would smell the same."
Rational ignorance

Very often we can hear from critics of the free market economy about alleged market failures caused by information asymmetry, or by the fact that someone does not know something, for example due to a lack of education, so that he is then unable to make a qualified decision; therefore, according to those concerned, a state is needed to correct the situation. Now let's leave aside that it doesn't fix and at best just consumes a lot of resources for nothing (at worst it damages); I would like to focus here on the alleged "market failure", which in my opinion is not really a market failure at all. It is important to realize that information and education are not free goods, as it is necessary to spend a minimum of time (and typically a little more) to acquire them; when someone does not have information, we often only see the disadvantages of that state, but we forget that the person saved resources that he did not have to spend to get it.
Basically, before we get some information, we can't know for sure whether the effort we spent to get it paid off or not, because we don't know it at that moment; there is nothing left for anyone but to try to guess using their own experience, since we do not have a crystal ball for predicting the future. And because people are different and our experiences (and personalities) are different, some simply prefer information over other things (like free time), others don't; however, this is definitely not a market failure, everyone simply chooses what they think is best for themselves. And calling information asymmetry a market failure is like saying the market failed when I missed the bus while the daily jogger caught it - we both chose what we think is best for us, which gives us different advantages and disadvantages in different life situations; and if we are not satisfied with it, we can change our lives.
Trade balance

A "positive" trade balance means that the price of goods exported from a country exceeds the price of goods imported; the opposite is called a "negative" trade balance. It is fixed in the consciousness of the people that we should strive for the first of the above states; but is it really desirable? A "positive" balance of trade means that goods are leaving the country whose market price is higher than that coming in; it is the opposite with money, however, if the country keeps a "positive" trade balance all the time, the money will only be devalued by inflation, because it will never be spent, because then the goods flowing into the country would have to have a higher value than what is leaving it. It can be compared to when you earn, you save, but you never spend the money, you just dissolve it in inflation; this analogy, by the way, explains why it makes no sense to argue that a "positive" trade balance creates jobs (yes, it does, but the goal is not work, but its products).
So is it appropriate to strive for a long-term "negative" trade balance? Well, that's a futile effort in the first place; it would be great if others were constantly giving us things with a greater market value than we are giving them, but this state of affairs is not sustainable. So what is desirable? After all, laissez-faire: The greater the interest in, for example, Czech goods in the world, the stronger the koruna will be, which will naturally increase the price of those goods, ergo the interest in them will decrease; on the contrary, little interest in Czech goods in the world will cause a weak koruna and low exchange rates, as a result of which the price of the goods will fall, which will again increase interest in them. We can keep track of the trade balance for the sake of interest (of course it is not desirable if it involves bugging businessmen by customs or the statistical office), but it is foolish to think that some official or economist can decide whether it is "correct" for it to be "positive" or "negative"; that's something that
only the market can
.

Guns are bad, huh?

Have you ever noticed how the majority of people who have never come into contact with firearms, have no particular interest in them, and don't even have anyone around them who owns any firearms and makes no secret of it? Based on many years of personal observation, I have to state that their relationship to firearms is typically very negative, although if they become more interested in the issue, or if they have a passionate shooter around them, their opinions usually change significantly; after all, it is not surprising when we consider that firearms are in principle the same as, for example, knives or sticks, only far more effective, but in principle they are tools like any other. And when it comes to the ability to easily and quickly kill as many people as possible, explosives, which are not so much a problem to make at home, will do just as well for a similar purpose; however, the vast majority of people simply do not desire such a thing.
So how is it possible that people who are not interested in the issue are so often a priori more or less biased against guns? I see no other explanation here than
omnipresent state propaganda, which tries to impress people from childhood
present firearms as something inappropriate or hostile to be wary of, and anti-gun activism as something noble; why does the state have this interest? Well, because an unarmed citizen is easier to control even in extreme situations; we can also notice that precisely for that reason, the same weapons in the hands of the police and the army are not presented and perceived negatively. Not to mention that the fewer people who own a gun, the less resistance there will be to constant (especially European, but not only) regulations, which unfortunately affect the shooter more and more; and we have one of the best gun laws in the world in terms of freedom. Hopefully it stays that way.
Transparency

A transparent environment around public funds is something that all politicians keep promising us, and many of them use it as a sort of fix-it-all charm; unfortunately, the voters (and especially the young and left-wing ones) very often believe them and often repeat it after them. However, transparency is not the solution to our problems for two reasons: First, we have public administration and the state in general is already so big that even with full transparency of all transactions, there will be such a large number of them that it will be impossible for anyone to control them (and if it happens, it means another sea of lost time and inefficiency); and secondly, apart from completely obvious and glaring cases, it is not clear even in a transparent environment what the state does in the interest of citizens and what it does not, because
directive (not market) controlled economy does not allow for economic calculation
. Therefore, transparency solves practically nothing in our situation; the only solution is shrinking the state.
Everyone subsidizes; we must too!

I often hear that "we" (apparently meaning the Czechs) have to subsidize "our" (probably Czech) farmers because other countries do it too, which gives them a competitive advantage; and related to this "logic", I wonder if the goal of agriculture is to have something to eat, or simply to have agriculture. What will happen if farmers subsidize all countries except the Czech Republic? Well, people in the Czech Republic will get the opportunity to buy goods that will be subsidized by taxpayers from foreign countries; and farmers? Well, some can compete with it (then there's no problem), others can't; but what does that mean? That these people obviously consume resources that people use for their business
they value more than the product these entrepreneurs supply them with
, ergo it is better for them to go do something else, or change their business in some way; we will not starve to death (if there was a threat, then these farmers would no doubt feed themselves).

Title business

"If the state didn't grant accreditation and didn't monitor who can issue degrees, everyone could set up a school in the free market and just sell diplomas," is a very common argument against
free market education
; and it also makes sense... that is, before you think about it for at least half a minute. Why is it possible to sell titles today? Well, simply because they have value in today's world; and who gives them here? State; precisely those accreditations, the "guarantee" of certain standards, state matriculation exams, but also the requirements for education for civil servants. If degrees are not given value by the state apparatus, the real value of a diploma will flow only from the reputation of the one who grants it; and if some entity starts selling diplomas just like that, it will devalue them, for which it will soon pay.
On the assumption that the state will not give any accreditations and each educational institution decides for itself under what conditions it will give its students which certificate, then employers will stop having requirements like "high school graduation" or "completed higher education", but will also start to be interested in which school the diploma comes from and what it actually means. It makes no sense to buy it from someone who will simply sell similar certificates, because everyone can immediately issue them to themselves, or come up with any title; in the free market, no one will prevent anyone from doing so, as a result of which the meaning of "having a degree" will be lost, but it will only matter who awarded it (and to prevent counterfeiting, each educational institution can, for example, provide a web interface where you can verify who actually graduated and how). So the argument about selling titles on the open market is absolute nonsense.
Nature and tradition

In this text I would like to deal with two very similar and quite often used arguments, which I find both absolutely equally stupid and meaningless; we can meet them mainly in debates about freedom, the state, homosexuality, pedophilia, but also interpersonal relations. According to the first, something is right because it is natural; the other tells us that something is right because generations of our ancestors have done it, so we should stick to it. Both sound reasonable at first glance, but upon closer reflection we find that neither makes sense. Of course, I'm not saying that if something is natural, or if the clouds have been doing it for generations before us, we shouldn't even consider whether it might not be a good idea - because very often it will be; on the other hand, I consider it a road to hell to accept such things thoughtlessly and use historical experience or nature as an argument.
Why? Well, it's natural, for example, that if we get an infection that our immune system can't deal with without antibiotics, we'll die; Should we therefore resign from medicine and die? Generations of our ancestors believed that the Earth was flat; should we take it for granted? No! Of course, there are many other cases in which what is natural, or proven by generations, really makes sense, but there are also quite a few where we simply invented a better way; for that reason the arguments of tradition and nature are worthless. They are roughly on the level of saying that if something is a means of transport, then it must necessarily be a car; it may or may not be true, ergo it cannot be rationally argued, it is simply necessary to come up with another defense of such a claim... and exactly the same applies to arguments based on nature or historical experience.
Bastiat on democracy, I on emotions

Claude Frédéric Bastiat declared almost two centuries ago: "Good God! What an effort it is to prove in political economy that two and two make four! And if you succeed, people will start shouting: "It is so obvious that it is boring." - And then they will proceed to vote as if you had not proved anything at all." Doesn't that remind us of something? Well, yes to me; but why does this keep happening over and over again? Because a huge number of people make decisions on the basis of emotions, and the rational basis for such decisions does not interest them at all, often even rather distracts them; how many times have you seen someone make a claim based on certain arguments that you later disproved and the person just went to find a new one to stand their ground? Alternatively, have you experienced someone defending their position with arguments that were mutually exclusive and conflicting?
This - perfectly normal - behavior says only one thing: None of the arguments such a person makes are the real reasons why he holds a certain point of view (if they were, their refutation would convince him); real reasons tend to be emotional. I have long lived under the belief that taking a stand based on emotion is inferior; in recent years my opinion has changed - i think it's ok (of course it's not ok to initiate violence based on it). But where am I going? Most people (and libertarians especially) dismiss and deride emotional reasons; then what is the result? Will it change anyone's thinking? No; the people in question somehow rationalize their positions and lie to everyone (especially themselves) that they have logical arguments, which does not help anything, on the contrary, it may seem meaningful to explain something logically to such a person, although it is impossible to succeed in this and another path must be chosen. Let's be careful of too quick judgments...
Efficient tax collection

Effective tax collection is the bane of many politicians, who, when they manage to collect more money in taxes than their competitors, tend to even brag about it; it is important to realize that this bragging is not equivalent to the joy of the owner of a private company from higher profits, because these mean (if the company is not connected to the state) voluntary payments from customers, ergo also quality work on the part of the service provider, which obviously satisfied the needs of its clients well. But when a politician levies higher taxes, it is not doing something for someone for which that person would give them their money, but simply forcing people to hand over even more resources to the state against their will, under threat of violence, without any increase in wealth in the process, on the contrary; bragging about such actions is then something like a robber bragging about how many people he has hurt and robbed.
One of the popular tricks to increase tax collection and still win the sympathy of a large part of the electorate is to raise taxes on the rich and big companies; even if we completely ignore the populism of such a move and the motivations of envious socialists who applaud such looting, this approach shows quite clearly that the goal of the state is nothing more than to grab as much as possible - more taxes from those from whom it expects to be milked a little more. So the next time you hear populist talk about progressive taxation and a more friendly tax system for small businesses and entrepreneurs, don't be fooled; it's not a favor from the state, but purely the fact that the tax burden is already so high that the taxpayers wouldn't have to bear it, so they need to be relieved a little so that they don't stop pouring completely (not that I don't agree with every tax cut, I'm just trying to show things in a wider context).
Sustainable development

Sustainable development is a doctrine that is very popular especially among young people, but not only among them, most consider it to be at least a good (though perhaps not very realistic) idea; for me personally this concept is nothing more than classic ill-conceived nonsense - these are very popular these days by the way (poses don't cost a lot of energy, thinking does). Our world is dynamic, society develops very quickly and technology even faster; sustainable development basically ignores this. Its advocates tell us that we should not use non-renewable resources because they are running out, but they ignore the technological development that, for example, a hundred years ago coal was the majority of consumption, today it is oil and no one knows what it will be in another hundred years; and development will absolutely logically reflect the shortcomings of the given time - the less oil is needed, the more its price will rise and the more the search for alternatives will pay off.
What if we mine everything, you ask? Well, those businessmen are not idiots who need a civil servant to guide them; the closer it gets to "extracting everything", the more society will lean towards renewable resources, because then it will also start to pay off financially (raw materials will be scarce and their price astronomical). Well, if that's what it's all about, why not switch to renewables now? Well, simply because it gets better the better the technology we have; therefore, it is not worth wasting resources on it now, when in tens or hundreds of years (it is hard to say when it will be necessary) the same result can be achieved with much less effort, or some completely different solution will appear that we cannot even imagine today (and in a market economy it will always be possible to make money from what is needed) - only an arrogant fool, a left-wing intellectual, a politician and the like feel that they can plan it better.
Worshipers of the state

"Absurd. For example, a loud football fan eats a football and insults educated hipsters in the humanities, but then they pay for a theater performance. And the same hipsters, for example, insult football fans as primitives and nags, and pay for the football matches. And the only thing they agree on is that it's reasonable and it simply wouldn't work otherwise, because we'd all shoot each other here. Oh yeah."
So sounds one very true and brilliantly worded
comment in Stoké
; and since I consider it to be of very high quality, I would hate for it to fit. Marek28 thus commented on state subsidies to support sports; and I would allow myself another thought.
For what reason do the two aforementioned groups agree on state interventions, instead of each voluntarily paying their own? In my opinion, simply because for both, a "good state" means that they can force their opponents to pay, while they will not pay them - let's look at the rhetoric of everyone who defends the state as such, but does not like where the funds are going right now ("The state is needed, but it should..."); they generally don't mind forcing someone to pay for something they don't want - they only mind when they're on the victim side, but they find the enslavement of others desirable. They don't say it in those words, but the meaning of their message is clear; What does this mean? They're either true ruthless thugs or they've been so massively hammered into their heads that it's okay to obfuscate the point; personally, I think the latter is the case for most people... so let's show them the truth.
Urza in the debate on the whistleblower protection bill

Communists yes, Nazis no?

Have you ever wondered why the Nazis are persecuted by the fools for every nonsense, uniformed monkeys search their apartments in the early hours of the morning, destroy their belongings and hurt them in the name of fighting a dangerous ideology, while the communists, who already profess more or less the same values (the only difference is which groups of people they want to persecute more and which less), are not only not banned, but even sit in parliament? The answer is quite simple: there are simply more Communists; and buzzing such a large group of people is not easy because they might resist. It is far better to find a similar ideology, which is professed by a few desperate people, whose social danger is currently minimal, because there are really few of them, however, it is all the easier to target them, show activity and pretend that we need monkeys in uniform because they protect us from them.
And what is the name of the principle on the basis of which the Nazi demented people were banned from their hobby, while the communist ones were not? Well, it is the right of the stronger; precisely the right of the stronger that many fear would prevail in anarchy. The catch, however, is that the law of the stronger still applies today, across various social institutions, the only difference being who is the "stronger"; somewhere among the bushmen it is the one with bigger muscles and a club, in capitalism the best or richest entrepreneur, in feudalism typically the one with better origins, in democracy it is the darling of the crowds with the most votes. Always and everywhere someone will be stronger and another weaker, with the former typically having more options (which of course can be at the expense of the latter, but it doesn't have to be); the question is how do we measure that "strength" - should the "strong" be the one who best satisfies the needs of the people or the biggest populist?
Vacation in the Protectorate

I recently watched on the Internet (albeit only sideways on the second monitor during other activities) the documentary historical reality show "Holiday in the Protectorate" (from 2014); the point of the show was that the selected family had to live for some time (weeks or months) in a simulated World War II environment (if anyone were to ask, I don't consider the series to be total shit, but I probably wouldn't recommend it to anyone more than as a soundtrack). The goal was to bring the viewer closer to how (terrible) life was back then; and although today we live in a wonderful time (in my opinion, probably the best in the entire history), I could not help but notice certain similarities, which the performers, most probably also the screenwriters, and I can imagine also the majority of the audience, completely missed, and therefore I would like to point them out.
One of the first horrors the family had to go through in their new environment was the censorship of textbooks, from which "unsuitable" authors and "dangerous" ideas had to disappear; one of the contestants even commented that it is something completely unimaginable nowadays. Really? Back then, Hitler simply banned Czech authors, today we ban Hitler. Another shock came when our family was hit with a twenty percent tax for the benefit of the Empire; people were justifiably indignant at how crazy this crap was, after filming was over, they were expected to return to normal life with a total tax burden of sixty to seventy percent. The icing on the cake was then a reminder of how Hitler seduced the poverty of the time into food speculators; this is also a big difference compared to today, where nobody accuses speculators of anything in such a populist way, right? Yes, we live a fairy tale these days; however, it still applies - beware of bullies.
Corruption, an eternal theme

Almost every political party has the fight against corruption in its agenda; why isn't it working? That the bad guys would always take over? Typically yes, but that's not the reason. Corruption is an inherent part of state power, because it stands and falls on the fact that its people have resources that are not theirs, but that the state has plundered from its subjects; such an environment creates the potential for corruption in itself by the existence of public funds. Every control body then runs into exactly the same problem, because it is itself corruptible; just by being tasked with fighting corruption, he has gained the power that gives him the incentive to allow himself to be corrupted. Is there any solution to this situation at all? Yes, sure; if the state does not have public means and resources, there is a complete lack of motivation to corrupt it. No control body, no politician with empty promises, simply no one will be able to stop corruption as long as there are public funds; when these disappear, the problem disappears with them.
Liberty Evening: An Introduction to Anarcho-Capitalism

Are you from Olomouc or the surrounding area? Come today at 6 pm to the Liberty Evening organized by Students for Liberty v
Bluesbar GARCH
.
Lucka Komárková and I will give a lecture about anarcho-capitalism there; the standard introduction will be followed by a debate where you can ask (and ideally counter) anything!
What causes poverty?

Sometimes we are faced with the following question: "What causes poverty?" But the answer – to the surprise of many – is that poverty is not caused by anything; it is a natural state. Men are by nature poor, and have nothing but what is freely around them; none of what we call wealth (or at least not poverty) is available in and of itself, all of these goods had to be produced by someone - and just because we're so covered in them at the moment, we feel like it's something everyone's entitled to (and many of us like to forget that in order to get something, someone has to produce it too). I do not think there is any point in asking what causes poverty, which is a natural state and is not caused by anything; for a far better question is, "What causes prosperity?"

lectures on anarcho-capitalism at the (de)Centrála club
was inequality.
