of the (de)Central club
.
Pretended time preferences of ecologists

The average Democratic politician's typical planning time horizon is about one term, so these parasites rule in a flood-after-us style; green eco-terrorists are no different from them in this, but as part of their media theme they pretend to have significantly lower time preferences when they explain to us that we should give up various goods in the present in order to help ourselves (or our descendants) in the distant future. Many people believe that the more you plan ahead, the better; but is it really so? It is not; for two main reasons. The first reason is that time preferences are a purely individual matter - some people prefer to feel better now and pay for it later, others the other way around; both of these approaches have their advantages and disadvantages, the assessment of which depends on each of us, and it is not possible to objectively decide which approach is "better".
The second reason, easily understandable for those who are not intimately familiar with the principles of the Austrian economic school, is the impossibility of predicting the future (and especially the distant future), which means that it is not excluded (in addition, it is sometimes very likely) that we will currently take some costly measures dictated to us by ecologists, so that in the end it turns out that it was completely unnecessary; for example, we will limit the production of materials that slowly decompose in nature, so that in a few (dozen) years we will find out that thanks to progress, we can not only decompose them, but also gain something from it. Of course, nothing like that may happen, but no one can know, we are all (even the most educated among us) left to the field of conjecture; therefore, everyone should make their own decisions without being forced by anyone (especially the government) to follow the ideas of eco-terrorists.
The fight against inequality

In the last many decades and especially years, the "fight against inequality", by which we typically mean wealth inequality, has grown enormously; for a moment, let's ignore how such a fight typically takes place, i.e. that the state takes by force from one to give something from the loot to someone else, embezzles a little and simply wastes a large part of the resources, and let's focus on what the fight is actually based on - it is a generally (and quite without thinking) accepted assumption that inequality is bad and we have to get rid of it. The first question is why inequality always automatically means wealth inequality; people are not equal in terms of mental and physical attributes, talents, talents, character traits, charisma, in fact inequality prevails in absolutely everything. So why artificially try to induce a kind of post-confidential equality in the aspect of wealth? Is it okay to turn the rich fool to the intelligent pauper? Isn't the other one already at an advantage?
However, I consider the question of why inequality is bad at all to be far more serious; almost everyone takes it as fact that there is no point in discussing it, but I refuse to accept it. Take, for example, complaints that workers in certain professions are poor because they have to toil many hours a day for little money; these complaints are only because there are other professions where this is not the case, but they completely ignore the fact that a few decades or hundreds of years ago most people worked in even worse conditions, which was acceptable then because many people were just as bad, whereas today it has become unacceptable only because it is no longer the standard and there is some demand for equality. However, can someone logically explain to me why a certain level of poverty is unacceptable not depending on its absolute level, but depending on how most people are doing at the time?
Cheap shunt

Someone recently asked me in a discussion how I, as a libertarian, would deal with the market failure of producers of all sorts of things driving their price down at the expense of quality, because customers hear low prices more than anything else; my answer was, understandably, that I would not solve it in any way, because it is not a market failure, but rather efficiency. If people prefer to buy cheap and low-quality products, it means that they prefer them to expensive, higher-quality ones; there can be many reasons: financial need, planning an upgrade (in the past, people bought washing machines or refrigerators for twenty years; today they don't, on the other hand, new products also offer new functions, designs, etc.), joy from more frequent purchases and product changes, preference for a larger number of low-quality items over a smaller number of higher-quality items, but also missing information (a customer may prefer a cheaper item because they do not know that the more expensive item will last much longer).
First, note that the market always responds to the wishes of consumers regardless of their reasons; this is only a good thing, because precisely thanks to market mechanisms, a change in consumer preference was revealed, which would be difficult for a central planner to estimate, since even people themselves often cannot formulate it (in fact, on the contrary - how many times do we hear begging for a low life span and how little praise is given to the benefits arising from it). Second - and this is very interesting - even a change in preferences due to lack of information is not a market failure, on the contrary! Even obtaining information costs something (at least time); and until we have the information, we typically can't know for sure whether it was useful to us, yet we have to decide whether or not to sacrifice time to get it. Therefore, those who buy uninformed are indeed in a worse situation from the point of view of purchase, but on the other hand, they have saved time that they could have used in other ways; is it worth it How to whom; so let's let everyone decide.
People are stupid, we have to protect them (from themselves)

You must have heard the phrase in the title of the article countless times; not necessarily expressed precisely in these words, but essentially hidden behind the rationale behind most regulations and laws. Now, let's ignore for a moment that the realization of such protection through the state is
immoral
a
effectively unfeasible
; suppose we have a tool that can seriously provide that protection. What will happen? The price people have to pay for making bad decisions will drop; as a result, the motivation to make good decisions also decreases (making good decisions takes time, effort, and sometimes education, which again requires time and effort; and above all, often requires responsibility). Quite logically, people become comfortable and become less responsible, but also more stupid (intelligence also needs to be developed and trained, an untrained brain stunts just like an untrained muscle); good, but they will be protected so it wouldn't be worth it after all, you think?
Um, let's look at the other implications; a society with more irresponsible and stupid people will need even more protection. And what happens when they get it? Of course, he will again become comfortable, lose some responsibility and cleverness, which will again lead to another need to mitigate the consequences of bad decisions; but what's worse? There will be more children raised by irresponsible parents, thus society will begin to degenerate in such a way that each succeeding generation will require a greater degree of protection from itself; and where will it all lead? To the absolutely stupid, uneducated and irresponsible dumb masses of people who can't even wipe their own asses; and we're still talking about conditions where there's a magical way to protect these people from themselves without it costing them anything. There's no such thing in the real world, unfortunately... or for goodness sake?
The most dangerous religion

Buddhism? Judaism? Christianity? Islam? Although people in the world have committed all kinds of atrocities in the name of many beliefs, none of the commonly known religions come even close to the most dangerous of all in the brutality and fanaticism of their believers; it is a religion that is responsible for the dead and sheep and fanatics clearly the most, theirs
indoctrination takes place all the time and in various places
, and it is extremely treacherous also because it is typically not even considered a religion, although it exhibits all its features – yes, you guessed it, it is statism. Like other religions, this too has its dogmas ("we need a state, otherwise we would kill each other"), which are practically not discussed and, above all, not critically thought about, sacred symbols (flag, anthem), priests (politicians), ceremonies (elections) and more holy wars have been and are still being fought in its name than in the name of anything else.
However, statism has one more peculiarity; it is the only religion which really has the characteristic (so often attributed to Islam of late) that it is aggressive by its very nature, and by principle requires violent propagation. How is that? Well, in all other religions, trends can arise (and do arise) that continue to recognize belief in God or some holy men, but do not demand the imposition of a given belief on others (we can argue about how significant this is a deviation from this or that holy book, but in practice it is a state that can be reached and achieved); however, in the absence of that element of coercion, statism simply ceases to be statism - whoever demands that the state have power only over those who voluntarily agree, essentially ceases to be a statist and begins to be a libertarian (in other words, actually the opposite of a statist, since he is de facto defined by imposing anything on others through the state).
Run the state like a business (and fuck the economic calculation)

Everyone has surely heard some smart guy expound on the wonderful idea of "running the state like a business"; and many even believe that libertarians must be on the hook for it. How did this idea come about? Well, the state has problems with inefficiency, private companies are often efficient, so why not try it? This is primarily because it is not possible - companies do not have any magic of efficiency, their clouds are absolutely inefficient; the whole "magic" lies in the fact that the ones that work poorly cannot make money on themselves, so they go bankrupt, ergo only the efficient ones stay afloat in the long run (and the moment they slow down, they are replaced by others on the free market). There is no such thing as "running a business" as there are a huge number of ways to run a business; and no one knows today what methods will be competitive tomorrow, but the market will mercilessly take them over, which is out of the question in the case of the state. Why?
Since the state collects funds for its functioning by force and provides services regardless of
there is no meaningful metric of state effectiveness
; and if someone "manages it like a company", it may mean a prosperous company, but far more likely a bankrupt company (which will never go bankrupt, because the losses will be paid by the taxpayers), while which of those possibilities occurred is in the stars, because it cannot be known even ex post (although it can be estimated). The entrepreneur is clear - as long as his company prospers in the free market, he manages it effectively, as soon as it stops prospering, it means the opposite; but what state? A politician starts to "run it like a business", but how do you know if it has helped and what is it good for compared to the previous state? You can look and guess by eye, or run a bunch of different statistics and look very scientific... but how do you evaluate the benefit? He doesn't even have units...
Collective guilt and scumbags

I have noticed that many people find it inconsistent the position of almost all anarcho-capitalists, who on the one hand vehemently reject collective guilt, but on the other hand are able to declare that the cops are pigs; why is this inconsistency only apparent? This is because collective guilt means blaming someone for what other members of the group to which the person belongs have committed; for example, to excuse Hiroshima and Nagasaki because of what happened before at Pearl Harbor is a typical example of collective guilt, because the specific people who attacked Pearl Harbor were overwhelmingly not the same people who massacred the atomic bombs a few years later, they just belonged to one nation. Of course, nation does not have to be the only criterion, it can be religious affiliation, skin color or other parameters; regardless of whether a person was born with them or acquired them during life, he is not responsible for the actions committed by someone else.
So is there an exception for uniformed monkeys? No. We also judge them only by their actions; but in order to be a policeman, a person has to do immoral things (starting with the fact that he signed up for the services of the largest criminal organization in the given territory as a rapist, ending with the fact that during his service he actually violates the principle of non-aggression every time he legitimizes someone, stops him in a car, etc.). Similarly, when I pass any judgments on murderers, robbers, thieves, or sexual predators, it is not for what other members of that group have committed, but for what each of them must have done to be included in such a group; it is actually a group defined by some action or behavior - and if we condemn this particular action, then it is not an application of collective guilt to condemn the whole group, since all its members committed exactly what we condemn. And it is precisely on this principle that the widespread condemnation of policemen as swine works.
Are we living in totality?

The vast majority of people will answer this question no, because we have a democracy; and with regard to the propaganda that the state pushes into us already during compulsory school attendance, such a naive answer is not surprising. First of all, let's clarify the difference between totalitarianism and dictatorship: One of those terms describes the extent of state power, while the other describes its concentration. Dictatorship means the concentration of power in the hands of an individual or a small political group without an opposition or other entity limiting that power; it doesn't matter how the rulers rule (mostly cruel and totalitarian, but not a requirement). Totality then describes a state where the state significantly intervenes in practically all aspects of the lives of its subjects; however, power in totality is not necessarily held by a single person or a small group. Totality often goes hand in hand with dictatorship, but both regimes can exist independently.
Democracy is indeed incompatible with dictatorship, because either the people or the monarch (or a select group) can have unlimited power, both cannot occur at the same time; however, the existence of a democratic system does not exclude totalitarianism, because even a democratic state can recklessly intervene in all sectors of the lives of its citizens. I am also personally convinced that the trend towards socialism (and as a result also towards totality) is
an inevitable inherent feature of every democracy
, in which the right to vote is not significantly restricted in any way; and the Czech Republic is a shining example of this - just look at the Civil Code or the Labor Code (and not only that). Whether you come to the conclusion that we live in totalitarianism or not, remember that although dictatorship is mutually exclusive with democracy, the same is not true of totalitarianism.
Voter shopping

Many people (including politicians) are very negative about "buying" votes and "bribing" voters; doing it openly and directly (paying someone to vote for me) is even against the law, so it's done through donuts and such. However, if politicians really wanted to exclude this phenomenon from society, it would be very easy; and as a side effect, only those who are really interested in the political situation and mean something to them would still vote: Let the state stop paying money to political parties for votes obtained (thereby depriving them of part of the funds for bribing voters) and use this money differently - let every citizen have a choice at the ballot box to either vote or receive cash. It would be almost impossible to bribe voters under such conditions with a donut or a sausage, because whoever would vote just for the sake of it would rather take money for not being elected (or both, after all, the elections are anonymous).
However, politicians will never push through something like this, because on the one hand they are concerned with the dregs of the elections, but above all it could also turn out that for the majority of people who still vote (and that the voter turnout is not exactly breathtaking even today), that vote is not worth even a few crowns; how far would voter turnout drop in that case? Not that I consider the whole thing a particularly good idea, it wouldn't save the misery of democracy anyway, but the problem of "buying" voters would be solved once and for all; but why doesn't anyone put such a thing into practice? Well, simply because politicians mostly don't care; they (and by no means only they) will keep talking about it, but they will never risk a drop in voter turnout from the current plus or minus half to maybe a tenth, because then someone might start questioning their legitimacy, so we will rather wait
Zeman's fines for not voting
.
Helping the poor?
Global warming

Even if we ignore the falsified statistics and pseudoscientists, they are already reaching for public money by fabricating evidence and creating catastrophic scenarios based on uncertain
weather forecast for tens or hundreds of years
forward, I admit the objective fact that in the last one hundred or one hundred and fifty years, when we measure the temperature, it has warmed a little; however, we have no evidence that human activity has a negligible effect on it. However, even if she had, it is questionable whether this is a problem at all; and if so, it is not clear by how large. On the other hand, we know demonstrably that the Earth has a tendency to cool enormously and warm itself - regardless of the existence of heavy industry, automobiles or other modern technologies (even without them there were ice ages, or green pastures in Greenland); the crucial question is how significant are the few degrees or tenths of degrees of warming possibly caused by humans compared to the tens of degrees caused by nature.
Unfortunately, no one knows the answer, everything is just more or less substantiated estimates, but de facto, on the one hand, no one can say what effect human activity has on the global weather, but above all, it is not at all clear what the really long-term (that is, not tens or hundreds, but thousands or more years) trend of temperature development is and what the greenhouse gases and other side effects of technology actually cause; are we adding to the already ongoing warming? Or are we delaying the next ice age? I'm afraid that with the current level of knowledge, nobody just knows. So how to approach it? Simply letting everyone make up their own mind; until there is proof that global warming is actually harming anyone (or will realistically harm anyone in the future), it is not acceptable to initiate violence against anyone who does so just because one thinks it might ever cause some harm.
Why don't machines take people's jobs?

Perhaps everyone has come across the fairly popular scare that machines and technology in general are taking people's jobs; and many believed this economically unsubstantiated claim. So let's show why this is not true; it can be explained simply like this: Human needs are practically endless (once we have food and drink, we want housing, when we have housing, we want a car, after the car, entertainment, then more free time, even more entertainment, and so on - this is of course just an example), so if some of them are provided by machines, there will not be unemployment, but a demand for more goods, which will again create jobs. Most proponents of theories about "taking away work with technology" will admit this, but the objection will immediately come that there will be work, but not for unskilled labor. But even that doesn't make sense; why?
Well, suppose the machines drive out of the market all the unskilled workers who become unemployed; what then? Even these people will have needs that need to be met (drink, food, clothing, a roof over their heads, and the like); that could be done by the rich with technology, but the unskilled workers have nothing to offer them (their work is not wanted by the machine owners), so basically two possibilities can arise: Either the rich will give them goods for free (which is not very likely, but if that happens, unemployment itself ceases to be a problem), or a group of unskilled unemployed will start asking and offering work to each other; they will be poorer, but not unemployed, because in the worst case they will essentially create a parallel economy, which will of course develop (among other things thanks to the know-how of the mechanized part of society). So you can sleep peacefully in connection with the machines.
A failure of capitalism?

We often hear around us that capitalism is failing; the current problems (typically caused by the state and its regulations, sometimes not obvious at first glance, but often are) that our society faces are presented as evidence. Why is this argument completely incorrect? Well, mainly because we simply don't live in capitalism, but in some kind of mix of capitalism and socialism, while problems appear mainly in those fields that the state regulates more (education, healthcare, etc.), on the other hand, those in which the state does not interfere much (for example, IT) are functional.
Capitalism is a system in which private individuals own the means of production and can do with them as they please; socialism, on the other hand, means that the means of production are owned or controlled by the state. Nowadays, although most of the means of production are still owned by private owners, it is no longer so hot to manage them; the state, by its regulations, limits the owners in how they may and may not use their means of production. After all, the fact that most of the money we earn, we hand over to the state and its central planning, the minority we keep for ourselves and spend on the market can also be considered a relatively authoritative indication - that's not capitalism, is it?
Not to mention that our society - despite the state and socialism - is still thriving; yes, sure, there are problems, but just look at what relatively poor people can afford even today: a roof over their heads, enough food, hot water, entertainment, information and education, free time, affordable means of transportation, lots of clothes. Who had access to such things a hundred years ago? Only the richest; and it is only thanks to capitalism that this prosperity has spread among the broad masses who are now so often opposed to it (although there is practically no one among them who does not use the gains of capitalism).
After all, what is capitalism actually based on? On the free market and voluntary exchanges! And the magic of voluntary exchange is that it increases the utility of both parties involved; if this were not the case, and the utility of at least one of the parties would fall from the exchange, that party would never enter into it voluntarily. Despite all the ambitions of central planners and regulators, each of whom knows best how the world should work properly, the best and easiest way to achieve prosperity is simply to let people act, willingly exchange goods and make their own decisions; well, this system is called capitalism.

Money as something inappropriate

Money
, income, debt and financial transactions in general represent a sensitive topic for many people; why is that? Well, I have observed two reasons: The first, which I completely understand, consists in the protection of private information, which can (especially in connection with the state) be easily used against each of us; however, I often see another reason, which is not just a simple lack of information – money is often perceived as something bad. I'm sure you've all heard the scornful statement that someone does something "just for the money"; but what's wrong with that if the thing itself doesn't hurt anyone? Prostitutes and prostitutes, porn actors and porn actresses, drug testers, sometimes even businessmen, they all tend to be
crossed fingers therefore
that they do their work "just for the money"; similarly, people who are "too much for money" are condemned. Not to mention the socialist fabrications that money is the root of all evil.
It is remarkable that despite this rather negative view of money, people find work mutually rewarding.
very easy to exchange
(and it happens on a massive scale day in and day out for billions of individuals around the world), for something very virtuous; while it is money that most people work for. Not to mention that their far more important function (than motivation) is to transmit information about the real world, which makes money in my opinion
one of mankind's greatest inventions
; therefore it is a shame that so often (and from early childhood, see fairy tales) we lead young children to have a negative attitude towards them. The limits of democracy

The vast majority of people, as a result of state propaganda, adore democracy; many even take her as
good by definition
. But what are its quantitative limits? It is evidently not true that when the majority of any number of people agree, the minority should submit; or perhaps there are supporters of each group of hooligans together with the victim being able to vote on who will walk away with the money? So is a larger number of individuals needed to minimize the risk of error? So why don't the people of the whole world vote on, for example, global redistribution? How many of Europe's lovers of democracy would voluntarily invite billions of bushmen from the poorer parts of the world to a vote on the forcible redistribution of wealth? And what would be their arguments, why not? Would something be said about primitives unable to understand our situation? But how many primitive voters in the Czech Republic influence things that they do not fully understand, just because they got a sausage or a doughnut?
So the question arises, why should a system of determining the legitimacy of human action, which shows absurd results on a small and global scale, be the ideal for nation-states? Why should it be correct at this granularity when it fails at every other? Of course, one cannot throw off the table without further arguments the possibility that, although democracy will lead to misery in most groups, it works well precisely at the level of nation-states; on the other hand, I see no reason why this should be the case, when states often represent quite artificial political constructs (for example, Czechoslovakia Masaryk compared to other powerful states). Isn't it all a coincidence that democracy is inherently amoral and unjust on every scale, and in borderline cases it can be seen at first glance, while in our reality it prevents a sober assessment of all the misery of state indoctrination we are exposed to since childhood?
Armed company

Although the Czech legislation regarding weapons is one of the less strict compared to other European states, freedom as such can only be spoken of rigidly, because one simply cannot legally go and buy a gun or ammunition just like that - you need a permit from the state (which for many weapons cannot even be obtained); not to mention that politicians and the media constantly try to stigmatize gun owners, make them into extremists, and often publicly state that owning a gun is not a right, but a privilege, while we hardly have a single politician on the political scene who welcomes and supports an armed society.
The libertarian rationale I encounter most often is that the government is afraid of an armed society because in such a society the military or police as a whole is not stronger than the civilians, so in the event of a civil war whoever controls the state's armed forces may not win. They are of course right about that, but I don't think that it would be the main reason, because I don't suppose that Czech politicians would seriously think about a civil war, because there is no such thing as a slippage (and if there is such a thing as "national nature", then the Czech one is quite at odds with it).
Personally, I think it's addiction first, responsibility second and self-confidence third; until the fourth for some other reasons (including civil war).
Dependency – unarmed citizens are dependent on the police; the armed ones are able to defend themselves and subsequently see even better how useless (and harmful) the uniformed monkeys are.
Responsibility - an armed citizen assumes a certain responsibility that he did not have until then, which can make him more responsible; and that is precisely what conflicts with the interests of most politicians.
Self-confidence – politicians want citizens to look up to them in case of problems; those who are armed can solve part of the problems (security) themselves, ergo they don't look, or look less.
An armed society means a freer society, for the people will accept some of the responsibility that the state assumed for them in an unarmed society; therefore, let's strive to make the thunder stick a completely normal part of life for as many people as possible. And let's not forget that the moment a government starts disarming its citizens, it means that they will soon need their weapons...
President Bush for the first and second time

Newspeak: poverty

Perhaps each of us sometimes reads - or hears - something about how many people live "below the poverty line"; usually we learn about it in connection with some alarming news in the sense that such people are increasing, or at least not decreasing. So does this mean that even though our society keeps getting richer, the poor have less and less, or still the same? No! Doesn't mean! Can you guess why? Well, the so-called "poverty line" is nothing more than a bureaucratic construct that is constantly being redefined to divide the population into rich and poor in whatever proportion suits the powers that be; yes, it's that simple - if we were to define "poverty" in the same way (and no libertarian definitions are needed, just use the bureaucratic standards of the past), we would find that the number of poor people is constantly decreasing.

If everyone took care of themselves...

"If everyone takes care of themselves, eventually everyone will be taken care of."
This sentence, in my opinion, perfectly illustrates the essence of most of the problems in the world today; everyone has a need to control everyone else's life, social engineers know best of all what is best for whom, socialists want to centrally plan absolutely everything. The idea of someone taking care of themselves is considered by the current establishment to be blasphemy against the biggest, most widespread and most dangerous religion of our time - statism.
Just look around at newspapers, politicians, various bloggers, read their articles; they mostly deal with mass problems at large and dictate what they should and shouldn't do to others as part of their solutions. At the same time, it would be enough for everyone to look at their own and not to invent nonsense: If you invent something for yourself and find out that you made a mistake and bear the consequences, you simply reconsider the decision, because you feel its consequences firsthand; but if someone makes decisions about others in this way, then even if his mistake is revealed, the person in question often stands behind him out of pure vanity, because someone else bears the consequences and no stranger's blood flows.
Of course, the typical objection is that some people can't take care of themselves; their loved ones or family can take responsibility for such people (which is not against anything), but even then there will be a certain (small) percentage of those who are not capable themselves and have no one else. Well, all the people who don't like the principle described above can take care of you (and some others too; I personally also donate part of my income to help people who, in my opinion, need it); however, nothing entitles anyone to come to someone and forcefully deprive them of funds that the person in question does not want to give himself.
Yes, I admit, the result will be that some one here and there will end up badly; on the other hand, it is happening now and will always happen. The difference is mainly that we currently pay an absurdly high tax to the state for it; and by that I don't just mean most of our income, but also the freedom that the state deprives us of with its laws. We have come so far that the idea that everyone should take care of themselves and not interfere in the lives of others (unless both parties agree) is considered extremism; please let's not be manipulated by this - it is right for people to make up their own minds.
State business despite

An acquaintance of mine likes South America very much, where he spends a month or two every year; sometimes he tells me about the conditions there and it's always interesting stuff. He recently told me that although official unemployment there is quite high, the eye of the authorities does not see that far; the consequence of this is that even the officially unemployed can earn a decent living - for example, he met a woman there who made a living by boiling a cauldron of food every morning, loading it on a cart and going out into the streets to sell, so that in the evening or afternoon she returned home with enough money to live comfortably.
How easy is it to make a living as an unemployed person when there is no state and no bureaucracy to bind everyone? Who couldn't cook a cauldron of stew, buy fresh bread and sell it at the stand? And when it stops bringing it out? Simply change the assortment, sell or produce anything else, start practically from scratch in a small way, without the need for larger investments; and it doesn't even have to be about cooking - anyone with a garden can buy chickens and sell eggs, everyone can learn to weave baskets, or thousands of other things. How many people would try this if it weren't for bureaucratic legal terror?
But under the current dictates of the state, which takes care of absolutely everything by law, such a person must obtain a permit, at least a trade certificate, another certificate for working with foodstuffs, familiarize himself with all standards and comply with them, register income, pay taxes, issue receipts, and now also have an EET. How many rounds of bureaucracy does he have to go through before he finds out if his idea is even profitable and feeds it? He'd better get rid of it, especially when he has a social system and benefits at his disposal, because socialist pies are also (or actually mainly) jobless.
Sure, it's best for politicians if the unemployed don't fend for themselves; they can then show activity, create the impression of their indispensability and within that
make people dependent on the state
. After all, as some cow from ANO taught us in connection with the introduction of EET, business only makes sense if the person in question pays taxes from it; if someone goes bankrupt who does not report his income, it is said to be no harm, because such a business was useless anyway. And as long as we elect representatives, they already have a similar view of business, unfortunately nothing will change in the whole matter; and when, for the worse.
Through the eyes of the outlaw

During my life, I had the honor of discussing with many freedom-restrictors and prohibitionists, whose motivations varied greatly, some were just afraid of something, while others I would describe as notorious prohibitionists who need to have absolutely everything covered by the law; as they arrived at their conclusions in very different ways, it has long seemed to me that they were quite different considerations, coincidentally leading to the same conclusion. Quite recently, however, I found out that there is one logical error in their thinking, which is common to almost all limiters and regulators (except for the downright actively evil ones, who are fully aware of the consequences of their actions; but in my opinion, they are a negligible minority); so what kind of mistake is it?
Well, this is a fairly widespread idea - when something is banned, people very often imagine that the thing will simply disappear; the basis of all their reasoning is based on the simple idea that when the state prohibits something, it is basically the same as if the given thing disappeared from the face of the earth and ceased to exist at the moment of prohibition. What more, at most, some more enlightened prohibitionist can see is the ineffectiveness of regulations; they typically understand that the disappearance will not be complete, but only partial, because not everyone obeys the law. However, virtually every prohibitionist ignores the costs of enforcing the restrictions, the negative side effects, and certainly not the restrictions on freedom or the distortion of the market; calling for bans is then a logical consequence of such thinking.
It is certainly interesting for the prohibitors to present these objections; he typically either downplays them, ridicules them (for example, many people respond to the objection that a typical ban implies the use of aggressive violence against innocents by declaring the absurdity of such a claim), or simply ignores them. However, it is evident from most of the reactions that the person in question did not try to compare the costs of regulation with its benefits at all (not that it is possible; we are referring to the interpersonal incomparability of benefits, but in order for the prohibitor to even understand this, he would first have to try to compare); he just sees something he doesn't like, so he automatically wants to ban it (gambling, drugs, Islam, prostitution and so on).
I know that not all of them are like that, some are among the outspoken villains who understand the consequences of their actions (and forbid for personal gain); however, I strongly believe that most banners do so for the above motives (they believe that banning will solve some problem). For that reason, all those who support bans on anything need to be constantly reminded of the cost of such measures; and the price is really high, because it is not only about the fact that the enforcers of the regulations could do something productive instead of their "work" (and their time is not free), but above all about the consequences - restriction of freedom, violence against the innocent, increasing the potential for corruption, possible creation of mafias (prohibition). Please, let's constantly highlight these costs to all banners; let us repeat again and again that almost every state ban in practice means the use of offensive violence against the innocent, although people don't want to hear much about it!
Ancient civilization

The ancient civilization is often spoken of as a model of virtue, a great society from which we could learn a lot and, for example, the famous Islam killer Bill Warner sets it up as the opposite of the barbaric Islamic world, which enslaved people since its inception; to mention slavery in this context appears to be quite absurd considering that the entire ancient civilization was based on slaves (free people were a minority in that society). Similarly distant from reality is also the romantic idea of duels between heroic Romans and the "barbarians" of the north; what was it really about? Well, the Roman legions were simply conquering more territory, whose original inhabitants were subjugated, massacred, enslaved and tortured in the process; the conquering practices of the Roman legionnaires were not matched by their cruelty even by the Nazis, who surpassed them in scale, but this was only due to population growth and technological progress.
Ancient Greece is often referred to as the cradle of democracy; and it really was in a certain limited sense, however, it was definitely not a democracy, which would mean "the government of (all) the people", because real democracy took place among a handful of privileged (free citizens), while the majority (slaves) did not participate in the decision-making process. Paradoxically, this was the reason why those first democracies exhibited
greater stability than the current ones
(not that both kinds aren't crap, though each a bit different); although it is of course true that ours gradually developed from such a civilization, it was in no way a society from which we should take an example - we have come a long way as humanity, we have learned from many mistakes, and we should not lose sight of the fact that idealizing the past can be quite dangerous in many ways.
Identity, identification, authorization, state and identity cards

Today, it is a matter of course for almost everyone that we have documents such as an identity card with which we can identify ourselves, the state has a central database of citizens and collects an inordinate amount of personal data about them; it's interesting how many people react with extreme irritation when private entities behave similarly (and even do it just for fun, the law forbids them), but in the case of the state, it leaves the same individuals cold. The existence of such measures is presented to us as a "necessity" without which society could not reasonably function; despite this propaganda, we easily overlook the fact that even a hundred years ago, ID cards were not compulsory (this was introduced by a certain Adolf, who helped to finally solve it), two hundred years ago they did not exist at all, and if we go back another hundred or two hundred years, we will come across the absence of records in the matrix - people were simply not registered in any way, yet no doom occurred.
Of course, it can be argued that in times when people did not travel nearly as much, everyone was in an environment where everyone knew them, identification was not needed, whereas in today's globalized world the requirements are higher; and of course that is true. On the other hand, in today's world we have cryptographic means, unknown to our ancestors, by which the problem can be completely solved;
exhaustive (and in my opinion underrated) article
OC wrote about it - one of the smartest and most uneducated anarcho-capitalists I know. Wondering why it doesn't work that way when it's so good? Well, simply because the state already does it in a different (albeit worse, more expensive, more exploitable and crappy) way, so there is no interest in spending additional funds on another system when the state system will exist anyway and we have to pay for it anyway; however, if this were to cease to exist, a market solution would replace it practically immediately.

Market and "fair" prices

The purpose of this text is not so much to convey a message, but rather to provoke a discussion on a topic that has been bothering me lately; I'd like to know what other libertarians think about this. Model situation: A person close to me gets into a critical situation in which it is necessary to perform a tracheotomy immediately in order to survive, but I cannot do this and I do not have the tools for it; there is only one doctor in the area who can perform the procedure and has the equipment for it (other help will not arrive in time); the person in question agrees to it, but demands all my property in exchange. We can all (libertarians) probably agree that he has a right to do that; however, my question is - is it a "pig house"? At first glance, I'd say yes, but...
So that the discussion does not go in a meaningless direction, I explicitly emphasize again that I am not solving here
NAP
; from the point of view of the principle of non-aggression, of course the doctor's actions are correct, he can do it, he does not violate anyone's rights, and I have no right to force him to perform the procedure by force (whether it be putting a gun to his head, or first promising him property, but then not doing anything to him and violently defending against his attempts to take what belongs to him). Of course, even NAP compliant stuff can be crap; for example, cheating on a partner, betraying someone's friendship, cheating on someone who has helped me for a long time, hurting someone's feelings for fun, and many other similar things can be done in accordance with the NAP.
At first glance, I would classify the actions of such a doctor in the same category, on the other hand, some time ago there was a discussion in Stoká in which someone said something to the effect that the doctor should charge the market price; and at that moment I thought: What is the market price in the given situation? Of course, this varies in time and place (the price of water in the desert is different than at a dam), ergo I wonder, isn't "all my property" really the market price? I'd almost say yes given the circumstances. And if the doctor has no relationship with me, why should he provide me with a service below the price? From this point of view, it seems pretty obvious to me that his actions are not "crap".
On the other hand, I would call it "crap" if a doctor in a similar situation, where it was my loved one, but not me (and no one he could hurt), let the injured person lie on the ground, stepped over him and went on (although he has the right to do so, of course); I perceive failure to provide first aid (if someone can do it and it does not pose a risk to them) as a disgusting act. But charging a market price for it (and perhaps negotiating it quickly, so that when a loved one of the injured person says that he will not give his entire property, but "only" a million, to perform the procedure) can hardly be bad, can it? The well-known example of selling "overpriced" gasoline in areas affected by a natural disaster, where the only gas station will remain untouched, can be demonstrated that such behavior is not only okay, but even desirable and "socially beneficial." Is there anything different here?
Taxes - mandatory or voluntary?

Have you ever wondered what happens if you don't pay your taxes? Well, it comes down to it - if it is a lot of money and you lie to the state about your income, you will be legally kidnapped and put in a dungeon straight away; if you simply do nothing, the state will call, then send bailiffs, and if you defend your property from them, there will also be sadistic monkeys in uniform, who, if you resist, will either snap you like a dog or put you in a dungeon for an even longer period than in the previous case. In fact, it's no different from a mob collecting firebombs; the difference lies only in the legality of one and the illegality of the other, in other words, in what some goons voted in parliament.
However, one can sometimes come across this statist argument: "But I pay taxes voluntarily."
Of course, we can doubt whether this is really the case, and whether the person in question would pay taxes in the amount demanded by the state even without the threat of force; but even if it were so, the taxes cannot be justified by it.
Why? Well, if this justification holds up, any act of violence for which there is at least one victim who doesn't mind being a victim and basically wants it that way can be excused this way.
For example, we could say that going to the park at night to rape women is okay, because there are those who would sleep with a rapist even without a knife to their neck.
Unfortunately, state propaganda can be seen incredibly clearly on the issue of taxes; not only is an action when someone simply refuses to hand over their money to the aggressor commonly considered "theft" in connection with taxes, but on top of that, many people think to argue that he pays taxes voluntarily, so everything is fine. Just imagine how absurd it would be in a different context - for example, you tell someone how you were robbed, only to find out from the person you are telling it to that nothing actually happened, because the last time they robbed him, he didn't really mind, so why are you complaining; but different standards apply to the state, as the teacher at school taught us...

Wasting food

You know those pictures of piles of food being thrown away while African children are starving? They are often accompanied by some deeply moral message about our selfishness and how we should be ashamed of throwing away something that is in need elsewhere; I have two major objections to these superficial messages, which I intend to refute completely:
1/ Food here and food in Africa are two different goods; the cost of transportation is astronomical compared to the cost of the discarded food, in many cases it would be cheaper to grow new food locally.
2/ Considering how much food our society consumes, it can be considered a miracle (of the free market) that there are so few surpluses; It's simply not possible to hit the mark on consumption exactly - so do you prefer surpluses or hunger?
After all, who wants to return to the previous regime of queues for meat? And even then there were surpluses.
Not to mention that there were times when even in Europe people were starving; but then came the industrial revolution and wild capitalism which solved this problem. Let us be glad for it and wish the same to Africans; however, let's not be ashamed of the fact that we have those surpluses - on the contrary, let's be grateful for them - it does no harm to anyone and is a natural consequence of the prosperity in which we live.
Alcohol does not belong behind the wheel?

I was just listening to a discussion about the drug problem in which some drug addict "refuted" the thesis that
drugs are different
, people do too, so the effects of using narcotics vary, ergo it's not fair to ban everyone the same; the person in question used the analogy that, for example, alcohol behind the wheel affects different people differently, yet the law applies to everyone the same and no one even thinks of questioning or discussing it. So not only has it occurred to me many times, I've even had such debates before, but I haven't written about it yet; and the fool, by taking the correctness of such a law as a given, led me to believe that a short text on the subject would do no harm.
Not only does alcohol affect different people differently, but above all it does not automatically make everyone a bad driver; only to some degree (which is itself very individual) does it reduce the abilities of the drunk. And there are undoubtedly people on the roads who will be even two per thousand better drivers than youngsters who have just left driving school; not to mention the fact that some people start reeling after a few drinks, while others just get into the mood after the same amount, with their motor skills and reaction time remaining virtually intact. So alcohol not only reduces the ability to drive in different people in different ways, but above all from a different basis (some are much better drivers than others).
From this point of view, it really seems absurd to punish people according to how many parts of alcohol they have in their blood, since some completely sober driver is more dangerous on the road than a drunk professional with millions of kilometers on the road; so what is the solution? Laissez faire, I say! Only the free market can come up with the answer. Perhaps private insurance companies and road owners would completely prohibit alcohol behind the wheel, perhaps they would allow a certain limit as a flat rate, or they would determine the dependence of permitted drunkenness on kilometers driven without accidents, or address it only in the event of an accident or not at all; and I think the most likely option is that they would come up with something that I didn't even think of here.
Not to mention that it's not even clear that the optimum lies at the point where alcohol causes the fewest accidents; we must not neglect the possibility that traffic participants will voluntarily undergo an increase in the risk of an accident in exchange for the benefit of other things (convenience and so on). And a similar possibility is not at all improbable, because, for example, everyone who leaves home and goes to a pub for a beer (even on foot) demonstrates his preference for taking certain risks to satisfy some needs; it is therefore not unrealistic for people to think similarly in connection with driving. The problem, of course, is that
without a free market we will never find a solution to the problem, because it is simply impossible
.
Let's shop at home

It's surprising how often one hears calls to buy "homemade" goods, especially food, even though it's been almost two hundred years since Frédéric Bastiat made it absolutely clear what nonsense it is; to those who happen to be unfamiliar with it, I warmly recommend the work "What is and what is not visible" (good news for those who do not like long texts, this is short and readable). However, patriotism is strong, emotional, and state-sponsored; not to mention that being visible, having influence and being able to convince others has, unfortunately, almost nothing to do with being right or preaching delusion.
Supermarkets are even being ordered by some new law to label food with flags to show what goods consumers are buying, as the belief that it is "right" to support "homemade" products enjoys a relatively non-negligible popularity; In this way, people are falsely convinced that they are actually somehow helping themselves by buying "domestic" goods, because the prosperity of "their" state means benefits for them personally. Not that it is not true to a certain (very small) extent, but these advantages are quite negligible compared to the disadvantages that market distortions bring with them.
There are many ways to refute these delusions, I will choose the one that seems easiest to me: What is the essence of the market? The best producers and suppliers of certain goods make the most money because people voluntarily pay them for those goods; the worst ones fail. And it is this principle that is the most advantageous for consumers, as it ensures that they get exactly the goods they want; if we prioritize "domestic" goods at the expense of foreign goods instead of monitoring other parameters, it can easily happen that we give a chance to a manufacturer or supplier who, although Czech, is not as good as a foreign one.
So I am definitely not saying that we should not buy Czech goods on purpose; only that if we choose only according to quality and price, while ignoring the country of origin, we will support the best manufacturers and suppliers regardless of where they are from, but if we include the country of origin in the criteria, we may get worse Czech goods or services instead of better foreign ones next time. Personally, in addition, when given the option of choosing between Czech and foreign goods with otherwise identical parameters, I take the foreign one in order to balance the various patriotic tastes of my fellow citizens xD
Students for Liberty: Urza versus Backa

Few trolls have the stamina of Mr. Backa; and because I recognize invincibility, I will face him tonight at Liberty evening organized by Students for Liberty in a duel on the topic: "Is the state legitimate?" Since Mr. Back's rhetorical skills can't be denied (not to mention his passion for making fools of people), I promise myself an interesting debate from the evening, from which I can take away a lot of embarrassment, so don't hesitate to come xD

How to move to a free market?

The goal is a free market, a stateless society, i.e. anarcho-capitalism... how to get there? Privatize? If so, how? Auction off state property? Give it away? To whom and how? All at once? What about opting out of government "services"? Of which? In what order? Creating parallel structures? I would be very interested in your opinions; and in as much detail as possible, as well as reasoned, including the options you considered and rejected (and why). Please share them in the discussion? For I believe that there is no "right" way; in my eyes they are just more and less bad. Although I am convinced that some are better than others, my goal now is not to influence, but rather to learn something.
If someone is not an anarchist and his goal is a small state (or at least smaller than the current one), it does not matter at all; describe the path you would like to take from your current state to your dream state.
People fooled by advertising

"People don't know what they want, they are manipulated by advertising, we need to regulate it to help them!" So goes the common objection against the consumerist market society; and I continue to be fascinated by the thought process of those who float it: "I am educated, aware, unmanipulated and wise, I am not affected by the corporate ads, I have seen through what millions of people have not; so now I will be the savior and help them...against their will, through violent state intervention." Sometimes such a person, if he is particularly conceited, will throw in the analogy of how parents bring up children; then he drinks the idea down with a latte from his favorite hipster cafe (but marketing doesn't apply to him, he's a hipster because he wants to). He lacks humility, respect for people and their wishes, tolerance for choosing a different lifestyle and the realization that he is not better than others - the more strongly these qualities are rooted in a person, the more the person in question promotes
free market
.
Traffic jams

Traffic jams seem to be the necessity of our time; and it is quite logical that when there are too many cars, the roads simply get clogged and the traffic is not smooth. How to solve it? I have no idea; no one else knows either, so it's probably a necessity. Such necessities have already existed; so, for example, there were times when traveling around the world in eighty days seemed almost a miracle, just as it was clear that objects heavier than air do not fly, talking to someone halfway across the world is impossible, and a person moving faster than sixty kilometers per hour will die. However, resourceful individuals with the motivation to do great things have always managed to find solutions through the thorny path of trial and error; and against such problems some traffic jam looks like a strumpet. But none of those who could solve it has the motivation to risk anything, because it has a warm place and everyone has already accepted constipation as an inevitability; so why bother and risk losing the favor of voters?
Safe colors

Cars of some colors can be seen better on the road, others less so; imagine - purely hypothetically - a regulation that bans "dangerous" car colors - red and yellow can be seen well, but away with grey. For some time now I have been seeking opinions on this regulation from proponents of (other) regulations with whom I debate; and guess what? Almost everyone is against it; even advocates of mandatory seat belts. I address the question of why this is so; it is a typical regulation, which consists in the prohibition of something "unnecessary and vain" (which no one so-called "needs", it is just a "whim") in the name of safety (and we also have the popular argument of endangering not only oneself, but also the surroundings), ergo there should be similar opinions on this as on alcohol or talking on the phone while driving, but they are not. So what's the difference? Personally, I think that this is just media massage and what is currently "modern" to ban. Do you have a better explanation?
Children of unschoolers

As many readers know, I work in
Freedom of learning
; and because its members and supporters often put their beliefs into practice (with great results, by the way), their children often do not go to school. This is not pure unschooling, the current legislation does not allow it, because children have to be tested; and that's where something fascinating happens. These children simply do not understand why they should go through the process; they ask if the examiner doesn't know what they're asking to help and explain (which would make sense), but then when they find out it's an "examination" they don't understand the point of the whole thing. Why should they prove what they can do to a stranger, from whom they want nothing? One would see such a mindset in a schoolboy; because he is trained to do things simply because he is ordered to do them - and trying is normal. At the same time, the question: "Why should anyone test me?" is an example of critical thinking; however, this (despite declarations to the contrary) is not desirable.
Urza in deCentral: The Non-Aggression Principle (NAP)

The topic of the past
lectures on anarcho-capitalism at the (de)Centrála club

Suicides

One possible—albeit somewhat morbid—way to gauge population satisfaction is to track suicide rates; of course, it has its pitfalls (it only measures the number of the least satisfied and a lot of other factors affect it), but also advantages ("survey" will not affect any lying). And what does this metric say about some popular claims that we were better off "under the communists"? Well, under the previous regime, an average of 24 people per hundred thousand inhabitants were killed annually (in the five years after 1968, even 28); since the revolution we have an average of 16 suicides for the same number of people. So people committed suicide "under the communists" fifty percent more often than today! Of course, I am not saying that a person who would otherwise be happy will kill himself just because of who is in the government (I personally do not believe this explanation even with Palach); however, I believe that the political system affects people's lives enough to make some (not all) reasons for suicide.

Is stealing BTC a violation of the NAP?

One of my readers asked me a question: When someone steals Bitcoin, they are in violation
non-aggression principle (NAP)
? The "theft" in itself (that is, sending a signed transaction that moves BTC from one address to another) is not, in my opinion, a violation of the NAP. No one can own a private key (it is a sequence of bits, in principle it cannot be owned, it can only be known and kept secret) or prevent others from signing transactions (thereby violating the NAP), therefore dealing with "foreign" BTC is not a violation of the NAP. The question, however, is how the "thief" got the key; there, most likely, a violation of the NAP has already occurred (even if he didn't break into anywhere, but hacked some device, it is still a violation of the NAP, because it involved dealing with someone else's property - that device - against the owner's will), although in theory it might not have to (if the "thief" had seen and remembered the key, for example).

Social engineers have a problem; and as it happens in a state-run society, we have it with them. However it happened, the state (again) made a mistake; and instead of correcting it by phasing out the pension system, he is trying to save the situation with more mistakes.
Child allowances, maternity allowances, tax write-offs for children, and now perhaps even a reduction in social insurance for more children, these are all measures intended to stimulate citizens to have more intensive procreation; something like when a farmer has cattle and needs more cattle for economic reasons, somehow the lords of power look at us. They devised some pension system based on the assumptions that once held; and that would play so well that now the plebs are disrupting their plans, no such thing, you will give birth nicely!

This move is advocated by the populist Daniel Herman. As? There is certainly interest in having a monument stand on the site; on the other hand, there is also an interest in having a piggy bank standing in the same place. What about that? The owner of the piggery makes a profit from it corresponding to how much benefit it brings to society as a whole (that is, to the people who eat the pigs); on the other hand, there is an intangible benefit to many people from a possible memorial. How to compare these two incommensurable values? Well, quite easily: Are those interested in the monument willing to fold and pay the owners of the piggy bank enough to give it up? If not, then apparently they want that memorial less than many want a piggery.
Unfortunately, nothing like that was heard in the duel. In principle, he makes exactly the same error in reasoning as his opponent: He puts his wishes and his subjective feeling above the preferences expressed by people through their actions in the market. If they consider Lety to be more important than other places, then it is not right to force them to build monuments elsewhere first. Twenty-three years since the death of Murray Newton Rothbard

Today it is exactly twenty-three years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers and geniuses left this world at the age of 69 - Murray Newton Rothbard, the "father of anarcho-capitalism"; his life's work was a consistent and logical introduction to the consequences of two trends that were seemingly not very related: anarchism and the Austrian school of economics. Anarchists were often wrong in economics, and the proponents of the Austrian school of economics did not apply their (correct) conclusions to the state; Murray Newton Rothbard corrected both and came to a brilliant conclusion: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." This knowledge and full understanding of it changed my life greatly; Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.

Uninsurable

In debates about the unnecessaryness of the state, one can relatively often encounter the question of what will happen to people who suffer from some serious and expensively treatable congenital disease, ideally one that can be detected before birth, which means that no insurance company will be interested in them; and what is my answer? Well, of course no one can predict the market, but I can imagine, for example, insurance for parents to whom the insurance company will offer a future contract for their child's insurance for an additional fee; I can also imagine insuring children even before conception and many other solutions. That similar services do not exist today? That is true, but why should they exist in a socialist health care system where everyone will be insured? Logically, there is no demand for something that the state offers for so-called "free"; if it stops happening, demand will arise - and where there is demand, there will also be an offer, because you can make money from it.
My fiancee called the principle "insurance against the uninsurable"; I consider this designation to be absolutely accurate. Insurance is similar to betting: If there is an event with a low probability of occurrence, I can bet for quite a bit of money that it will occur, and when it does, I can win far more (because the chance of winning was small); and as long as people are willing to bet, there is no reason why those bets should not be made by someone who calculates the statistical odds and designs favorable terms for himself. Why shouldn't it then be possible to bet that if a child is born to me affected by disease X, I will receive Y crowns, where Y is the price of treatment? If I am willing to bet significantly more than Y times the odds that the newborn will have disease X, someone rich will be found to make the bet because it is profitable; after all... if people come to you and offer 100 crowns for the fact that you will pay them 900 crowns with a 1:10 chance, will you refuse?
Compulsory war

One does not have to go far for the idea that conscription should be reintroduced; however, I am not entirely sure that all those who ask for this really fully understand what they are asking for, because the state propaganda has gone so far that many people no longer even think about what is hidden behind each of the euphemisms used by the government. So what is conscription? So, above all, it is about slavery; true, typically time-limited, but the gist is that conscripts are forced (!) to submit to the whims of other people the military designates as their superiors. Whether they bully them or treat them quite "well" is irrelevant; a slave owner who does not abuse his slaves and is "good" to them as much as possible does not cease to be a slave owner. Are you, then, supporters of compulsory war, really supporters of slavery? I think mostly not, you just think it's an exaggeration to call military service that; but is it really so?
If you tell someone in an African country where female circumcision is a common practice that it is a disgusting barbaric atrocity, they will probably also find it exaggerated, because in their reality it is a quite normal thing; she will probably answer something along the lines of: "I went through it as a child too, and at least I'm not fucking myself." A chilling analogy to the notorious: "I was in the army, I was bullied, but it benefited me, at least I'm not such a slob like today's young people." What do I mean by that? That the way we perceive something emotionally is influenced to an extremely strong extent by how common that thing is in the environment where we live - if we get used to it, even absolutely horrible things no longer shock us; in such a case, let's forget about emotions and follow logic: Even if we don't have to perceive war as slavery, in reality it is (a person is forcibly forced to obey someone's orders); and how can such an atrocity be justified?

Although I certainly don't consider not voting to be stupid or wrong, I personally have always voted; and I will vote as long as the message I would send by not voting is perceived as disinterest, not disapproval.
I categorically reject the thesis that I would legitimize democracy or the state with my vote.
Although it is not clear to me who you should vote for, I dare to say that the most dangerous is the vote for Babiš; in my opinion, the choice of the People's Party or KSČSSD is slightly better (although still terrible); I consider voting for SPD or Úsvit, Zelené, TOPka or STAN rather stupid (but again slightly better); I don't consider the choice of the other parties to be so bad, because they are too small to cause real damage or a "lesser evil" (compared to the rest). If you want to vote "against the Socans or Babiš" - or "so that the vote doesn't go to waste" - and you want to avoid voting for a small party, I would probably (with reservations) recommend the ODS, because it can perhaps be described as the least evil of the "big ones"; although in the past it has sharply shied away from the fight against a very large state (despite promises), thereby tripping up its voters, lately it is perhaps trying to make amends (I judge from watching their votes and speeches), but it will still take some time before they gain at least a shred of my trust. However, I consider the argument of the "loss" of the vote to be wrong, because the vote will almost certainly "lose" anyway ("it won't be lost" only if the election turned out at least a little differently without it, which is almost impossible). Hundreds of hours of researching party programs, the credibility of politicians, the basics of economics, predicting the effects of this or that law; assuming you don't have this as a hobby, this is an extreme expense. And what is the profit from the "correct" (conscious) choice? Well, none; unless the "right" candidate loses by one vote (which has probably never happened anywhere), the outcome of the election is exactly the same for each individual regardless of how they voted. Nocebo: The State Causes Cancer!

Nocebo is the opposite of placebo; while the placebo effect consists of healing based on the patient's belief that he is being treated (when in fact he is not), the nocebo effect worsens his condition based on perhaps expecting negative side effects of the drug (which he is not actually receiving). Disgusting pictures and warnings about all the horrible ways cigarettes can harm our health are now required by law to appear on every cigarette pack; why shouldn't the nocebo effect show up here? Every time a smoker takes his cigarette from a pack colorfully depicting the potential negative health consequences of his action, he is convinced that he will get sick; and if he believes it, his mind can seriously cause the disease. So not only the state
inexcusably violates proprietary rights
cigarette manufacturers when it regulates the appearance of their boxes, but even more so it harms the smokers it declaratively protects.

The mafia called the state

Gift markets

You can buy goods in the regular market; it goes something like this: You conclude a purchase contract with the seller (note, the contract is not a signed paper, but an agreement; the paper is only proof that it took place), you pay him the money, he hands over the goods to you... then he has to register this transaction electronically with Babiš. In the gift market, you don't buy, you give yourself a gift; it goes completely differently: You conclude two gift contracts with the marketer (not the seller) - the subject of one is your gift of money to the person in question, the subject of the second is that the good man presents you with his goods... and that's the end of it, because no one has yet implemented electronic records of donations. Donation markets have already been successfully held in Hradec Králové and Letohrad; another fifty cities are interested in organizing a similar event. Great so far! What do you think will come next? Oxford University has sent out new rules to students in its regular newsletter aimed at curbing racial intolerance; is it really needed there? And if so, how do the rules help? Let's take a look at them. For example, students may not ask a student of color where they originally came from; but even "better" is that they can't even avoid eye contact! It is said to be "micro-racism". Therefore, if a man glances at a woman of another race, she must return his glances, but in the case of the same race she does not have this obligation; and this is no longer micro-racism... this is racism like a cow! Don't all those politically correct geniuses realize that these kinds of measures accentuate racial differences? Don't they understand that in this way they can make racists out of those who have never dealt with any race at all? One can only hope that other institutions will not follow the example of the University of Oxford.
Sobotka shares the loot

Although the elections are still quite far away, they are slowly approaching; and Sobotka needs to buy votes, but why would he do so on his own, when he has the stolen money of all of us at his disposal - so he wants to increase the salaries of civil servants. It's not unlike a hood of pirates splitting it up,
what they looted
; After all, the additions should be made (apart from firefighters) primarily to policemen, customs officers and bailiffs, i.e. executive rapists, who already form the front line of state oppression and the acquisition of resources through robbery.
