he lectured in Polis some time ago
: Politicians promise people that they will take care of them (at someone else's expense), which if they do, the number of dependents on the state (and civil servants) will increase; an increase in dependents on the state means more votes for politicians who promise people to take care of them (at someone else's expense). The circle closes: Democracy inevitably leads to socialism.
The Pope on the libertarian invasion

I occasionally hear a joke among foreign libertarians that I would translate roughly as follows: "Libertarians are busily plotting to take over the world and leave you alone." (You can google “libertarians diligently plotting leave you alone” in the pictures.) Guess who took this little bit seriously? Pope Franciscus. He warned the world against the invasion (sic!) of libertarian values on our culture and education system. The danger of our delusional paradigms is said to be that we are not interested in the "public good" and in our belief that "only individuals assign value to things and human relationships, ergo only individuals decide what is good and what is bad"; he said that - surprisingly - very nicely, maybe I'll use it somewhere... I understand that he doesn't like it that much, because he would prefer to have the monopoly on what is good and what is bad; and his church always got along better with the state than with the libertarians xD
I am a Christian, but not a Catholic, because I am building a personal relationship with the Lord, for which I do not need a mediator in the form of a priest and certainly not a pope; in such moments I am glad for it, because the Pope's speech does not evoke a dilemma in me, but an infinite joy. Why joy? Dear ones, the head of the church, which surely has over a billion sheep, is talking about us! That means we do what we do well! As Gandhi said, "First they will ignore you. Then they will laugh at you. Then they will fight you. Then you will win." And this Pope's speech is the first swallow of that third phase; if the late Rothbard had lived to see it, he would surely have been glad. So let us continue our efforts; let's write, talk, spread, explain, try to understand people and not be rude to them, let's do our best. For this is the way to freedom; i don't believe i'll live to see a free market society, but i'll do my best... get involved too!
The right to children

Who decides whether we deny a woman who wants a child the possibilities of modern medicine? The state, how else... and the powers that be have determined that if the person in question is not married, she is unlucky. František Adámek, a deputy from the left-wing ČSSD, tried to change this – unfortunately unsuccessfully; Jitka Chalánková from the so-called right-wing TOP09 was most strongly opposed, as she herself is married, has four children, and would like to impose her values on others, and the state gives her that power. Her reasoning: "The right to a child is not a basic human right." Well, how about? Does this mean that what is not a "fundamental human right" is prohibited by the state? She and other members of parliament agreed that it was not a medical issue, but an ethical one. Well of course! It is whether people are free to enter into voluntary transactions or the state will come in and start prohibiting them; the ethical question is: "Is it legitimate for Mrs. Chalánková, together with the other deputies, to decide from a position of power who and how is allowed to reproduce?"
You have the word: Become a cyber spy

Almost every episode of "You Have a Word" is a massacre (except for the boring ones about diets and the like); mostly statism and the results of indoctrination by state propaganda abound there, but in the last part about cyber espionage, to those classic bon mots ("Whoever has done nothing wrong, has nothing to fear.") there was added lying manipulation of such dimensions that it surprised me (and I think similarly everyone who has at least a little idea about network security). A proponent of government wiretapping of citizens' network communications argued that foreign hackers could attack our power plants, chemical plants, water plants, and other strategic targets; someone from the audience and the presenter said that it is of course possible, because today everything is controlled via "those computers". It was simply a classic professional discussion in which all knowledge is drawn from hacker action movies; Of course, I don't blame anyone for ignorance, the problem is that in a democracy everyone has a voice.
No matter how skilled a hacker is, he can only attack "those computers" he can physically connect to over the network. So if the computer is not connected to the Internet, the person concerned is out of luck; as one of my teachers used to say: "The best firewall is a meter of air." (This statement no longer has as clear a point in the days of Wi-Fi as it did in his youth.) Of course, those who deal with the security of a nuclear power plant know this; so critical systems run offline. Unfortunately, this did not come up in the discussion for long, until after a while the tragic representative of the Pirate Party spoke uncertainly, and embarrassedly objected; however, the professional uncertainty emanated from it so much that the opponent wiped it out with the Stuxnet virus (attacking industrial systems running on Simatic), which is a completely irrelevant argument (monitoring network communication does not protect against a virus transmitted from a flash drive to an offline machine). But the Pirate was so insecure (he had been wiped out by the given opponent before) that he preferred to leave the topic alone.

I can think of several possibilities, I can't agree with any of them; and I would really like to know how many such people live among us... unfortunately even that one seems more than enough to me. I will not, however, class this story among those which would be laughable, if they were not, of course, to cry; Why not? Because in the end it was a joke after all: The uniformed monkeys came there, found the fiscal identification code on the receipt, the crooks showed it and he walked away in shame; this story was worth the money it cost me in taxes xD

I have a right to a pub

Unfortunately, the ban on smoking in pubs has passed and there is nothing we can do about it, because the laws in practice are constantly increasing, but with exceptions, no one cancels them, ergo, we thus solemnly join the "developed" countries of the EU, which are often argued against; however, even more common is the argument, which I call at work: "I have the right to a pub," which is often explained with the words: "There is only one pub in our village." The best answer to it came from Stok's comments from the author of TaxationISTheft: "So what? If I go to a bookstore and they don't have the book I want, should I start asking the state to make it there?" It is precisely such a senseless demand even in the case of those pubs; not to mention a pretty accurate summary of the current state of the sprawling state I read recently, I don't even know where: "I wouldn't want to own a pub. The idea of someone getting drunk in it, lighting a fire, and me kicking them out before giving them a receipt is a real nightmare."
The best president is a bad president

In my opinion, the position of the president of the Czech Republic has an amazing ratio of prestige to real power; the head of state is a media-exposed figure, but he doesn't have that much power (not that he doesn't have any at all, for example, he appoints the members of the Banking Council of the CNB) - in other words, given how much he is seen, he can't do that much damage. That's why I think it's not so bad from a libertarian point of view if the president is already a total badass; why? It provokes people, to whom it is easier to explain the absurdity of democracy and state propaganda; for example, such a Zeman represents from this point of view a president who constantly does exactly what I want him to do - namely, shame. But his election period is slowly coming to an end, and I really would not like to see any Karl (the same evil, which looks more acceptable at first glance); however, according to my information, a candidate will be presented soon, who should playfully trump Zeman in embarrassing... and whoever thinks it's not possible, let them watch the media xD

It is May 2000; uniformed monkeys forcefully (against the law) break into the Mironet company, confiscate computers, accounting and accuse the owner of software piracy, only to find out after two years that... sorry like, a bug crept in, you're innocent, sir, so goodbye. However, the person in question is not a sheep and tries to defend himself against this will; he is suing the state for 626 million, which is like a fuck off, you get 23 megabytes and still be happy, keep quiet and shuffle your feet, filthy subject, says the High Court in Prague. Election 2017: Another crackdown on property rights

For the first time this year, the pre-election campaign will be governed by the latest amendment to the electoral law; the head of the Office for Financial Control of Political Parties, Vojtěch Weiss, declared that anyone who wants to stick their own (!) poster with a political theme on their own (!) fence, shop window or window (that is, not only the promotion of a political party or movement, but also its defamation) must register in his office's tampering database - those who do not do so will be
sanctioned
a fine of ten to one hundred thousand crowns. That registration is also not a piece of cake, one either needs a transparent account, a website and other essentials for it, or one has to be registered by a political party; this will especially affect those who do not want to do a campaign, but an anti-campaign (for example, various haters of Babiš); I'm wondering if this also applies to Stoky, which is certainly not a poster or a large-scale device, but I don't know if it is a "communication medium" according to the law... what do the lawyers here think about it?
And now in Stoká we will once again visit the waters where there are things that would be laughable if they weren't crying: Deputy Speaker of the Chamber of Deputies Jan Bartošek (KDU) declared: "I find it strange to interpret the law in such a way that everyone who places a banner on the fence must register as a supporter." The head of the Constitutional and Legal Committee of the House of Representatives, Jeroným Tejc (ČSSD), responded: "It is not possible to interpret the law ad absurdum and ask people not to be able to express their opinion. The two geniuses approved the moronic law (and in addition to their parties ANO and Úsvit - let's point to them); that's how law-making works in our country (and unfortunately not only here): A bunch of incompetent idiots approve something, somehow imagine it in practice, but when they find out that another incompetent bureaucrat puts the law into practice differently, they sigh that it's up to them, because "the law is the law" (yes... and where does it come from).

Terror to inclusion

The state has invented that it is simply good for many disabled children to go to normal schools; however, some parents have the audacity to think they know their child better than the official, which is why they refuse to integrate them. And it is precisely these brats that the socialite will take to task; why? Well, because refusing inclusion is against the child's interest... and who judges what is the child's best interest? Yes, that's right - the state, who else. Not that I think inclusion is bad in all cases, however, it should not be decided by the government, but by children, parents and schools;
education should be voluntary
– and that comprehensively (so no one should deny anyone the opportunity to get an education, or force them to get an education; and the exact same thing should also apply to educational institutions), while the last institution that should interfere in this is a band of robbers – called the state – living off the money.
Let's prevent the indoctrination of our children
, as we can.
The new Freedom of Learning website

manifesto

Let's not expose our children to the same and try to prevent the state from indoctrinating them!
The state crushes the Czech roll

The company Rohlík.cz delivers food to people that they order via the Internet; receives and processes three to four thousand orders in Prague every day (I saw an advertisement on one of their cars that said they had already delivered over a million of them). Something like this is clearly a great initiative, because the customers get food at favorable conditions (otherwise they wouldn't order it), the employees earn the best they can within their means (if not, they work elsewhere) and the business owners also get their money's worth; as long as they don't hurt anyone, that is
clearly beneficial
completely regardless of what some politicians or officials think about the conditions under which people work there, as long as they do so voluntarily (and of course regardless of whether they pay taxes or obey other laws, as long as they do not harm anyone). Why should anyone be bothered by this? For what reason should anyone object?
However, the armed fist of the state decided to crush Rohlík.cz, because it does not like that foreigners work in their warehouses under conditions that, in the opinion of officials, contradict the laws; a lot has already been written about why the Benga behave disgustingly as always (first they arrested dozens of people, thereby paralyzing the company's activities, then they legitimized them and found out who actually broke the law and who didn't - even the innocent were therefore restricted in their freedom). However, the criticism that the state is going too hard seems insufficient to me; I see the biggest problem in the fact that such things happen at all, and people who voluntarily cooperate for the benefit of everyone, without harming anyone, are persecuted for their activities by idiots, who already parasitize on their activities, which is all defended by the fact that something is in the laws. Something like this should definitely not be an argument for using violence against someone who has done nothing to anyone and, on the contrary, is beneficial.

We bought a lift for a disabled person

Kevin Preiß is a wheelchair-bound young German libertarian; however, since his home is not barrier-free, he has been able to go out for years only if his loved ones take him there and back. The lifting platform that would solve the situation costs a quarter of a mega (that is, in crowns); and although the state presents itself as an entity that cares for the disabled, it has kicked Kevin out (well... it would have paid him the lift if it had cost half, which would have been possible, but in another house; it won't even pay him half that way). When my ex-girlfriend found out about the situation (she lives in Germany and knows a lot of libertarians there), she thought of doing a fundraiser... most of the needed amount was raised in three days, a quarter mega within a week; Kevin gets a lift, problem solved.
Although libertarians are often accused of being callous and unwilling to help others, I think the opposite is true; not only because I myself devote quite a bit of my resources to help those who need it (in my opinion), and I am far from alone among libertarians in this approach, but above all it makes sense - when you think that the weak should be taken care of by the state, you don't have that much motivation to do it personally (of course, it is individual and there are many of those motivations), while if you live in the belief that solidarity should be voluntary, you simply have a tendency to be simply voluntarily solidary (again, not without exceptions). This won't just be the case for libertarians, though; if solidarity is not enforced by the state, people will feel more responsible for the state of the world around them... when there is no possibility of calling a politician to solve problems, the tendency to solve them by oneself will increase.
Guess... golf?

We have over a hundred golf courses in the Czech Republic and more are constantly being built; however, the number of players is decreasing, which logically puts golf resorts in financial trouble. Whoever thought that the solution would be to let the unneeded go bankrupt while the popular ones prosper is probably a little old-fashioned; current politics understandably dictates: "Let's give the successful and subsidize the unsuccessful!!" That's what motivates people; and so the EU pours hundreds of millions of crowns in subsidies to these failed golf course operators. Remember that the next time you hear from someone how the balance of money that we send to the EU and that we get back is favorable for us; yes, it comes out that way in accounting, but the money collected from taxes appears on the outgoing side
under threat of violence
, while nonsense is being financed on the income side. It's like someone taking a thousand from you to buy us something you absolutely don't want, don't need, and can't sell for two thousand; will you thank him?
Gore-Tex? Prohibit!

Most of us are probably familiar with Gore-Tex; amazing (and quite expensive) clothing material, which, although waterproof, is breathable and therefore breathable - absolutely priceless for chundras (similar materials are used not only for jackets and trousers, but also for shoes). I applied some myself; and I was lucky because in my tramping days there wasn't yet a wise almighty EU to ban it. But now the situation has changed and the ban is on the table; well, finally - what else would we do? Reasons? Toxicity (so now I'm seriously worried about what years of wearing Gore-Tex will do to me) and ecology - it takes too long to decompose. Well, even if, I really wonder what it will do to ban this; we produce an incredible amount of glass and plastic that will decompose...well...maybe never, while banning Gore-Tex and similar materials, which are produced like spitting in the sea compared to the above, will save it exactly. Logical...
The state destroyed, the state subsidizes

Small grocery stores are dying; dozens to hundreds of them are closed every year in the Czech Republic. Why? Although there are undoubtedly more reasons, one of the indisputable ones is the regulations that increase operational costs intolerably - hygiene regulations, occupational safety, employee protection, inspection reports and many others, plus all the red tape that follows; you can't just open a shop and start selling, the law forbids that. Of course, the same laws apply to supermarkets, but they have entire accounting, legal and HR departments that deal with it; as a result, the exact same regulations affect small players much worse, because the difficulty of the duties associated with it is certainly not linear with respect to profit or turnover, so larger entities are favored by the state (small shops simply cannot afford to allocate even one person to take care of these things).
Current solution? The state subsidizes these small establishments; just like Ronald Reagan said: "If it moves, tax it. If it keeps moving, regulate it. And when it stops moving, subsidize it." A reasonable solution? Cancellation of regulations (
ideally also taxes
) and bureaucratic duties associated with it; small shops can then
to compete freely in the free market
and see what people actually want. And what about Miloslav Hlavsa, director of the cooperative network Konzum? "I don't like subsidies." Great so far; unfortunately, the person in question continues: "Operating food stores in small villages is not a business and should be included in the law as a public service." As an entrepreneur, he does not want subsidies; however, he misses the good old pre-revolutionary practices. What to say to that? The whole thing is so absurd that I don't even know; but if the state did not distort the market, who would the politicians actually save?

Urza in Polis: Democracy

Two weeks ago, the topic was mine
lectures in Parallel Polis
culture, art and we also touched on the protection of monuments and works of art; since the period of exams and viruses was over, over a hundred people showed up again. Considering the topic, I was very pleased to see how many of the attendees were artists who had a lively discussion with me; many of them came to my lecture for the first time, so I was busy re-explaining the basics of the Austrian school of economics, so as not to bore those who already know them as much as possible.

Unfreedom or status quo?

In my efforts to show people the benefits of a free society and the inherent evil that lies in states as such, I mainly come across propaganda and indoctrination on the subject of "the state is necessary", where this firmly rooted thesis often completely overwhelms any logical arguments, which are then swept off the table a priori; however, there is also the popular and ubiquitous "it wouldn't work" argument, which I have mentioned many times before and would now like to discuss in a little more detail.
Before I get into that, I can't help but mention one observation I've made over the years of debates about freedom: Against the general distrust of people in freedom in the real world stands a fairly significant confidence in the freedom of the Internet in the virtual world by the same people. Did you notice that? When politicians come up with regulations outside the Internet, they are often supported in activities that limit freedom of expression (and not only that); however, when it comes to Internet censorship, most people are far more sensitive. Why do you think this is so?
One explanation occurred to me - while the real world is so over-regulated that no one can even imagine it without regulations, the Internet is currently quite free and everyone can see that there is no doom and things work even without a central authority. The amount of regulation outside the Internet has exceeded all limits, so that people have been forced to integrate it into their lives, which the majority of the population can no longer imagine well enough without them; rather, it requires a huge amount of imagination and the necessity to accept the fact that the outcome cannot even be predicted well enough, because the free market is unpredictable, so the most daring ideas will be just one of many hypothetical versions of the future.
In connection with this, an urgent question arises: How much do people fundamentally reject freedom and how much change as a result of state propaganda? In an unfree world, these two things can merge - the one who is an enemy of change can appear to be an opponent of freedom, which of course also applies vice versa. What role does fear of the unknown play? Everyone can see that a free Internet does not mean the end of civilization; however, many are convinced that a stateless society would bring about the end of civilization. Do you think that if these people were able to imagine some alternatives, that would change their attitudes?

The spirit of freedom

I thank the libertarian Robert Higgs for the inspiration to write this text.
Dear readers, have you ever heard or used any of the following arguments?
1/ Look around you, there is a state in every society; Do you know of one that isn't there?
2/ The state is a thousand-year-old institution, it has existed since time immemorial; if it's so bad, why aren't stateless societies emerging?
3/ Without states, people would behave like animals, be dangerous and unable to take care of themselves; they need their rulers!
4/ Without states, economic collapse would occur; the economy stands and falls by laws.
5/ The abolition of states would cost great bloodshed; then they would still spawn again at the cost of more blood.
6/ Free people in various parts of the world are even worse off than the citizens of our state; and they should be happy for what they have.
7/ Conditions in the States may improve; rather than abolishing states, let's try to reform them.
8/ A world without states is nothing but a utopia; it can never work, which is clear to all but a few naive fools.
Let's go back in time a few hundred years and look at a few arguments against the abolition of slavery:
1/ Look around you, there is slavery in every society; Do you know of one that isn't there?
2/ Slavery is a thousand-year-old institution, it has existed since time immemorial; if it's so bad, why don't neo-slave societies emerge?
3/ Slaves would behave like animals without their masters, would be dangerous and unable to take care of themselves; they need their slavers!
4/ Without slavery there would be an economic collapse; the economy stands and falls with slavery.
5/ The abolition of slavery would cost great bloodshed; then it would still spawn again at the cost of more blood.
6/ Free people in different parts of the world are even worse off than our slaves; and they should be happy for what they have.
7/ The conditions of slaves may improve; rather than the abolition of slavery, let us try to improve their living conditions.
8/ A world without slavers is nothing but a utopia; it can never work, which is clear to all but a few naive fools.
These are real arguments of real people (A. Lincoln, G. Washington, T. Jefferson, G. Fitzhugh, T. Carlyle and many others).
How "strong" does the first eight arguments appear compared to the second? And how many more years will pass before people find them just as absurd?

What definitely wouldn't work?

The focus of most debates on anarchy tends to be a discussion of what could or could not function without state power; anarcho-capitalists try to predict (although they themselves admit that it is impossible to say with certainty) how the free market could theoretically replace individual functions of the state, while statists bring various objections as to why this would not actually be possible. However, I believe that the world (and the free market) works in a much more fascinating way than anyone could ever imagine (including anarchists who are aware of it); I would like to give two examples here.
Let's imagine that there was a law according to which a policeman would have to be present in every restaurant to make sure that someone does not run away without paying, or refuses to pay after a meal; how would statists defend such a law? Well, they'd probably argue that if it wasn't there, everyone would definitely be abusing it, doom would ensue and all the restaurants would go out of business; the guests would leave in droves without paying, after the meal they would pretend that they didn't have money, or they wouldn't take it with them on purpose - and then what would the poor waiters do about it? And now anarchists, hand on heart: How many of you would invent some complex construct, how the market would solve this "problem"? I certainly do; I would argue, for example, that restaurants could require a deposit from unknown customers, while only regulars would pay after the meal. Still... realistically, it's simply not necessary; except for exceptional excesses, it works even without any special measures.
Now suppose the Internet were not anonymous; anyone's online activity would be publicly traceable to their true identity. E-shops would definitely start using something like this to verify the identity of their customers. How would statists defend this? Here they would most likely come up with the fact that an e-shop simply cannot work on the anonymous Internet, because anyone could order goods on delivery in a foreign name, shops would be spammed with orders and would have to start demanding payment in advance; but then again everyone would start setting up fake e-shops en masse, cashing money, but never sending the goods. So it would be "clear to everyone" that no one would simply ever sell or buy anything on the anonymous Internet, because users would not be able to trust each other; and now - in the world of the non-anonymous Internet - try to refute those statists (or e-shop owners)!
I believe that many of the problems for which we are currently struggling to imagine how they might be solved without the state actually have far more straightforward and incredible solutions than we would ever imagine.

laws

According to Marks, to make the pension system "fairer", the childless should pay more social insurance than people with children; at first glance it sounds quite logical, if a little monstrous - whoever raises more taxpayers should pay less. Such reasoning would perhaps even make some sense if social insurance had at least some characteristics of insurance (apart from the name) and was not simply just (another involuntary) tax; the amount of the social "insurance" payment does not depend on the risks or the amount of performance, but on the income of the person who pays it, which lacks any meaning from the point of view of any theoretical "justice" (especially because people with higher incomes statistically less often need the "performance" of that "insurance" from the state).
If we completely ignore the moral side of the matter, i.e. that the whole social insurance is legalized robbery, and we will assume that it is a legitimate system (which is not true by any chance, but let's assume it), then it is true that people with children "produce" additional payers, thus they actually "deserve" benefits, but according to this logic, when we are not dealing with needs, but merits, it makes exactly the same sense to benefit people with very above-average incomes, because they themselves (not perhaps once their children) contribute far more money to the system than most; to ensure "fairness" in such an inherently unfair system by disadvantaging the childless is about like ensuring "fairness" to bullied schoolchildren by padding classroom walls. Theory and practice

Anarcho-capitalism is often the target of statist ridicule, according to which it is only a theory that cannot be put into practice; if you start talking in front of them about private courts or something similar to the police, they usually react by pointing out the fact that nowhere is the law handled completely privately, because the state can do it better and it "wouldn't work" at all.
The typical answers of anarcho-capitalists then mostly consist of a theoretical (and mostly absolutely correct) explanation of why and how it could work; however, any such speculations are often dismissed by simply pointing out that nothing of the sort is currently being implemented anywhere, resulting in a debate in which the libertarian defends something and the statist scoffs at it, automatically putting himself in a much more advantageous position.
As things really stand, I find this mode of debate quite absurd; why?
Well, in recent history we got a look at what a centrally controlled economy looks like - and it was appalling. We were also able to see in various states that any economic segment that any state allowed itself to leave to the market began to function better than before; on the contrary, it has probably never happened that the state stopped managing something, which would lead to the fulfillment of all those catastrophic statist predictions about market failure.
Imagine knowing two fundamentally different ways of solving problems; you first try to solve everything with one and it's not very good, then you start to solve individual things with the other and you always get better. Will you then try to maintain the status quo at all costs, or will you try for (further) improvement?
There are essentially two ways to control the course of things: Either let free people act, or have their lives centrally planned by force from the position of the state. So far, central planning has always failed; and each time it was replaced by free market principles, there were positive changes.
So what actually works and what fails? Who should question and who should defend? On whom should the burden of proof lie? So what is theory and what is practice?
The reality is that there are a huge number of industries where the state has failed across the board while the private sector has succeeded; on the contrary, there is probably no industry that thrives in private hands and only begins to flourish thanks to the state.
So based on what empirical experience can anyone claim about something that we need the state to do it because the free market "wouldn't work"?
In a rational discussion uninfluenced by state propaganda, the statist should, on the contrary, explain to the anarchist why this or that sector should be the rare exception that requires a central plan for its functioning.

Another logical flaw in this argument should be seen better than anyone else by libertarians; it is indeed possible (and I also assume it) that in a free society people would currently cope with the situation surrounding the immigration crisis by natural free market discrimination (whether at work, in the provision of services, or in closed communities, the possible form of which can be found in the works of Hans-Hermann Hoppe), but we cannot know for sure, because

Murray Newton Rothbard; requiescat in pace

Today it is exactly twenty-one years since one of the greatest thinkers, economists, philosophers and geniuses of the twentieth century and, in my opinion, of all time left this world at the age of 69 - Murray Newton Rothbard, the "father of anarcho-capitalism"; the importance of his work lies in the incredibly consistent unification of two seemingly unrelated trends: the Austrian school of economics and anarchism. His teacher, the outstanding economist Ludwig von Mises, proved the impossibility of economic calculation in central planning, thus proving beyond doubt the superiority of the free market economy over the socialist one, he still assumed that the free market would be ensured by the state; on the other hand, various anarchists pointed to the ethical indefensibleness of the state as a monopoly on violence, but their solution was typically various communist utopias lacking economic foundations.
In his life's work, Murray Newton Rothbard consistently combined these two directions into a consistent anarcho-capitalism, because he understood that the obstacle to anarchy and the free market is the state, while the absence of a monopoly on violence means anarchy and a free market, which he expressed as follows: "Capitalism is the fullest expression of anarchism, and anarchism is the fullest expression of capitalism. Not only are they compatible, but you can't really have one without the other. True anarchism will be capitalism, and true capitalism will be anarchism." He was a man of sharp analytical mind with an absolute sense of logic, but at the same time very emotional; an implacable hatred of evil, whose greatest contemporary embodiment is the state, permeated his entire work. He died when I was not yet ten years old; however, later on, what he created greatly influenced my life and opened my eyes. Thank you, Mr. Rothbard.

In case of a conflict between the settings, the user "wins" (» change account data «), however there is an option (the very first one) that can reverse it (ie the user's appearance will correspond to what he chose in the menu » appearance «); you can use this to turn off Stok sounds at work (the black-and-white appearance without images is also without sounds), which some readers have asked me to do. comment
, which in turn several people wrote to me that I should insert it as a standard "article"; since in my opinion it is long enough for Stoky, here (a little more generally) I describe its point - how we lose our freedom.
Phase One:
We have some freedom (speech, movement, business, arms, ...); people are not willing to give it up (yet) and anyone who would try to limit this freedom because of some bureaucratic bullshit will be sent somewhere, he will start losing voters and all his colleagues will give up on him. If, by chance, someone just passes a law that cancels this freedom, everyone who promises to repeal this legislation will do better in the next election.
Phase Two:
Prohibitionists present a strong emotional reason to limit this freedom (terrorist attack, mass-raped children, radioactivity, biological weapons, and so on, just about anything that evokes strong feelings, even though it may be only marginally related to the freedom in question); if it is a major intervention in our lives, he promises that it is a temporary change. I assume that we are all familiar with such arguments on the topic that during war one is allowed or does this and that (giving war as an example of moral heights is also laughable). The hysteria will completely overshadow any reasonable debate on the subject, so the ban will pass.
Phase Three:
As soon as people have become accustomed to the fact that the given freedom is already somewhat restricted, the social engineers will come up with a proposal to reduce the number of murders, rapes, robberies, and the like, if this freedom is suppressed a little more; these efforts sometimes fail, but after a while they still succeed (note that once a regulation is in place, it is virtually never repealed). When that happens, that freedom will begin to be restricted without the interest of the public, even because of every fool and bureaucratic whim; although it was a no-brainer at first, it leaves practically everyone (except a few crazy libertarians) cold at this point.
Phase Four:
Processes (within the public and private sectors), services, goods and norms arise, which are based on the fact that the given freedom is somehow limited; these are then used as arguments why that freedom must remain suppressed. Even if the original reason disappears, or turns out to be pointless from the very beginning, it really doesn't matter anymore. No one is interested in this freedom anymore, moreover, "it is clear to everyone" that it must be limited, because otherwise "it wouldn't work" (because of all the processes that count on that limitation).

State like a house

In connection with the issue of migration, we often hear the comparison that a state is like a house; just as the owner decides who to let home and who not, the state should supposedly decide who to let across the border and who stays outside. Although such a comparison may seem logical at first glance, it is actually one of the most false analogies I have ever come across; what I find very unique about it is that the compared statement denies the one to which it is compared.
As? Well, if the state decides who is allowed to cross the border, it also prevents me from inviting home whoever I see fit (because in some cases it leaves him completely out of the state). Isn't that paradoxical? The analogy is based on the fact that it is good to be able to decide for myself who I let into the house, but this principle that she uses as a model would be canceled by the principle that she is trying to enforce; it's hard for me to let whoever I want into the house when the person in question doesn't even have to cross the border.
Another problem with this analogy is that while a house typically has an owner who legally makes decisions, the state does not. A far more accurate analogy would be with the apartment building in which I own an apartment: Can the neighbors, by majority vote, ban me from inviting a visitor they don't like? Um... suddenly it's not so clear anymore, huh? Not that they couldn't make such an agreement in advance, but if it doesn't apply at the moment when I bought an apartment in that building, it suddenly becomes a rather tricky matter, and I quite doubt that anyone would still use the analogy like that (although it is more accurate in every way).
But the city resembles the state even more than the house; and here we are already on downright thin ice, because it is quite unheard of for the citizens of the city to vote on who can come there for work, for example. Do not take this text as a defense of any European Union quotas for refugees, because it would be even more absurd than my neighbors forbidding me who can visit me, if they ordered me who I must accept into my home; I'm just pointing out that the analogy of state borders with land borders makes practically no sense, and even contradicts itself.

Imagine how absurd it would be if someone asked people for money to buy "alcohol goggles" and put them on journalists and let them drive between cones... but why ask when there's another way, huh?
And finally, just on a side note, I'm wondering if it's illegal to drive with "alcohol glasses". Does the applicable legislation forbid me to wear glasses behind the wheel that significantly distort my vision? Of course, in case I crash because of it, it's clear; but as long as I drive without an accident, can a monkey in uniform slap me with a fine? If not, why not? If it really is as equivalent to drunkenness as the buffoons claim, why is one forbidden and the other allowed? Does it even make sense? I am afraid that it is again some purely arbitrary decision of politicians with a patent on what is best for us.

Political correctness as a cow

The Chicago Blackhawks hockey club and the Washington Redskins American football club have a common problem; what? Well, they have a picture of an Indian in their emblem, which, for example (and far from only) is racist according to Obama and shows disrespect for the original inhabitants of North America; so I don't know, I don't have the schools for this, nor the "correct" political mindset, but how can disrespect for someone be expressed by someone putting it in a club emblem or naming their sports team after it? I have no connection to American football, but if someone founded, for example, "Washington Anarchists" and put a yellow-black anarcho-capitalist flag in their emblem, I would think of many things, but hardly anything related to disrespect...
However, the American Indians are said to see it differently, they are said to be offended by it; I believe that someone like that can be found, but is it really such a topic among them? We probably won't find out through the media mask of political correctness. But even if it offends everyone, what right do they have to ban the owners from naming the club as they see fit? Limiting someone's freedom on the basis that their speech "offends" someone is a road to hell, because anything can offend anyone, so applying this principle we would probably end up having to seriously ban everything; not to mention the fact that assessing what offends whom and how much is not realistically possible in practice.
Daniel Snyder, the owner of the Washington Redskins club, first sent the politically correct activists to the appropriate places, now he has to defend himself against them in court; however, I find the arguments of his lawyers a bit hot and maybe a bit dangerous - they argue that the Washington Redskins should not be renamed because there are even more racist or offensive trademarks, for example Baked By a Negro Cookie Company (cookies from a Negro), or Dirty Whooore Clothing Company (clothing for dirty girls; I really like this, because I like light girls - even those that at least they dress) - I'm a little afraid that it won't end up with a ban not only on redheads, but also on all whores and blacks...
Political correctness is spreading everywhere like a plague, some time ago it was found officially offensive (and therefore prohibited) to display the confederate flag, so nothing stands in the way of banning Native American motifs in the logos or names of sports clubs; basically, the comrades in the USA have reached a point (and not that we are any significantly different) in which bans on activities that offend someone are considered correct, so freedom itself is not so much discussed anymore (they wrote it off a long time ago; and it was such a land of freedom), but the debate is only about what and how much offends how many people.
Freedom of speech in Britain

BBC presenter Ursula Presgrave is unlikely to be a fragile soul who loves sick children; on her Facebook profile she posted a controversial (and in my opinion quite demented) opinion about the uselessness of some of them: "Anyone born with Down syndrome should be euthanized. It's just cruel to let them lead a useless vegetable life." People reacted quite logically to this with many comments to the effect that she was just trying to get attention and that she was disgusting; I quite agree with the second conclusion, in the case of the first I have my doubts, as the person in question has more than enough attention as a BBC star.
Domenica Lawson, Princess Diana's goddaughter with Down syndrome, feels offended by this statement because she says she lives like normal people (which I also have some doubts about; on the other hand, it's purely her business); and many other famous people experience it too, I'm not famous personally, so I'd just conclude that Ursula Presgrave is probably a cow. It is understandable that it will most likely cost her her job, but what is much worse is that someone sued her, the court recognized her guilt, and the person in question will go sulking for six months; and that's much closer than the whole famous statement about children with down syndrome, because it was just talk.
Before the court, of course, the person in question was indirectly forced to pour ashes on her head, apologize, take back her statement, bitterly regret it, and the like; I don't believe in the sincerity of such behavior, but I don't condemn it in any way, because nothing like this would most likely not have happened at all if the person in question had not tried to accept a lesser punishment. But how can anyone believe in freedom of speech in a society where people are sent to prison just for expressing stupid and callous opinions in public? Of course, freedom of speech is not just about letting people express reasonable and emotionally mature opinions; for real freedom is when everyone is allowed to show himself as an insensitive fool without being penalized for it.
Fortunately, we are not that far in the Czech Republic, although our comrades
trying their best to get closer to the British ones
; where will it all end? We will see the creation of a Ministry of Truth, which will approve which views are the "correct" and permissible, and no one will be allowed to publicly hold otherwise; eventually maybe not even privately. However, I am sure that even if something like this happens, we will still live in a declarative free speech society; and just like today, even in that case we will of course have that freedom, but it will be clear to everyone that it cannot be unlimited - exactly as the state propaganda is currently serving it to us.
Massacre in Paris

Last night there were several coordinated massacres in Paris where a handful of terrorists opened fire on crowds of people; the number of dead is tentatively estimated to be in the tens (allegedly there are more than a hundred victims). Although there were also bomb attacks, according to the available information, it seems that the vast majority of those murdered were shot (that is, they did not die in the explosion). The terrorists attacked several places at the same time (a full concert hall, a football stadium, a restaurant, generally places where people go for entertainment); by the shouts of "Allahu Akbar" it can be judged that these were Islamic radicals.
The reactions of politicians and the public are quite predictable - the French government has declared a state of emergency, closed the borders (both ways) and is preparing "further steps"; the public (mainly the Czech one) defines itself against Islam, for Konvička and Hample it will be a real feast, I assume that they are both happy without each other. From the opposite camp, the following thought came to me in particular (paraphrasing freely): "There are 6M Muslims living in France; if a tenth of them were radical jihadists, we would have 600k attackers; if only one percent of them were radicals, 60k people would attack; and even if it was only a tenth of a percent, it would mean 6k attackers."
The problem is that even those few terrorists were enough; and no matter how many measures we impose at the borders or anywhere else, we will never be able to eliminate them all. The only way to defend yourself is to increase the ratio of terrorists needed to murder a person; Yesterday, a group of goons attacked and killed dozens of people. Why? Because they had nothing to fire back. If nine out of ten people had one arm long, I expect the casualty-to-terrorist ratio would drop pretty damn low; quite possibly by order of magnitude - after all, the attacks took place in a place where the police were more or less around, under "more favorable" conditions, Breivik achieved an appalling ratio of 77:1 (these terrorists are around 10:1; and I am convinced that in an armed society they would not get past 2:1 in the long term).
Now around us we will hear calls for the banning of Islam and other totalitarian measures, which in the long run prove to be not very effective (often completely counterproductive); the only meaningful solution is an armed and free society, in which everyone can bring anyone they see fit to their land, but no one will be obliged to take care of them, give them anything, employ them, serve them in their business, etc., weapons will be freely available without state permission and ammunition will be freely available. Even in such a society, of course, there are goons who will go shoot people at a concert, but they simply don't kill that many.
Attacker with knife at school

In Merced, California, another tragedy occurred at a school marked with a gun free zone sign; one of the students ran there in the morning with a knife (ergo he even respected the ban on firearms), stabbed five people, after which the police arrived and shot him dead. I have no reservations about the work of the police here, shooting the attacker is of course perfectly fine; but the question is, of course, why did he manage to attack five people? Benga had to get there first, obviously they can't be everywhere (and that's actually a good thing, as they usually do more harm than good; this example was an exception).
But what if the school was not a gun free zone? What if students or teachers could be armed at school? How many people would the attacker manage to stab? He only had a knife! One can certainly imagine that the first victim will be stabbed so suddenly that no one has time to react; before anyone recovers, perhaps the predator will attack someone else, maybe a third person at the most, if he chooses a great position to attack and everyone will be shocked. However, if almost everyone had a thunder stick at their waist, I can't imagine how a student could stab five people at school; quite possibly they would have stopped him before or after the first victim.
Uniformed monkeys with the best training simply must naturally react an order of magnitude (!) slower than armed humans on the spot; even most superheroes, if they existed, wouldn't be able to intervene in time! The attacker typically does not respect the gun free zone, but even if he accidentally does (perhaps this one was exemplary and only took a knife), the consequences are dire. The only real effect of a gun free zone is to disarm potential victims; it is something like a henhouse secured in such a way that, although no hen could escape, every marten had convenient access inside.
So why do gun free zones even exist? I'm afraid that the only reason is some kind of reality-detached dreams of prohibitionists, who imagine the functioning of the world in such a way that whatever the state prohibits, everyone will automatically respect it; these people absolutely do not realize that if someone wants to commit such a heinous crime as murder undoubtedly is, it will be difficult to stop him if he has to break some insignificant regulation in the process. To not see or ignore this trivial principle really requires an extreme level of blindness from state propaganda, according to which every problem can be solved by restricting freedom.
Referendum on leaving the EU

"If elections could change anything, they would have been banned a long time ago," is a sign spray-painted on a building I pass about once a week. It is quite possible that Czech politicians also go there, because the government rejected the proposal of the Úsvit MPs (not that they were any better, but this time they happened to be right) to organize a referendum on leaving the EU; membership in the EU is said to be one of the Czech Republic's basic starting points in foreign policy, and withdrawal would be in sharp conflict with the interests of the state. Not that I don't consider democracy to be
crap
,
idolatry
a
factory for incompetence
, however, it's funny how even this can be suppressed when it suits the powers that be (which only confirms my words in the linked articles).
The Government Office has issued a statement for its ministers, in which it also points out that it is not entirely wise to hold a referendum on leaving the EU at a time of migration crisis; Well, sure, it's not entirely wise if we're interested in a specific result, but otherwise it's exactly the opposite - considering leaving the European Union makes the most sense precisely when a reason appears; waiting to make a decision until this has passed can be described as pure dementia (or in this case, calculation).
Polls show that if a referendum were held today, citizens would vote to leave the EU; and although it is not advisable to trust statistics that you do not falsify yourself, these seem quite credible to me, because the government itself is so afraid of such a referendum that it quite openly denies its subjects to express their opinion on this matter. Something similar could be expected, but I wouldn't see it so bleakly, because Eurosceptics are more or less on the right track; after all, as Gandhi said, "First they will ignore you; then they will laugh at you; then they will fight you; and in the end you will win."
In my opinion, our membership in the EU (and most likely the EU itself) is reaching its inevitable end; the question is how much longer it will last and how it will end - it would be good to get all four. If the dictates of the EU were to be replaced by a totalitarian government of monsters like Petr Hampl or Martin Konvička, we would not help ourselves much (rather the opposite); on the other hand, if we finally get it to a referendum (although not under the current government, but there will be others) initiated by someone who is not so extremely dangerous at the same time (which could easily be the fools from Úsvit, but also perhaps Svobodní), we can celebrate a partial victory.
Home freedom: intervention, sunk!

Another state attack on our freedoms this time comes from a rather unexpected place; the Ministry of the Environment is coming up with a law that allows municipal authorities to inspect households that are drowning in all kinds of unapproved garbage. Inspectors (I ask myself, what kind of "people" can do this job; shame on them) will gain the right to enter private homes, poke around in other people's stoves, take samples of other people's ashes, which will then be analyzed in a laboratory; whoever refuses to let these pigs cross the threshold will be fined up to fifty thousand kroner (and the law does not say anything about the fact that the same control cannot follow with the same penalty).
Of course, the government promises that the checks will not be "bullying" (interestingly, probably no politician in history has ever introduced a law declaring that it would be "bullying"; but hey, somehow we've managed to look around and see one legal shenanigan next to another); of course, everyone is concerned only with our health, the health of our children, the health of our children's children and the health of their children's children. The social democrat Jiří Dienstbier assures us that controls will of course be the last resort after all other attempts at correction have failed; I can see it completely, because it is completely out of the question that it could hypothetically work like, for example, cashiering in the traffic police.
The Minister of the Environment, a member of the party of fools led by the big fool Babiš, Richard Brabec, honors his name and the party with the following statement (I quote): "Our opinion has been confirmed that the inviolability of housing is not unlimited." That's an opinion, sir! If I made a living by robbing houses, I would stop at the Brab family's house at night, whitewash them from the basement to the attic, and leave a message: "Dear Minister, I hereby confirm your opinion that the inviolability of the home is not unlimited." I completely understand that morons like Mr. Brabec hold these views, but I consider the state of society in which the person in question still boasts of such reprehensible views to be very sad.
"And what is the market solution?" As usual, I first emphasize that the free market cannot be predicted; however, if I had to guess, I expect that if someone was bothered by it, they would simply wait for the wind to blow the smoke from the neighbor's property over theirs, capture it, and analyze the smoke (repeated measurements from different locations would hopefully prove contamination). It is also worth noting that if the state did not waste resources, society would be richer and fewer people would have the motivation to burn with harmful materials. And finally, the most important thing - if in a free society someone broke into another's house and it was found that it was wrong, the attacker should compensate the victim; not that something similar couldn't apply even now (if the law isn't "bullying" after all, so what's the point, they certainly won't break into anyone's house), but of course Mr. Brabec doesn't want that, because it smells like the state should be responsible for its actions.
Even more social engineering!

The Ministry of the Interior came up with another brilliant law, according to which everyone should have a permanent residence where they actually live; and whoever is caught not having it there will pay a fine of up to fifteen thousand crowns. The official justification for this fiddling for fiddling is the efficiency of public services provided and crisis planning in the event of natural disasters such as floods. According to the drafters of the law, three hundred thousand people live in the Czech Republic whose real residence does not correspond to their permanent residence; the interesting thing is, if they already know it anyway, why bother with such bureaucratic nonsense?
The proxies for the introduction of this law are truly absurd. Improving the quality of public services? Phew! Which of the private companies making money in a market way has access to such information as the state? And what would happen if any of them provided services as bad as the public ones? Well, she simply wouldn't make a living and was forced to quit. The reality is that
without the possibility of economic calculation
public services will always cost a fart no matter how much information the state coerces from its subjects; on the contrary
the free market can provide them better
even without unnecessary fuss.
And crisis planning? Well, years ago I was among the volunteers who helped firefighters evacuate people trapped in houses on the banks of the flooded Radbuza; and I can say that the very last thing anyone was interested in at that time was some unreliable information from unnecessary officials. And if it is a matter of more mass planning (capacity of various shelters and the like), then it must be taken into account that three hundred thousand people are three percent of the population; and are any reserves really planned so closely? After all, even just a normal commute to work will make many times greater differences between where people actually are and where they have permanent residence (for example, the Central Bohemian region becomes substantially depopulated during the day when people go to work in Prague, where there are therefore more of them to return at night).
In reality, this is nothing more than social engineering and other state-buzzing of citizens; the real reason will then sound something like this: "Ordnung muss sein."
In any case, I wonder how the state wants to enforce and control compliance with this law; will officials or uniformed monkeys go from house to house at night and find out if those who are reported to the office are present? Or will some more advanced tampering tools be deployed? In any case, we have a lot to look forward to...
Fluctuate the amount of social insurance

The Ministry of Labor came up with a brilliant proposal for social insurance; the more children, the lower the amount one has to pay. The "logic" behind it is said to be that those who raise taxpayers should get a discount, because they also pay a decent amount to the state for insurance over the course of their lives; well... or not, because I can imagine all kinds of socially excluded families, who, among other things, acquire them as an additional "source of income", but not in the sense that they would take care of them in adulthood, but also because of the money that the state will give them for it, regardless of any tax breaks, or there are also people who simply have it on the hook, they don't use contraception much and whatever the devil wants, sometimes something is born.
There is, of course, a public debate about the issue, and it is similarly fruitless, as debates on similar topics typically tend to be in our democratic society; in particular, how many children a person has, how much they will or will not pay taxes, how much money they will pay to the state in total with their children, and the like. Some feel unfairly disadvantaged when the state is taxed for their decision not to have children, while others are themselves harmed because their descendants should pay for their pensions not only for them, but also for other people who have allowed themselves to have no children; the positions of both parties are understandable in a way, but they completely ignore the essence of the problem.
So what is the problem? Well, primarily in the fact that there is any social "insurance" at all; what if the state simply did not interfere and
he left everyone to take care of his own pension
in a way of your own choosing? Someone can save (whether for a mattress, or trust some institution... and of course bear risks that can be reduced, for example, by diversifying investments), someone else will raise productive children who will take care of him in his old age (of course, there are some risks here too, but that's life), someone else will start a prosperous company (the risk here is of course huge), or there will certainly be people who somehow combine the above methods.
That people will then lose their certainties? Yes and no. No one is ever completely certain (everyone can be hit by a car), but anyone who really cares can reduce the level of risk so that it is close to zero; of course it's not free, but it's certainly not even if it's provided by the state (which is probably even more expensive). The problem is that today the state orders everyone to buy (incredibly overpriced) "certainties", so those who want to invest their money differently (and take risks) are simply out of luck. Not to mention all the other disadvantages of the unfairness of this system, which are shown, for example, in discussions about this law - in fact, there is no way to set a "fair" amount of that "insurance" (especially as long as its amount depends proportionally on the income of the person concerned).
Compulsory kindergarten

I consider the indoctrination of children, who are obliged to go to school, where the state propaganda of democracy and the establishment is hammered into their heads from an early age, to be one of the biggest pieces of crap by the state; but compulsory school attendance as we know it now is clearly not enough for the government - it came up with an amendment to the Education Act, according to which parents will be forced to send their preschool children to kindergarten for at least one more year. The coalition MPs gave the green light to the proposal, now the question is how the situation will develop further; but I'm afraid that this is another one of those laws that, even if they don't pass once or twice, they will eventually be pushed through, and then no one will ever repeal it.
However, it is interesting how the opposition argues against this law; it is said that it is not good for the state to constantly interfere in everything and change the rules of the game, they are unnecessary bureaucratic measures, it is not necessary to order something like that, education belongs to the family, not to the kindergarten, the parents are responsible for the healthy development of the child. Well then, I laugh at that, gentlemen of the opposition; Your words should be set in stone. The question, however, is whether these are truly seriously expressed opinions of those concerned, or whether it is simply that they do not like those who propose the law, so they would take any random argument that they could throw at them as a thank you.
If the opposition politicians really thought that the parents are responsible for the healthy development of the child, that their education belongs to the family and that the state should not constantly interfere in everything, then the question is why we actually have standard compulsory schooling, because their arguments are of course completely applicable against it; I wish they were taken seriously and not just as fluff for politicking. In fact, we have come so far that reasonable ideas seem so absurd to the powerful that when they say them themselves, they don't even think that there might be some truth in them...
An interesting question, by the way, is how much compulsory schooling will expand in the future; of course, it would be best to cancel it completely, but we probably won't see that. On the contrary, it will rather be extended, I just thought until now that the procedure would consist of artificially increasing the number of high school graduates and university students (which is already happening), until their numbers increase in this way to such an extent that the given type of education can be declared compulsory and almost no one will be against it, because such a regulation will in practice change the lives of only a small number of people; but the ways of the state are unfathomable, now they try it from the youngest.
How the hell he shot people

Before Christmas 2014, a drunk policeman Pavel Koblížek burst into a disco, where he started waving his city card and demanding free entry for himself and two friends; such an incident beautifully shows how the uniformed monkeys perceive themselves - as superhumans, whom others have to accommodate and entertain them for free, because they are sycophants of the state. However, the gorillas in the club did not give a shit about the fizzle, they took it out in their teeth and bequeathed it to the appropriate limits; however, the person in question did not like it, because the subjects dare to oppose the henchmen of the powerful, so the police aggressive brute entered there again and sprayed it with tear gas.
This understandably pissed off the club's security and they decided to put the scumbag in the booth; so they began to chase him, which culminated in the person in question starting to shoot at them, killing one of them, wounding another, and the third preferred to run away. And this is where the accounts begin to diverge, because while the security claims that the victim simply turned around and started shooting, Fizl maintains that he only fired after the physical attack took place - he is said to have been knocked to the ground, kneed and strangled by the gorillas, as a result of which he feared for his life, so he fired in danger of his life. Well, the fact that the statements diverge is not so surprising.
Fízl, however, got away with the witness; he first testified that the security guard from the disco caught up with Koblížek and beat him up, but when asked directly if he saw it, he answered: "I think so, after all, when they chase someone, they jump on them, don't they?" Convincing, huh? Anyway, what I find far more interesting than the witness statement is the fact that there was no fizzle DNA on the gorillas' hands and no DNA from any of the victims was found on the body of the killer; how is that possible when he allegedly knelt on him and strangled him? Another remarkable fact is that, although the city policeman shot with his right hand someone who was allegedly kneeling on him and strangling him, he hit the person in question from the other side (that is, in the victim's right side, which would correspond to the shooter's left hand).
Here I would be very interested in the motivation of the witness to testify as he did; does he really think he saw what he said he saw? And what about the strange wording about the fact that when someone chases someone, they also jump on them? I understand that it was dark, there was confusion, it was difficult to find your way around, the statements logically diverge. Or was there any influence at the gym in favor of a colleague? Hard to say. However, DNA is DNA and it is difficult to shoot someone in the hip with one hand. Even if that wasn't the case, what about the aspect of a drunken punk who walks into a disco and demands free entry on the basis of some punk card?
Schoolboys - immigrant henchmen; or the state?

As expected, Islamophobic people (of course also here in the Czech Republic) can go crazy because of this, they call the whole incident outrageous, and on social networks you can read threats of violence to the principals of their children's schools, if something similar occurs to them; I personally agree with the Islam killers here, the whole situation is completely intolerable and I consider it outrageous that children are modern-day slaves and servants of someone depending on what their teachers (or ministerial officials) feel like doing. It's perfectly fine to be concerned about solar propaganda, but it's not fine to simply replace it with another one; the only correct solution is not to prescribe to the schools what they should teach and let the parents choose the educational facilities that suit their child.
In principle, there is no difference at all between an institution that compulsorily educates children to love refugees and an institution that compulsorily educates children to love democracy; it's just a matter of what one agrees with and what one's opinion is, however immigrant-hating parents should have exactly the same options as democracy-hating parents (not having their children indoctrinated against their beliefs). Let every parent teach his child what he sees fit; the state should not have the slightest right to interfere in any way and decide what is right and what is wrong for the child.
Hell is going through the city!

Prague: The police were filling their own pockets with fines!
Random checks by the police officers in Prague revealed fraudsters who were already falsifying block fines by giving the fined person a block for a litre, they also took it from him, but they made it look like the fine was only for a kilo at the forgery. Beroun: Sixteen out of eighteen police officers accused of abusing the powers of an official!

Don't you happen to know about something?
At the eaten shop

Do you also, dear readers, miss the queues for bananas and are downright bored of the damn bourgeois market, where you can buy goods practically at any time, even on holidays? If so, I bring great news: Our noble deputies will save us, because no stranger's blood flows! MPs from the KDU-ČSL informed us that they welcome this proposal as a contribution to a better combination of work and family life. What about the fact that people do not buy, what about the fact that workers who already want to work will not earn, and those who have no family will sit at home on holidays instead of working for extra pay. But why should MPs be interested in what problems they caused to whom with their demented laws? They bear no responsibility, they can do whatever they want, approve any bullshit, no one will ever force them to answer, after all we elected them in democratic elections, so what?
Although some people (probably in vain) protest against this, virtually all arguments on the subject are utilitarian; almost no one will stop to note that the primary and fundamental immorality of this law is not who ever buys, but the threat of violence by the state against anyone who does not submit to this disgusting will.
